about: Made by design/passes-near/to_site.py from design/passes-near/passes-near.json: every stretch between neighbouring stations with any of it in England ([a, b, metres]) and one item per stretch. The network is from OpenStreetMap (see passes-near-LICENCE.md).

AAP-BOP.text: Your train passes near Bounds Green tube station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1932 on the Piccadilly line's extension to Cockfosters. Its eight-sided entrance was designed by C. H. James in the style of Charles Holden, a well-preserved example of London Transport's modern look of the 1930s.

AAP-HRN.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Tower, on the train's {side}, all that is left of Hornsey's medieval parish church and the oldest building in Hornsey. Its date isn't known; the antiquarian Daniel Lysons seems to have been the first to put it at about 1500.

AAP-NSG.text: Your train passes near Bluebell Wood, on the train's {side}, just over an acre of oak wood that is the last fragment of Tottenham Wood, which covered about 388 acres in 1619. Despite its name, no native bluebells grow there.

ABW-BVD.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Lesnes Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1178 for a small group of canons regular, on rising ground above what was once marshland. The ruins are a scheduled monument, and part of the woods beside them is a geological Site of Special Scientific Interest, important for fossils.

ABW-PLU.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church, Plumstead, on the train's {side}, on a site with a church since about the 10th century. Its oldest part, now the south aisle, is 12th and 13th century, and its tower dates from 1664; it was badly damaged by flying bombs in 1944 and 1945.

ABW-WWC.text: Your train passes near the Royal Arsenal's Grand Store, on the train's {side}, a great three-sided range of riverside warehouses built in 1805 to 1813 to James Wyatt's design. Wooden piles were used instead of the stone foundations he specified, and the buildings suffered from subsidence for many years.

ACC-SAT.text: Your train passes near where Eden Studios stood, on the train's {side}, a recording studio in Beaumont Road, Chiswick, from 1972 until it closed in 2007. Elvis Costello, Madness, the Smiths and Kylie Minogue are among those who recorded there; the site was then cleared for housing.

ACC-WIJ.text: Your train passes near the former works of Park Ward, on the train's {side}, a coachbuilder founded in 1919 that made car bodies for Bentley and Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce bought it in 1939, and in 1961 it merged with H. J. Mulliner to become Mulliner Park Ward.

ACT-BAG.text: Your train passes along Bagshot Park, on the train's {side}, a royal home whose house was built in 1879 for Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught. An earlier lodge here was rebuilt for Charles I by Inigo Jones.

ACT-MAO.text: Your train passes near Englemere House, on the train's {side}, an Italianate house of about 1815 that was the home of Field Marshal Lord Roberts from 1903 until his death in 1914.

ACT-SNG.text: Your train passes near Charters, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco house built in 1938 for the industrialist Frank Parkinson. His guests included Winston Churchill and the Duke and Duchess of Windsor.

ADM-AYH.text: Your train passes near Aylesham, on the train's {side}, a village begun in 1926 for miners at the newly sunk Snowdown Colliery. Its planner, Sir Patrick Abercrombie, meant it to grow into a town of up to 30,000 people.

ADM-BKS.text: Your train passes the site of Bekesbourne Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, which had the railway along its northern edge. It began in 1916 as a landing ground for the Royal Flying Corps, and from December 1918 its squadron was commanded by Arthur Harris, later Marshal of the Royal Air Force.

ADV-GRT.text: Your train passes near Marlborough Lines, on the train's {side}, home of Army Headquarters, the staff who support the head of the British Army.

ADV-WCH.text: Your train passes near Andover Museum and Museum of the Iron Age, on the train's {side}, in a Georgian town house of the 1750s, with finds from the nearby Danebury hill fort.

AFK-CHG.text: Your train passes near the Archbishop's Palace at Charing, on the train's {side}, one of the earliest properties of the archbishops of Canterbury. In 1520 Henry VIII stayed here with an entourage of more than 5,000 on his way to the Field of the Cloth of Gold.

AFK-EBD.text: Your train crosses the River Medway on the viaduct of the high-speed line to the Channel Tunnel, finished in 2002 beside the two bridges of the M2. In 2003 a specially formed Eurostar crossed it at 208 mph, a new speed record for Britain's railways.

AFK-FNR.text: Your train passes near the White Horse Stone, on the train's {side}, a sarsen stone on Blue Bell Hill. Excavators found a Neolithic longhouse just south of it, 18 metres long, in use some time between about 4100 and 3500 BC.

AFK-HMT.text: Your train passes Newtown, on the train's {side}, built by the South Eastern Railway from 1847 for the workers at its Ashford works. It was first called Alfred Town, and was laid out round a green.

AFK-PLC.text: Your train runs beside Godinton Park, on the train's {side}. Its Jacobean house was home to the Toke family for about 455 years, and its garden has one of the longest yew hedges in England.

AFK-WHA.text: Your train passes Westenhanger Castle, on the train's {side}, a fortified manor house of the 14th century. In 1588 Elizabeth I used it as the headquarters for Kent's 14,000 troops against the Spanish Armada.

AFK-WYE.text: Your train passes near Wye College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1447 by Cardinal John Kempe as a chantry college that taught local children. It later became an agricultural college of the University of London, and closed in 2009.

AFS-FEL.text: Your train passes near Bedfont Lakes Country Park, on the train's {side}, 72.5 hectares of lakes, meadows and woodland. Gravel was dug here from the 1860s and it was a landfill site until 1973; it became a nature reserve in 2000, and is home to 156 species of bird.

AFS-SNS.text: Your train passes HM Prison Bronzefield, on the train's {side}, the largest women's prison in Europe. The site was first a residential school for orphans from London, opened in 1872.

AGT-HOV.text: Your train passes the site of the Goldstone Ground, on the train's {side}, home of Brighton & Hove Albion from 1902 to 1997. It hosted football at the 1948 Olympic Games, and David Beckham made his professional debut here in 1992.

AGT-PLD.text: Your train passes near the Goldstone Pumping Station in Hove, on the train's {side}, a set of High Victorian Gothic buildings begun in 1866. It pumped water for Hove and Brighton for more than a century, and later became the British Engineerium, a museum of engineering and steam power.

AHD-EPS.text: Your train passes through Epsom, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. In the late 17th century a spring on Epsom Common was thought to heal, and its water was rich in what became known as Epsom salts.

AHD-LHD.text: Your train passes near Ashtead Common, on the train's {side}, a wood with more than 2,300 pollarded oaks, many of them 300 to 400 years old. It belongs to the City of London, and much of it is a National Nature Reserve.

AHS-CWN.text: Your train passes Cowden Meadow, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest whose grassland has not been cultivated for many years, so it keeps flowers such as quaking grass, oxeye daisy and pepper saxifrage.

AHS-ERI.text: Your train passes near Harrison's Rocks, on the train's {side}, a line of sandstone crags in the woods south of Groombridge. Climbers own them, through the British Mountaineering Council since 2009, and the soft rock has about 400 short climbs, all done on a top rope.

AHT-AHV.text: Your train passes near Aldershot Military Cemetery, on the train's {side}, laid out in the 1850s when the Army made Aldershot its permanent training base. Nearly 17,000 service people of nine nations are buried there.

AHT-ASH.text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church in Aldershot, on the train's {side}, built between 1875 and 1878, the first new church in a town that had grown fast once the Army arrived in the 1850s.

AHT-FNH.text: Your train passes near the site of Badshot Lea Long Barrow, on the train's {side}, an earthen burial mound probably built more than 5,000 years ago, the only long barrow known in Surrey. Little was left by 1936, when it was excavated because a chalk quarry was about to swallow the rest.

AHV-BKO.text: Your train passes near Brookwood American Cemetery, on the train's {side}, the only American military cemetery of the First World War in the British Isles. Its chapel, opened in 1929, bears the names of 563 missing, most of them lost at sea.

AHV-FML.text: Your train passes near Frimley Green Windmill, on the train's {side}, a brick tower mill first recorded in 1784. From 1803 it belonged to the Royal Military College at Sandhurst; it stopped work by 1870 and became a house in 1914.

AML-EAL.text: Your train passes near Ealing Village, on the train's {side}: five Art Deco blocks of flats built from 1934 to 1936 to tempt film stars from Ealing Studios. In the end, most of the flats went to film crews.

AML-PAD.text: Your train passes near Kensal Green Cemetery, on the train's {side}, where Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the engineer who built this railway, is buried with his father, Marc.

AMR-CFO.text: Your train passes Little Chalfont, on the train's {side}, a village that grew up in the 20th century round its station. The station opened in 1889 as Chalfont Road, among isolated farms, and was renamed Chalfont & Latimer in 1915.

AMR-GMN.text: Your train passes near Gipsy House, on the train's {side}, the home of the writer Roald Dahl and his family for several decades. He and his wife, the actor Patricia Neal, bought it at auction for £4,500 in 1954.

AMT-MDG.text: Your train passes near Aldermaston Lock, on the train's {side}, built between 1718 and 1723 and later given unusual scalloped brick walls.

AMT-THE.text: Your train passes near Folly Farm, on the train's {side}, a house that Edwin Lutyens extended around 1906 and 1912, with gardens he designed with Gertrude Jekyll.

AMY-ARU.text: Your train passes near Amberley Museum, on the train's {side}, an open-air museum of industry in an old chalk quarry. The quarry had its own railway, linked to the main line at Amberley station; the museum runs passenger trains on a narrow-gauge line today.

AMY-PUL.text: Your train passes near St Botolph's Church at Hardham, on the train's {side}, whose 12th-century wall paintings are the earliest nearly complete series in England. Among them is the earliest known picture of St George in the country.

ANF-BEU.text: Your train passes near Denny Lodge, on the train's {side}, the remote building that names a large New Forest parish with no towns, villages, churches or schools.

ANF-TTN.text: Your train passes near Eling Tide Mill, on the train's {side}, one of only two working tide mills left in the United Kingdom.

ANG-FOD.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church at Poling, on the train's {side}, a flint church whose nave dates from Saxon times. A Saxon window found in its north wall in 1917 still has part of its original wooden shutter.

ANG-GBS.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Goring-by-Sea, on the train's {side}, a Norman church given its present Gothic Revival look by Decimus Burton in 1837. Inside is a mural painted in 1954 by the German artist Hans Feibusch, which caused controversy at the time.

ANG-LIT.text: Your train passes near Littlehampton, on the train's {side}, a fishing town at the mouth of the Arun that became a port and resort, with a ferry across the Channel to Honfleur. Its population grew tenfold in the 1800s, from 584 in 1801 to 5,954 in 1901.

ANZ-NWD.text: Your train passes near Anerley Town Hall, on the train's {side}, an Italianate building by George Elkington, opened on April 30th 1879 as the vestry hall of St Paul's, Anerley. It became the headquarters of Penge Urban District in 1900; its assembly hall has an unusual hammerbeam roof tied with wrought-iron rods.

ANZ-PNW.text: Your train is following the course of the Croydon Canal, which crossed Penge Common along what is now this line through Penge West; a stretch of it survives in Betts Park, on the train's {side}. After the canal closed, the London and Croydon Railway, at first an atmospheric railway, was built largely along its course and opened in 1839.

AON-BTY.text: Your train passes near St Lawrence's Church in Alton, on the train's {side}, probably begun not long after 1066. On December 13th 1643, in the Civil War, Royalist soldiers made their last stand in it before Parliament's troops broke through the west door.

APD-HMT.text: Your train crosses the Royal Military Canal, dug from 1804 along the edge of Romney Marsh as a barrier against Napoleon's planned invasion. Early in the Second World War it was fortified again, and many of its pillboxes survive.

APD-RYE.text: Your train passes near the Landgate at Rye, on the train's {side}, the only one left of the town's four fortified gateways, dating from 1329. In 2015 some 25 tonnes of pigeon droppings had to be cleared from its arch.

APF-CUM.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Appleford Railway Bridge. The first bridge here, of timber, was finished in 1844; today's steel one dates from 1927.

APF-DID.text: Your train passes Didcot Railway Centre, on the train's {side}, a railway museum in what was once a Great Western Railway engine shed.

APF-SWI.text: Your train passes near Priory Cottages at Steventon, on the train's {side}, a manor house of the 1300s that was a grange of the Abbey of Bec in Normandy. A group of women philanthropists, Ferguson's Gang, gave it to the National Trust in 1939.

ARU-FOD.text: Your train passes near Lyminster church, on the train's {side}, home of the Slayer's Slab, a medieval gravestone with a cross on it and no name. Legend says it marks the grave of the man who killed the Knucker, the dragon of the nearby knuckerhole.

ARU-LIT.text: Your train passes near Littlehampton Lifeboat Station, on the train's {side}, on the east bank of the Arun. The RNLI opened a station here in 1884; its inshore lifeboat of 1967 was paid for by an appeal on BBC TV's Blue Peter and named Blue Peter I.

ASC-CNM.text: Your train passes near Christ Church in Cheltenham, on the train's {side}, a Gothic Revival church begun in 1837 and consecrated in 1840. Inside hangs a glass cross engraved by the artist Bryant Fedden.

ASC-WOP.text: Your train passes near Bredon Barn, on the train's {side}, a 14th-century barn built for the Bishops of Worcester. The National Trust has had it since 1951; it was badly damaged by fire in 1979 and restored by 1983.

ASC-WOS.text: Your train passes near the park of Croome Court, on the train's {side}: the first landscape designed by Capability Brown, who also designed the house, for the Earl of Coventry in the 1700s.

ASD-FIT.text: Your train passes near the New Orphan Houses on Ashley Down, on the train's {side}, built between 1849 and 1870 by George Müller. Their five houses held 2,050 children at a time, and Müller never asked anyone for money to run them.

ASD-SRD.text: Your train passes near St Werburgh's Church, on the train's {side}, a medieval church that stood in Corn Street in the old city until 1879, when it was taken down and rebuilt here. Its 14th-century tower was moved stone by stone; the church is now a climbing centre.

ASH-NCM.text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church in Ash, on the train's {side}, which dates back to the 12th century. Domesday Book records a church here, probably built of wood.

ASH-WAN.text: Your train passes near the site of a Romano-Celtic temple at Wanborough, on the train's {side}. It was looted between 1983 and 1985; more than a thousand of its silver coins are now in the British Museum.

ASN-BFN.text: Your train passes near the London Bus Museum at Brooklands, on the train's {side}. About 35 of its buses and coaches are on show, from Victorian horse-drawn omnibuses to Routemasters, including the only surviving wartime utility bus that ran in London.

ASN-CHY.text: Your train passes near the site of Chertsey Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 666 by Saint Erkenwald. King Henry VI was buried here before his body was moved to St George's Chapel, Windsor.

ASN-WYB.text: Your train passes near Coxes Lock on the Wey Navigation, on the train's {side}, built between 1651 and 1653. Its mill pond is the biggest on the navigation, and its old mill buildings are now flats.

AUW-CBY.text: Your train passes near the mound of Ascot d'Oilly Castle, on the train's {side}, named after Roger d'Oilly, who was given the land by William the Conqueror. His brother built Oxford Castle.

AUW-SIP.text: Your train passes near the mound of Ascott Earl Castle, on the train's {side}, a motte-and-bailey castle built on Iron Age earthworks. A second castle, Ascot d'Oilly, stands at the other end of the village.

AVF-BOA.text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church in Bradford-on-Avon, on the train's {side}, one of very few Anglo-Saxon churches in England without later medieval changes. For many years it was used as a school and a cottage, until William Jones, rector of the parish church of Holy Trinity, rediscovered it in 1856.

AVF-FFD.text: Your train passes under Avoncliff Aqueduct, next to Avoncliff station, which carries the Kennet and Avon Canal over the River Avon and the railway. It was built by John Rennie and John Thomas between 1797 and 1801.

AVN-PRI.text: Your train passes near Pill, across the river on the train's {side}, where the RNLI kept a lifeboat for little more than three years, from July 1971 to November 1974.

AVN-SAR.text: Your train passes near Avonmouth Docks, on the train's {side}, part of the Port of Bristol where the Avon meets the Severn estuary. Today they are one of the UK's main ports for chilled foods, especially fruit and vegetables.

AVP-AYS.text: Your train passes the site of a Roman settlement at Fleet Marston, on the train's {side}, on the line of Akeman Street, the Roman road. In 2022 archaeologists working on HS2 found a Roman cemetery in the parish, with about 425 burials and 1,200 coins.

AXM-CKN.text: Your train passes near Forde Abbey, on the train's {side}, a Cistercian monastery whose last abbot surrendered it to the Crown in 1539; it became a house. The philosopher Jeremy Bentham rented it in 1815.

AXM-HON.text: Your train passes through the site of Newenham Abbey, a Cistercian abbey founded in 1247 by Reginald de Mohun, a short way south-west of Axminster.

AYH-SWO.text: Your train passes near Snowdown, on the train's {side}, a hamlet that was home to one of the four chief collieries of the Kent coalfield. The colliery closed in 1987.

AYL-MDB.text: Your train passes near Allington Castle, on the train's {side}, home of Sir Thomas Wyatt the Younger until the Crown seized it in 1554, after his rebellion against Queen Mary. Largely a ruin by the early 1900s, it was saved and restored by Sir Martin Conway and his wife.

AYL-NHE.text: Your train passes near Aylesford Priory, The Friars, on the train's {side}, founded in 1242 by Carmelite friars who came from Mount Carmel in the Holy Land. The Carmelites came back in 1949, and it is a place of pilgrimage once more.

AYP-BXY.text: Your train passes near the King's Head, on the train's {side}, a pub on Bexley High Street in a building dating back to the 16th or early 17th century. It is listed Grade II.

AYP-SID.text: Your train passes near Lamorbey Park, on the train's {side}, a park set round Lamorbey House, a Grade II listed mansion. The estate's earliest recorded owner, in 1495, was a reeve named Thomas Sparrow, and a later owner was Charles FitzRoy, a son of Charles II; parts of it are now Rose Bruford College, two schools and a golf club, and its 1920s Glade has a large lake.

AYS-LTK.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church in Little Kimble, on the train's {side}. Inside are the remains of early 14th-century wall paintings of saints, among them St Francis preaching to the birds and a large St George.

AYS-SKM.text: Your train passes near Stoke Mandeville Stadium, on the train's {side}, the National Centre for Disability Sport. It grew out of the Stoke Mandeville Games, the forerunner of the Paralympic Games, started in 1948 by the neurosurgeon Ludwig Guttmann at the hospital next door.

BAA-BOG.text: Your train passes near Bognor Regis, on the train's {side}, a resort laid out by Sir Richard Hotham in the late 18th century on an empty stretch of coast. King George V spent three months recovering here in 1929, and the town was given the name "Regis" later that year.

BAA-CCH.text: Your train passes near Chichester Cross, on the train's {side}, an elaborate stone market cross about 50 feet tall, where the city's four main streets meet. Its inscription says Bishop Edward Story built it, so that poor people would have somewhere to sell their wares.

BAA-FOD.text: Your train passes near John Baker's Mill at Barnham, on the train's {side}, a flint and stone tower windmill built in 1829. It was worked by wind until the early 1920s and by engine until 1963.

BAB-HHE.text: Your train crosses the Ouse Valley Viaduct, 96 feet high and carried on 37 arches, with stone balustrades along the top. It opened to trains in July 1841, and has been called "probably the most elegant viaduct in Britain".

BAB-TBD.text: Your train passes near Worth Forest, on the train's {side}, an ancient wood in a ghyll, a narrow valley that a stream has cut into soft sandstone. Its wet valley floor is carpeted with sphagnum moss.

BAD-BLM.text: Your train passes near the Gally Hills on Banstead Downs, on the train's {side}, where Saxon burial mounds survive. Bronze Age axes and Iron Age and Roman pottery have also been found on the downs.

BAD-EPD.text: Your train passes near Epsom College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1853 as the Royal Medical Benevolent College, to house pensioned doctors and to educate the sons of poor or deceased doctors.

BAG-CAM.text: Your train passes near the Camberley Obelisk, on the train's {side}, which is really a square brick tower, built on a wooded hill in about 1765 to 1770 by the merchant John Norris. It once stood much taller.

BAL-MTC.text: Your train passes near the site of Battersea Grammar School, on the train's {side}. Founded in Battersea in 1875, the school moved to larger premises in Streatham in 1936, and closed in 1977 when it merged with Rosa Bassett School, a girls' grammar school, to form Furzedown Secondary School in Tooting.

BAL-SRC.text: Your train passes Tooting Bec Lido, on the train's {side}, opened in 1906 and the largest freshwater swimming pool by surface area in the UK, 100 yards long and 33 yards wide. Brad Pitt's pool scene in the film Snatch was shot here.

BAL-SRH.text: Your train passes near Du Cane Court, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco block of 677 flats on Balham High Road. When it was built in 1937 it was thought to be the largest privately owned block of flats in Europe, and many music hall stars of the 1930s and 1940s lived there, among them the comedian Tommy Trinder.

BAL-TOO.text: Your train passes near The Bedford in Balham, on the train's {side}, a listed pub rebuilt in about 1931 and known for comedy and music. The Clash, U2 and Ed Sheeran have all played early gigs there.

BAL-WSW.text: Your train passes near Chez Bruce, on the train's {side}, a restaurant opened in 1995 that has held a Michelin star since 1999. It is on the site of Harveys, Marco Pierre White's former restaurant.

BAS-BFE.text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church in Bere Ferrers, on the train's {side}, whose stained glass is the oldest in Devon outside Exeter Cathedral.

BAS-CSK.text: Your train crosses the Tamar between Devon and Cornwall on Calstock Viaduct, 120 feet high, with 12 arches built from 11,148 concrete blocks between 1904 and 1907.

BAT-CWU.text: Your train passes near Senlac Hill, on the train's {side}, where Harold is generally thought to have placed his army for the Battle of Hastings on October 14th 1066. Battle Abbey was later built on top of it.

BAT-RBR.text: Your train passes near the site of Glottenham Castle, on the train's {side}, built in the late 13th century with stone walls, two square towers and a gatehouse. It belonged to the de Etchingham family and was abandoned by the 17th century.

BAW-FNN.text: Your train passes near St Michael's Abbey in Farnborough, on the train's {side}, founded by the exiled Empress Eugénie as a memorial to her family. She is buried there beside her husband, Napoleon III, and their son.

BAW-SND.text: Your train passes near the Concrete Elephant, on the train's {side}, a sculpture by Barbara Jones made for the Lord Mayor's Show in London in 1963, to show off a builder's use of reinforced concrete. It now stands beside the A30 in Camberley.

BBL-OTF.text: Your train passes near the site of a Roman villa at Otford, on the train's {side}, abandoned in the fourth century. Its remains were found and dug in the 1930s, and again in 2015.

BBL-SEV.text: Your train passes near the Sevenoaks Wildlife Reserve, on the train's {side}, made from old gravel pits by the Harrison family. It was the first gravel pit in the United Kingdom turned into a nature reserve, and has five lakes filled from the River Darent.

BCE-MAO.text: Your train passes near the former RAF Staff College at Bracknell, on the train's {side}, where the Royal Air Force trained its staff officers from 1945 to 1997, in a Victorian house called Ramslade House.

BCE-WKM.text: Your train passes near Ranelagh School in Bracknell, on the train's {side}, a Church of England school founded by Lord Ranelagh in 1709.

BCF-HWY.text: Your train passes near Wycombe Abbey, on the train's {side}, a girls' boarding school founded in 1896 by Dame Frances Dove. Its grounds of woods, gardens and a lake include a Cold War bunker.

BCF-SRG.text: Your train passes near Bekonscot, on the train's {side}, a model village built in the 1920s by Roland Callingham at one inch to one foot, often called the oldest surviving model village in Britain. It helped inspire Enid Blyton.

BCH-HNB.text: Your train passes near the Church of St Mary the Virgin at Hillborough, on the train's {side}, built between 1876 and 1878. It includes materials from the church founded in 669 inside the Roman fort at Reculver, which was mostly pulled down in 1809.

BCH-WGA.text: Your train passes near the Carlton Cinema in Westgate-on-Sea, on the train's {side}. It was built in 1910 as the town hall, but within two years it had become a cinema, and it still shows films today.

BCS-HDM.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Ludgershall, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church dating from the 14th century. The Bible scholar John Wycliffe is reported to have been one of its early vicars.

BCS-KGS.text: Your train passes near the church at Kings Sutton, on the train's {side}, whose spire, added in the late 14th century, rises to 198 feet (60 metres). Nikolaus Pevsner thought it "one of the finest, if not the finest, spire in this county of spires".

BCU-BEU.text: Your train crosses Bishop's Dyke, an earthwork round land of the Bishop of Winchester. Legend says King John told the bishop he could have as much land as he could crawl round, and the bishop, who was rather fat, managed a large area.

BCU-LYT.text: Your train passes near Buckland Rings, on the train's {side}, an Iron Age hill fort whose banks and ditches can still be clearly seen.

BCU-SWY.text: Your train passes near the site of a First World War hospital, on the train's {side}, run by New Zealand's army medical corps. It was set up in Brockenhurst in 1916, in two large hotels taken for the purpose.

BCV-SVS.text: Your train passes near the Marcus Garvey Library, on the train's {side}, opened in 1987 and named after the activist Marcus Garvey, whose son, Marcus Garvey III, laid its foundation stone. Its Black Literature and Marcus Garvey collections are used by the local Black community.

BCV-WHL.text: Your train passes near Bruce Castle, on the train's {side}, a 16th-century manor house and one of the oldest surviving English brick houses. The postal reformer Sir Rowland Hill lived there; it is now a museum, and its grounds, a park since 1892, are Tottenham's oldest.

BCY-HPA.text: Your train passes near the Rivoli Ballroom, on the train's {side}, opened in July 1913 as the Crofton Park Picture Palace. After its last film in 1957 it became a dance hall, reopening on Boxing Day 1959 with a sprung floor of Canadian maple, and it keeps its red velvet, flock wallpaper and chandeliers.

BCY-NXG.text: Your train passes near New Cross Gate Cutting, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of more than four hectares beside the line. It is a remnant of the Great North Wood, on the site once known as Hatcham Wood, and deer live there; the London Wildlife Trust manages it and usually opens it only on open days.

BDH-CSA.text: Your train passes near The Elms in Old Bedhampton, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century house given a Gothic Revival makeover in the 18th. Its owner, Sir Theophilus Lee, invited his relative the Duke of Wellington to dine here, and had a room made in his honour.

BDH-HAV.text: Your train passes near the middle of Havant, on the train's {side}, once home to the leading parchment works in southern England, which closed in 1936. The Treaty of Versailles was written on Havant parchment.

BDH-HLS.text: Your train passes the site of Portsmouth Airport, on the train's {side}, opened in 1932 with three grass runways between Hilsea and Langstone Harbour. From here ran the first air ferry in the south of England, to Ryde on the Isle of Wight; the last flight left on December 31st 1973.

BDN-SAB.text: Your train passes near Nunwell House, on the train's {side}, home of the Oglander family for centuries. Sir John Oglander, a Royalist, hosted Charles I here on the King's last night of freedom.

BDN-SAN.text: Your train passes near Brading Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, found in 1879 when a farmer making holes for a sheep pen struck a mosaic floor. The villa grew around three sides of a courtyard, and its mosaics are on show under a cover building.

BDS-PAD.text: Your train passes near Marble Arch, on the train's {side}, designed by John Nash in 1827 as the state entrance to the courtyard of Buckingham Palace. It was moved here, near the corner of Hyde Park, in 1851, when Queen Victoria enlarged the palace.

BDS-TCR.text: Your train passes near 25 Brook Street, on the train's {side}, where the composer George Frideric Handel lived from 1723 until his death in 1759 and wrote almost all his later works. Jimi Hendrix lived next door at number 23; the two houses are now the museum Handel Hendrix House.

BDW-HGD.text: Your train passes near the Somerset Hospital at Froxfield, on the train's {side}: almshouses for widows left by Sarah, Duchess of Somerset, the oldest part built in 1694.

BDW-PEW.text: Your train passes Crofton Pumping Station, on the train's {side}. Its Boulton & Watt steam engine of 1812 is the oldest working beam engine in the world still in its original engine house.

BEC-BGM.text: Your train passes near the site of Catford Studios, on the train's {side}, a film studio built in 1914. During the First World War it made Tom Brown's Schooldays and The Man Who Bought London, the first film of an Edgar Wallace story, and it closed in 1921.

BEC-RVB.text: Your train passes near Beckenham Place Park, on the train's {side}, a large park laid out by John Cator the younger in the second half of the 18th century. Its Palladian mansion, which gave the park its name, is now a community centre and café.

BEG-PDW.text: Your train passes the John Brunt V.C. pub in Paddock Wood, on the train's {side}. Once the Kent Arms, it was renamed in 1947 after John Brunt, who spent his teenage years in the town and won the Victoria Cross in the Second World War.

BEG-YAL.text: Your train passes near the Hop Farm at Beltring, on the train's {side}, where hops have been grown since at least the 16th century. It has the largest collection of oast houses in the world, and once grew hops for Whitbread.

BET-CBH.text: Your train passes near the Young V&A, on the train's {side}, the V&A's museum for children, opened in 1872 as the Bethnal Green Museum. Its iron frame was first put up in South Kensington in 1856 to 1857; the museum won Museum of the Year in 2024.

BET-LST.text: Your train passes near All Hallows-on-the-Wall, on the train's {side}, a church beside the line of London's old city wall. The present building was designed by George Dance the Younger in 1767, when he was only 24; the church before it was known for the hermits who lived in cells there.

BET-SRA.text: Your train passes near the ArcelorMittal Orbit, on the train's {side}, a 114.5-metre sculpture and observation tower by Anish Kapoor and Cecil Balmond, built for the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. It is Britain's largest piece of public art; in 2016 a slide, then the world's longest, was added.

BEX-CLL.text: Your train passes near the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, on the train's {side}, built in 1935 and described by Historic England as the UK's first public building in the Modernist style. Since 2005 it has been an arts centre.

BEX-WLD.text: Your train passes near Bulverhythe, on the train's {side}, where a German submarine from the First World War, UB-131, was wrecked in January 1921 while being towed from Harwich to Falmouth for explosive trials. The wreck was sold for £655 and broken up where it lay.

BFD-KWB.text: Your train passes near the London Museum of Water & Steam, on the train's {side}, in Kew Bridge Pumping Station, opened in 1838 to supply west London with drinking water. It has the world's largest collection of Cornish engines, including the largest surviving single-cylinder beam engine in the world.

BFD-SYL.text: Your train passes the site of the Firestone Tyre Factory, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco landmark on the Great West Road opened in 1928. It was demolished over the August bank holiday in 1980, reportedly before it could be listed, which led to the listing of 150 interwar buildings; its gates and railings survive.

BFE-SBV.text: Your train crosses the mouth of the River Tavy, just before it joins the Tamar, on the Tavy Bridge, 453 metres long.

BFN-WBY.text: Your train passes near Brooklands, on the train's {side}, opened in 1907 as the world's first purpose-built banked motor racing circuit, and one of Britain's first airfields. Its last race was in August 1939.

BFN-WYB.text: Your train passes near Brooklands Museum, on the train's {side}, home to Concorde G-BBDG, built for testing before the planes carried passengers. It first flew in February 1974, last flew on Christmas Eve 1981, and came here by road in 2003.

BGL-LUX.text: Your train passes near Luxulyan, on the train's {side}, which gives its name to luxulyanite, a rare Cornish granite used for the Duke of Wellington's sarcophagus in St Paul's Cathedral.

BGL-ROC.text: Your train passes near an old holy well north-west of Roche station, on the train's {side}, protected as a scheduled monument.

BGM-CTF.text: Your train passes near the Fellowship Inn, on the train's {side}, built in 1923 and 1924 as the first pub on a London housing estate. Fleetwood Mac played there, and the boxer Henry Cooper trained and lived there before his 1963 fight against Cassius Clay.

BHK-EDR.text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, Edmonton, on the train's {side}, first recorded in the 12th century and rebuilt in the 15th; its west tower still has its medieval outside. The essayist Charles Lamb and his sister Mary, a writer, are buried there.

BHK-ENF.text: Your train passes near Barclays Bank in Enfield, on the train's {side}, where the world's first cash machine was put in, in 1967. A gold-coloured cash machine and a plaque have marked the spot since 2017; the building itself was finished in 1897.

BIG-CHH.text: Your train passes near Christ's Hospital, on the train's {side}, a school founded in London in 1552 as a charity for poor children. Its pupils still wear a Tudor uniform of long blue coats and yellow socks, worn since 1553.

BIG-PUL.text: Your train passes near the Old Swan Bridge over the River Arun at Pulborough, on the train's {side}, built in 1787 in a medieval style. It replaced a line of timber bridges, and before them a ferry.

BIK-BKJ.text: Your train passes near Beckenham Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1876 as the Crystal Palace District Cemetery. The cricketer W. G. Grace and the businessman Thomas Crapper are buried there.

BIK-CYP.text: Your train passes near the National Sports Centre, on the train's {side}, opened in Crystal Palace Park in 1964. It stands on the site of the ground where FA Cup finals were played from 1895 to 1914, and its athletics stadium has also staged concerts by Bruce Springsteen and the Sex Pistols.

BIP-NVH.text: Your train passes near Tide Mills, on the train's {side}, a village beside a tide mill begun here in 1762. The village was condemned as unfit to live in in 1936 and abandoned in 1939.

BIP-SEF.text: Your train passes near St Leonard's Church, Seaford, on the train's {side}, parts of which are Norman work of the 11th century. In the Middle Ages Seaford was one of the main ports of southern England, but its harbour silted up and the French burned the town several times between 1350 and 1550.

BIT-BLY.text: Your train passes near Bletchley Park, on the train's {side}, where codebreakers including Alan Turing broke the German Enigma and Lorenz ciphers during the Second World War.

BIT-HDM.text: Your train passes near the remains of Notley Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded for Augustinian canons in the 12th century and one of the richest in the Oxford area. Laurence Olivier and Vivien Leigh later owned it.

BIT-ISP.text: Your train crosses the site of Alchester, a Roman town at a crossroads of Roman roads whose Roman name isn't known. Excavations have shown it was one of the earliest legionary fortresses in Britain after the invasion of AD 43.

BKA-EFF.text: Your train passes near Bookham Commons, on the train's {side}, woods and grassland owned by the National Trust and mentioned in the Domesday Book. A group of houses on the commons is called the Isle of Wight.

BKA-LHD.text: Your train passes near the Leatherhead Theatre, on the train's {side}, built inside a disused 1930s cinema and opened by Princess Margaret in 1969 as the Thorndike Theatre. It was named after the actor Dame Sybil Thorndike.

BKG-WEH.text: Your train passes near the site of the Memorial Grounds, on the train's {side}, opened on Jubilee Day, June 22nd 1897, as the home of Thames Ironworks Football Club. The club played on there as West Ham United until it moved to the Boleyn Ground in 1904; the grounds also had a cycle track and one of England's largest open-air swimming pools.

BKG-WGR.text: Your train passes near London Sri Murugan Temple, on the train's {side}, a Hindu temple in Manor Park built of marble in the Dravidian style. Founded as a charity in 1975 and first consecrated in 1984, it gained its present building, with a temple tower 50 feet high, in 2005, and holds a chariot festival every August.

BKH-CTN.text: Your train passes near Morden College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1695 by Sir John Morden as a home for merchants who had fallen on hard times. Its design is sometimes said to be by Sir Christopher Wren; it is still a retirement home, and its day centre won the Stirling Prize in 2023.

BKH-KDB.text: Your train passes near the Paragon, on the train's {side}, a curved crescent of 14 large houses on the edge of the heath at Blackheath, designed by Michael Searles and begun in 1794. It is seven pairs of houses linked by six single-storey colonnades, said to use pillars from the demolished Wricklemarsh mansion, and it is listed Grade I.

BKH-LEW.text: Your train passes near Blackheath Quaker Meeting House, on the train's {side}, designed by Trevor Dannatt and used by Quakers since 1972. It is thought to be the only Quaker meeting house in Britain built in the Brutalist style, and has been called a “Brutalist jewel”.

BKJ-KTH.text: Your train passes near St George's Church, Beckenham, on the train's {side}. First built in the 12th century, it was rebuilt from 1885 to 1887 by the local architect W. Gibbs Bartleet, and its pinnacled tower, finished in 1903, is the focal point of Beckenham High Street.

BKJ-NBC.text: Your train passes near Beckenham Cricket Club's ground in Foxgrove Road, on the train's {side}, where the Kent Championships, a grass-court tennis tournament, were played in the first half of June from 1886 to 1996.

BKJ-SRT.text: Your train passes near the former Bishop Challoner School, on the train's {side}, a Roman Catholic independent day school that began as a junior school and added a senior wing in 1956. It closed on July 4th 2025.

BKL-BMS.text: Your train passes near St Blaise's Well, on the train's {side}, a holy well in the grounds of the old palace of the Bishops of Rochester, now part of Bromley Civic Centre. Its water, with traces of iron, was believed to heal, and it became a place of pilgrimage with an oratory to St Blaise beside it.

BKL-PET.text: Your train passes near Jubilee Country Park, on the train's {side}, bought by Bromley Council to mark the Queen's Silver Jubilee in 1977 and opened as a park in 1981. A local nature reserve of grassland and ancient woodland, it has a large population of the rare corkyfruit water dropwort, and the London Loop walk runs through it.

BKL-SMY.text: Your train passes near Chislehurst Junction, on the train's {side}, where the South Eastern and Chatham main lines pass over each other. Loops joining them were built after the two railway companies merged in 1899; the first, the down Bickley Loop, opened on September 8th 1902.

BKO-FNB.text: Your train runs beside the Basingstoke Canal, on the train's {side}, finished in 1794 to link Basingstoke with the Thames. It never made money, became derelict, and was reopened in 1991 after years of restoration.

BKO-WOK.text: Your train passes Brookwood Cemetery, on the train's {side}, the largest in the United Kingdom, opened in 1854 for London's dead. Coffins and mourners came out from a special station beside Waterloo, on a branch line into the cemetery.

BKS-CBE.text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church, on the train's {side}, the oldest church building in England still in use as a church. It was Queen Bertha of Kent's private chapel before Augustine arrived from Rome in 597, and is part of Canterbury's World Heritage Site.

BLM-SUO.text: Your train passes Belmont Pastures, on the train's {side}, a narrow strip of old meadow beside the line that once belonged to Belmont Hospital. Now a nature reserve, its chalk grassland has wild flowers such as bladder campion and knapweed, and grasshoppers and crickets.

BLY-FEN.text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church in Fenny Stratford, on the train's {side}, built by Browne Willis, its first stone laid on St Martin's Day 1724. Every St Martin's Day, November 11th, the Fenny Poppers, six small ceremonial cannon, are fired with blank charges at noon, 2pm and 4pm.

BLY-LBZ.text: Your train runs through Linslade Tunnel, whose three bores are the only tunnel on the London and Birmingham Railway built on a bend: local landowners refused to let the line pass closer to Leighton Buzzard. The first bore opened in 1837.

BLY-MKC.text: Your train passes near the National Bowl, on the train's {side}, an open-air arena made from an old clay pit for brick-making. It opened in 1979; Queen played here in 1982, and Michael Jackson drew 60,000 fans on each of three nights.

BMD-ENL.text: Your train passes near Enfield Power Station, on the train's {side}, a 442-megawatt gas-fired station on part of the site of the old Brimsdown Power Station. Building started in September 1997, and it was running by December 1999.

BMD-PON.text: Your train passes near Beavertown Brewery, on the train's {side}, founded in 2011 by Logan Plant, son of Led Zeppelin's Robert Plant. Its name comes from De Beauvoir Town, where its first beer was brewed; its Enfield brewery opened in 2020.

BMG-EML.text: Your train passes near the fruit research station at East Malling, on the train's {side}, set up in 1913. Its research, above all on rootstocks for fruit trees, earned it a worldwide reputation.

BMG-MDE.text: Your train passes near Maidstone Museum, on the train's {side}, built round Chillington Manor, an Elizabethan house finished in 1577. It opened in 1858 with the collections of a local doctor, and has one of the most important Japanese collections outside London.

BMH-BSM.text: Your train crosses one of the two Bourne Valley Viaducts over the River Bourne, built in 1888 and 1893; the other is now disused.

BMH-POK.text: Your train passes St Clement's Church, on the train's {side}, built from 1871 to 1873: the first major church designed by J. D. Sedding, and one of three Grade I listed churches in Bournemouth.

BMN-SUP.text: Your train passes near Bromley College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1666 under the will of John Warner, Bishop of Rochester, to house 20 widows of clergy. Its almshouses were built round a quadrangle in 1670 to 1672 and are the oldest building in Bromley, listed Grade I; it still provides homes for retired clergy and their families.

BMS-SRT.text: Your train passes near the site of Simpson's Place, on the train's {side}, a moated medieval manor house; in the reign of Henry V, William Clark asked for a licence to build it with crenellated walls and a deep moat. It was demolished around 1870, and its name lives on in Simpsons Road.

BMT-BRI.text: Your train passes near St Mary Redcliffe, on the train's {side}, whose spire is 274 feet high. Elizabeth I is said to have called it "the fairest, goodliest and most famous parish church in England" on a visit in 1574.

BMT-PSN.text: Your train passes near the site of St John the Baptist's Church in Bedminster, on the train's {side}, one of Bristol's oldest churches, first recorded in 1003. It was gutted in the Blitz in November 1940 and in 1967 the council approved the demolition of its ruins.

BMY-BSK.text: Your train passes near the ruins of the Holy Ghost Chapel, on the train's {side}: a chapel stood here by 1244, and Lord Sandys added a family chapel in 1524.

BMY-MOR.text: Mortimer station, at one end of this stretch, keeps its Brunel-designed Great Western Railway buildings, still in use.

BNE-COO.text: Your train crosses the River Thames at Bourne End, on a bridge first built in wood by Isambard Kingdom Brunel for the line's opening in 1854 and rebuilt in steel in 1895.

BNE-MLW.text: Your train passes near Marlow Bridge, on the train's {side}, a suspension bridge over the Thames built between 1829 and 1832 by William Tierney Clark, who also designed the Chain Bridge over the Danube in Budapest.

BNH-BXH.text: Barnehurst station, at one end of this stretch, opened on May 1st 1895, when the Bexley Heath Railway opened its line from Blackheath to Slade Green. Its platforms sit just east of the bridge that carries Barnehurst Lane over the line.

BNH-SGR.text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Church, Slade Green, on the train's {side}, founded in 1900 as a daughter church of St Paulinus in Crayford and a parish of its own from 1925. In the Second World War it sheltered families bombed out of east London; it was rebuilt after a direct hit in 1944, and again after a fire in 1991.

BNI-BNS.text: Your train passes near the Bull's Head, on the train's {side}, a riverside pub in Barnes, rebuilt in 1846, that opened as a jazz venue in 1959. It became one of the most important jazz venues in Britain, known as the suburban Ronnie Scott's.

BNI-CHK.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Barnes Railway Bridge, first opened in 1849 to Joseph Locke's design; it also carries a footpath. It is a landmark of the Boat Race, and its coat of arms has a light blue oar for Cambridge and a dark blue oar for Oxford.

BNM-SLO.text: Your train passes near the site of William Herschel's house, on the train's {side}, where he and his sister Caroline built his 40-foot telescope, the largest in the world for 50 years. With it he found two of Saturn's moons in 1789.

BNM-TAP.text: Your train passes near Burnham Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1266 by Richard, Earl of Cornwall, brother of King Henry III. Anglican nuns made it their home from 1916.

BNP-CPN.text: Your train passes near Barnstaple's Long Bridge over the River Taw, on the train's {side}, one of the largest medieval bridges in Britain. A will of 1274 left money for its upkeep.

BNS-MTL.text: Your train passes near the tomb of the explorer Sir Richard Burton, on the train's {side}, a mausoleum of marble and stone shaped like a tent, designed by his wife Isabel. Their coffins can be seen through a glass panel at the back.

BNS-PUT.text: Your train passes near The Pines, on the train's {side}, a house on Putney Hill where the poet Algernon Charles Swinburne lived with his friend Theodore Watts-Dunton until his death in 1909. Max Beerbohm, who often visited, described it as 'but a few steps from the railway-station'.

BOA-TRO.text: Your train passes near the tithe barn at Barton Farm, on the train's {side}, built in the 1330s for the nuns of Shaftesbury Abbey, the richest nunnery in England. It is listed Grade I and looked after by English Heritage.

BOD-LOS.text: Your train passes near Restormel Castle, on the train's {side}, a Norman castle known for its perfectly circular design.

BOD-LSK.text: Your train crosses Moorswater Viaduct. Beside it stand the stone piers of the earlier viaduct, which carried the line on timber, as Brunel advised for Cornwall's valleys.

BOE-FRM.text: Your train passes the old Funtley Deviation, on the train's {side}, a two-mile line opened in 1904 to avoid the unstable Fareham tunnel. It had troubles of its own, and closed in May 1973, when trains went back through the tunnel; it is now a footpath.

BOE-HDE.text: Your train passes near Shamblehurst Farmhouse, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house partly from the 1600s, its upper floor jutting out over the lower. It now goes by the name Strawberry Cottage.

BOH-FSB.text: Your train passes near Fishbourne Roman Palace, on the train's {side}, the largest known Roman home north of the Alps, built around AD 75. Its mosaics include the Dolphin mosaic, and it burnt down in about 270, after which it was abandoned.

BOH-NUT.text: Your train passes near Nutbourne, on the train's {side}, a village at the northern tip of Thorney Channel, an inlet of Chichester Harbour. Its name probably comes from the South Saxons' hnutu burna, the stream overhung by nut trees.

BOP-PAL.text: Your train passes near Broomfield House, on the train's {side}, in Broomfield Park. Bought by the London merchant Joseph Jackson in 1624, it was damaged by fires in 1984, 1993, 1994 and 2019, and plans to restore it had made no progress by January 2024.

BPW-FIT.text: Your train passes near Stoke Gifford depot, on the train's {side}, built on a triangle of land between three railway lines. It was built to look after Great Western Railway's Class 800 trains, which entered service in 2017.

BPW-PWY.text: Your train crosses Gipsy Patch Lane on a bridge built in 2020. It replaced a narrow dark-brick arch, so that the road could have a bus lane each way.

BPW-SWI.text: Your train passes near the Health Hydro in Swindon, on the train's {side}, built for the Great Western Railway's Medical Fund Society. Its Turkish baths carry on a service begun for railway workers and their families in 1868, the longest-surviving Victorian Turkish baths in the world; in 1948 the fund's medical services became part of the new NHS.

BPW-YAE.text: Your train crosses the Huckford Viaduct, built by the Great Western Railway in 1902 about 100 feet above the River Frome, which runs through one of its arches.

BRG-KMS.text: Your train passes near the Iron Age hillfort on Oldbury Hill, on the train's {side}, thought to have been built around 100 BC. At 123 acres it was the largest of a line of forts across Kent and Surrey, and flint tools from the Palaeolithic have been found there too.

BRG-WMA.text: Your train passes near Malling Abbey in West Malling, on the train's {side}, founded for Benedictine nuns around 1090 by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester. It was dissolved in 1538, became a monastery again in the late 19th century, and is now home to Anglican Benedictine nuns.

BRI-KYN.text: Your train passes near the old Somerdale chocolate factory, on the train's {side}, built for Fry's from 1924 and closed in 2011. Remains of a Roman settlement were found on the site.

BRI-LWH.text: Your train passes near Brunel's original Temple Meads station, on the train's {side}, opened on August 31st 1840 as the western end of the Great Western Railway. It is listed Grade I and no longer used by trains.

BRK-GLY.text: Your train passes near Glynde Place, on the train's {side}, an Elizabethan manor house built in 1569 and still the family home of the Viscounts Hampden. Since 2013 its grounds have held the Love Supreme Jazz Festival every summer.

BRK-PLG.text: Your train passes near Ovenden's Mill in Polegate, on the train's {side}, a four-storey brick tower mill built in 1817. It worked by wind until 1943, and then by engine until 1965.

BRS-NEM.text: Your train passes near New Malden High Street, on the train's {side}, known for its many Korean shops and restaurants: New Malden has the largest community of South Koreans in Europe.

BRS-SUR.text: Surbiton station, at one end of this stretch, was rebuilt in 1937 in an Art Deco style designed by James Robb Scott, and has been called one of the finest modernist stations in Britain. It appears in the very first episode of ITV's Agatha Christie's Poirot.

BRU-CLC.text: Your train passes near the Bruton Dovecote, on the train's {side}, a stone tower built between the 15th and 17th centuries that may have been a lookout before it housed pigeons.

BRU-FRO.text: Your train passes near Marston Moat, on the train's {side}, the moat of a fortified manor house held by the Bigot family before 1195. There is some evidence they fortified it without the king's licence; that, and an insult to the king's messenger, cost Richard Bigot his lands.

BRU-PEW.text: Your train passes near Sexey's Hospital in Bruton, on the train's {side}, almshouses built in about 1630 from the will of Hugh Sexey, an auditor of the Exchequer to James I. People still live there.

BRU-WSB.text: Your train passes the site of Witham Priory, on the train's {side}, founded in 1178 or 1179 as the first Carthusian monastery in England.

BSD-HBN.text: Your train passes near Holy Cross Church, Bearsted, on the train's {side}, begun in the 13th century. Three stone beasts sit on the corners of its tower, replacing worn originals that may have shown wolves from a family coat of arms.

BSD-MDE.text: Your train passes near Mote Park, on the train's {side}, a public park of about 450 acres in Maidstone. Its name comes from an Old English word for a place of assembly, and it has a boating lake and a miniature railway.

BSK-HOK.text: Your train passes near Basing House, on the train's {side}, a Tudor palace built from 1531 for William Paulet, Marquess of Winchester, that once rivalled Hampton Court. Cromwell's troops stormed it in October 1645 after a long siege, and local people were encouraged to carry off its bricks.

BSK-MIC.text: Your train passes near where the Basingstoke and Alton Light Railway set off, on the train's {side}: opened in 1901, the first English railway built under the Light Railway laws. Its track was taken up in 1917 for use in France.

BSK-OVR.text: Your train passes Milestones Museum, on the train's {side}, where streets of Victorian and 1930s Hampshire have been recreated indoors. It opened in 2000.

BSM-PKS.text: Your train passes near St Aldhelm's Church, on the train's {side}, which began as a Sunday mission to the area's pottery workers in a school room in the 1870s.

BSP-BSY.text: Your train passes near the Kiln Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened on Kilburn High Road in 1980 as the Tricycle and renamed in 2018. It became known for plays made from the words spoken at public inquiries, as well as new writing.

BSP-KNR.text: Your train passes near Islamia Primary School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1983 by the singer Yusuf Islam, known before as Cat Stevens. In 1998 it became the first Muslim school in Britain to be granted public funding, after a campaign of 13 years.

BSR-DMP.text: Your train passes near the Dickens House Museum in Broadstairs, on the train's {side}. The cottage was the home of Mary Pearson Strong, whom Charles Dickens visited on his family holidays here and who inspired Betsey Trotwood in David Copperfield.

BSR-MAR.text: Your train passes near the Scenic Railway at Dreamland in Margate, on the train's {side}, a wooden roller coaster opened in 1920, with a brakeman riding on each train to control its speed. When it was listed at Grade II* in 2011 it was the oldest working roller coaster in the UK.

BSY-WHD.text: Your train passes near the former Decca Studios, on the train's {side}, at 165 Broadhurst Gardens, where Decca made its recordings from 1937. David Bowie recorded his first single there in 1964, and the Zombies their hit 'She's Not There'.

BTE-SDN.text: Your train passes near Bitterne Manor, on the train's {side}, the site of the Roman settlement of Clausentum, the forerunner of Southampton. The manor house was built from its stones.

BTE-WLS.text: Your train passes near where the Woolston Floating Bridge crossed the River Itchen, on the train's {side}: a cable ferry that ran from 1836 until 1977, when the Itchen Bridge opened.

BTH-CPM.text: While your train is in Box Tunnel, the government's secret Cold War headquarters, built in an old stone quarry, lies just to the train's {side}.

BTH-FFD.text: Your train passes near Claverton Pumping Station, on the train's {side}, built by John Rennie between 1809 and 1813. The River Avon turns its great water wheel, which pumps water 48 feet up to the Kennet and Avon Canal, on the other side of the railway.

BTH-OLF.text: Your train passes near the Roman Baths, on the train's {side}, where the Romans built a temple at the hot spring between AD 60 and 70.

BTN-HOV.text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church in Brighton, on the train's {side}, opened in 1874. It has no tower or spire, but its roof rises 135 feet; one of its critics called it "a Noah's Ark in brick".

BTN-LRB.text: Your train passes near the Brighton Toy and Model Museum, on the train's {side}, which fills four Victorian arches under the forecourt of Brighton station. Founded in 1991, it holds more than 10,000 toys and models.

BTN-PRP.text: Your train passes near the London Road Viaduct, on the train's {side}, which carries the line to Lewes across a valley in Brighton. Built in 1846, it curves sharply on 27 arches and took about ten million bricks.

BTO-DPD.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Betchworth Castle, on the train's {side}, a medieval fortified manor house on a sandstone spur above the River Mole.

BTO-REI.text: Your train passes near Reigate Priory, on the train's {side}, founded in the 1200s as an Augustinian priory. After the Dissolution it became a house; one later owner was Charles Howard, who led the English fleet against the Spanish Armada.

BTY-FNH.text: Your train passes near the William Cobbett pub in Farnham, on the train's {side}, once the Jolly Farmer, where the radical writer and MP William Cobbett was born in 1763. It was renamed after him.

BUG-HSK.text: Your train passes near St John the Evangelist's Church in Burgess Hill, on the train's {side}, a Gothic Revival church of local brick consecrated in 1863. It was the town's first Church of England church.

BUG-WVF.text: Your train passes through Burgess Hill, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. Until the 19th century much of it was St John's Common, grazing land where a Midsummer Fair was held every June 24th.

BUO-HME.text: Your train passes near the Jolly Sailor at Bursledon, on the train's {side}, an 18th-century pub on the River Hamble that you can reach by boat. It was built as a vicarage and has been a pub since 1845.

BUO-SNW.text: Your train passes near the wreck of the Grace Dieu in the River Hamble, on the train's {side}: Henry V's flagship, launched in 1418 and twice the size of the Mary Rose. She made only one voyage and burned after being struck by lightning in 1439.

BVD-ERH.text: Your train passes near Erith Town Hall, on the train's {side}, designed in the Italian Renaissance style by Harold Hind, the council's surveyor, and opened on June 2nd 1932. It replaced Walnut Tree House, the old house the council had moved into in 1902, and its pediment carries the town's coat of arms.

BWB-FEN.text: Your train passes near the site of Magiovinium, on the train's {side}, a Roman town and fort at Dropshot Farm, at the edge of Fenny Stratford. Two hoards of Roman silver coins were found at or near the site, in 1967 and 1987.

BWB-WOB.text: Your train passes near the factory of Red Bull Racing, on the train's {side}, the Formula One team based in Milton Keynes since 2004. It won the Constructors' Championship four years running from 2010, with Sebastian Vettel, and again in 2022 and 2023.

BWT-HIG.text: Your train passes near Castle Street in Bridgwater, on the train's {side}, built in the 1720s for the Duke of Chandos on the site of Bridgwater Castle. Many of its houses are listed Grade I.

BWT-TAU.text: Your train passes near Taunton Castle, on the train's {side}, now the Museum of Somerset. In its Great Hall in 1685 Judge Jeffreys held the Bloody Assizes after the Monmouth Rebellion, and 144 men were hanged.

BXD-COH.text: Your train passes near the remains of an iron furnace, on the train's {side}, a scheduled monument from the days when the Weald made England's iron. Buxted was at the heart of it: the first cast-iron cannon made in England was cast near the village in 1543, by Ralf Hogge.

BXD-UCK.text: Your train passes near Buxted, on the train's {side}. In the early 1800s the Prime Minister Lord Liverpool bought Buxted Park and enlarged it, pressing the villagers to leave their houses: by 1836 the old village centre had gone, and only its church stayed in the park.

BXH-WLI.text: Your train passes near Park View Road, on the train's {side}, the football ground at Welling, named after the stretch of road beside Danson Park, where Welling United have played since 1977. Football has been played there since the 1920s; Erith & Belvedere have shared the ground since 1999, after the main stand at their own ground burnt down.

BXW-DKG.text: Your train passes near Denbies Wine Estate, on the train's {side}, the largest vineyard in England, with more than a tenth of all the vines planted in the United Kingdom. It takes its name from John Denby, who owned the farmhouse here in the 16th century.

BXW-LHD.text: Your train passes near the Running Horse in Leatherhead, on the train's {side}, a pub by the River Mole dating back to 1403. It was first known as Rummings House, after Eleynor Rumminge, the subject of a poem by John Skelton, Henry VIII's poet; the poem is on a wall inside.

BXY-CRY.text: Your train passes near Hall Place, on the train's {side}, a house built in 1537 for Sir John Champneys, a merchant and former Lord Mayor of London, partly from stone taken from Lesnes Abbey. Its walls have a chequerboard pattern of flint and rubble, and a red-brick wing was added by Sir Robert Austen, who bought it in 1649; it is listed Grade I.

CAM-FML.text: Your train passes near the old Staff College at Camberley, on the train's {side}, which trained the Army's staff officers until 1997. It grew out of a college opened in High Wycombe in 1799.

CAT-WHS.text: Your train passes the former home of Caterham Cars, on the train's {side}, beside Caterham station. The firm bought the rights to the Lotus Seven in 1973 and still makes the Caterham Seven; its factory was in Caterham until 1987 and its showroom here until 2013.

CAU-SDP.text: Your train runs along the valley of the East Looe River, beside the remains of the Liskeard and Looe Union Canal. It was finished in 1828 with 24 locks, and fell out of use after the railway was built in 1860.

CAU-SKN.text: St Keyne Wishing Well Halt, at one end of this stretch, shares its name with St Keyne's holy well. In Victorian times it was said that whichever of a newly married couple drank from it first would have the upper hand.

CBB-LEL.text: Your train passes Lelant's parish church of St Uny, on the train's {side}, listed Grade I, with Norman work in its nave arcades.

CBB-SIV.text: Your train passes near Trewyn Studio, on the train's {side}, which the sculptor Barbara Hepworth bought in 1949. She lived and worked there until her death in 1975; it is now a museum and sculpture garden.

CBE-SEG.text: Your train passes Canterbury Castle, on the train's {side}, one of the three royal castles of Kent built soon after the Battle of Hastings. Its great stone keep went up in the reign of Henry I; by the 19th century a gas company was using it for storage.

CBH-LOF.text: Your train passes near Keeling House, on the train's {side}, a 16-storey block designed by Denys Lasdun and finished in 1957. He grouped four blocks of maisonettes round a central tower, hoping to keep the neighbourliness of Victorian terraced streets; it was renovated in 2001 with a new penthouse floor.

CBK-PIN.text: Your train passes near Pinhoe, on the train's {side}, where the men of Devon and Somerset fought the Danes in 1001. The Danes broke through and burned the village.

CBK-WHM.text: Your train passes Cranbrook, on the train's {side}, a new town built on what was farmland. Its first houses were lived in from 2012.

CBN-HYL.text: Your train passes near Trevithick Cottage, on the train's {side}, childhood home of the Cornish engineer Richard Trevithick, now cared for by the National Trust.

CBN-RED.text: Your train passes near the hill of Carn Brea, on the train's {side}, with a Neolithic enclosure, a medieval castle and old mine workings on it.

CBP-DRG.text: Your train passes near the old Cuckoo Schools, on the train's {side}, opened in 1857 for children of destitute families from London. A working farm educated and fed them until the school closed in 1933.

CBP-SGN.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Perivale, on the train's {side}, a church of the 12th or 13th century, once the smallest in Middlesex. Cut off from its parish by the A40, it is now an arts centre.

CBR-LWS.text: Your train passes near Lewes Castle, on the train's {side}, built by William de Warenne after the Norman Conquest. Unusually it has two mottes, or mounds; the only other castle in England like it is Lincoln Castle.

CBR-PMP.text: Your train passes near East Chiltington, on the train's {side}, a village whose church is 13th century in origin. A Roman road, the Sussex Greensand Way, runs through the middle of its parish.

CBW-CRT.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Chartham, on the train's {side}, begun in about 1285, perhaps with the help of Michael of Canterbury, the master mason at Canterbury Cathedral. Its tower was added in the 14th century.

CBW-STU.text: Your train passes near St Dunstan's Church, on the train's {side}, which dates from the 11th century. In 1174 Henry II changed into sackcloth here before walking to Thomas Becket's tomb in the cathedral, as penance.

CBY-FIN.text: Your train runs along the edge of Cornbury Park, on the train's {side}, once a royal hunting estate: Domesday Book calls it a "demesne forest of the king". It still holds a remnant of the Wychwood Forest.

CCH-FSB.text: Your train passes near Chichester Cathedral, on the train's {side}, founded in 1075. It is the only medieval cathedral in England with a bell tower standing apart from the church, and its spire is the only one of a medieval English cathedral that can be seen from the sea.

CDI-NTC.text: Your train passes near the parish church of Newton St Cyres, on the train's {side}, built in the 15th century of a reddish local volcanic stone. Inside is a standing effigy of John Northcote, who died in 1632.

CDI-YEO.text: Your train passes near Crediton's Church of the Holy Cross, on the train's {side}, on the site of the cathedral of the bishops of Crediton until the see moved to Exeter in 1050.

CDN-CDS.text: Your train passes near an embankment of the Croydon, Merstham and Godstone Railway, on the train's {side}. Opened in 1805 as an extension of the horse-drawn Surrey Iron Railway, the line ran to quarries near Merstham until 1838; this embankment at Coulsdon is eight metres high.

CDN-ELD.text: Your train passes near Farthing Downs, on the train's {side}, the largest area of semi-natural downland left in Greater London, owned by the City of London Corporation. Early medieval burial mounds survive at its north end.

CDN-RHM.text: Your train passes the site of Coulsdon North station, on the train's {side}. It opened on November 5th 1899 as "Stoats Nest and Cane Hill", changed its name three times, and closed on October 3rd 1983 when the line to Brighton was resignalled.

CDN-WME.text: Coulsdon Town station opened as Smitham on January 1st 1904 and kept that name until May 22nd 2011. It sits on a sharp curve, where the line to Tattenham Corner swings away westwards from the main line to Brighton.

CDS-MHM.text: Your train runs through Merstham Tunnel under the North Downs, opened in 1841 for the first railway from London to Brighton. Nearly 60 years later the Quarry Tunnel was built beside it, which most fast trains now use.

CDT-PIL.text: Your train runs through the Severn Tunnel under the estuary of the River Severn, opened in 1886. It is 7,008 metres long, and until 1987 it was the longest underwater tunnel in the world.

CDU-CNM.text: Your train passes near Stonehouse Court, on the train's {side}, a manor house of 1601 that is now a hotel. An earlier owner of the manor, John Maltravers, was found guilty of a part in the murder of Edward II in 1327.

CDU-GCR.text: Your train passes near the barn at Frocester Court, on the train's {side}, a late 13th-century estate barn listed Grade I. The remains of a Roman villa have been found in the grounds.

CDU-YAE.text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity, Wickwar's parish church, on the train's {side}. It stands on a small hill, reached by a raised path called the Stank, meaning "dam": there were fish ponds here until the 1800s.

CED-LBZ.text: Your train crosses Bridego Bridge, now officially Mentmore Bridge, where in August 1963 the Great Train Robbers stopped a Royal Mail train from Glasgow to London and escaped with more than £2.6 million. Most of the money was never found.

CED-TRI.text: Your train runs through Tring Cutting, two and a half miles long and up to 60 feet deep, on the boundary of Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire. It was dug for the London and Birmingham Railway, opened in 1837, whose engineer, Robert Stephenson, was determined to keep its gradients as gentle as possible.

CFB-LAD.text: Your train passes near the Alex Yee Ladywell Arena, on the train's {side}, an athletics stadium renamed on November 22nd 2024 after the Olympic triathlete Alex Yee, who trained on its track early in his career. He asked for "Ladywell" to be kept in the name.

CFB-LSY.text: Your train passes near the Private Banks Sports Ground, on the train's {side}, used by Kent for first-class cricket from 1875 to 1921. In 2012 it was sold to the educational foundation of nearby St Dunstan's College and renamed the Jubilee Ground.

CFN-RDA.text: Your train passes near the Lido in Clifton, on the train's {side}, opened as the Clifton Victoria Baths in 1850. It closed in 1990 and was considered for demolition, but was restored and reopened in 2008.

CFN-SML.text: Your train runs through the site of Abona, a small Roman port town at the mouth of the River Trym. Much Roman material was dug up when the dock at Sea Mills was built.

CFO-CLW.text: Between Chalfont & Latimer and Chorleywood, your train passes from Buckinghamshire into Hertfordshire.
CFO-CLW.textReverse: Between Chorleywood and Chalfont & Latimer, your train passes from Hertfordshire into Buckinghamshire.

CFR-ESL.text: Your train passes near the middle of Eastleigh, on the train's {side}, a town that grew up in the 1800s around the London and South Western Railway. A Saxon village called East Leah was recorded here as long ago as 932.

CFR-ROM.text: Your train passes near King John's House in Romsey, on the train's {side}, said to have been King John's hunting lodge. It was in fact built in 1256, some 40 years after he died, though some of its beams may come from an older building.

CFT-CTF.text: Your train passes near the site of Catford Stadium, on the train's {side}, a greyhound track built in 1932 on Southern Railway land between two commuter lines. At its first meeting, on July 30th 1932, the greyhound Mick the Miller was paraded round the track.

CFT-NHD.text: Your train passes near the Brockley Jack Theatre, on the train's {side}, which shares a building with the Brockley Jack pub. It opened in 1992 with two Chekhov pieces, On the Harmful Effects of Tobacco and Swansong, and puts on new writing as well as established works.

CHE-EWE.text: Your train passes near the site of Nonsuch Palace, on the train's {side}, begun by Henry VIII in 1538 to rival the French king's Château de Chambord. It was pulled down in 1682 and 1683 by Barbara, Countess of Castlemaine, who sold the materials to pay her gambling debts.

CHE-SUO.text: Your train passes near Whitehall, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house in Cheam village thought to have been built around 1500 as a yeoman farmer's house. It is now a museum, with a room about Henry VIII's nearby Nonsuch Palace.

CHG-LEN.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Lenham, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 14th century after a fire destroyed the one before. It and the nearby tithe barn are both Grade I listed.

CHH-HRH.text: Your train passes near Chesworth House, on the train's {side}, a Tudor manor house of the Dukes of Norfolk. Catherine Howard spent her childhood here before she married Henry VIII, who had stayed here himself in 1519.

CHK-KWB.text: Your train passes the site of the Q Theatre, on the train's {side}, by Kew Bridge, which put on new plays from 1924 to 1958. Vivien Leigh, Dirk Bogarde and Joan Collins began their stage careers here, and it staged Terence Rattigan's first plays.

CHL-GOM.text: Your train passes near the ruins of the Chilworth gunpowder mills, on the train's {side}, set up by the East India Company in 1625 beside the Tillingbourne. They supplied gunpowder to the government and closed in 1920.

CHL-SFR.text: Your train passes near Shalford Mill, on the train's {side}, an 18th-century watermill on the River Tillingbourne. In 1932 it was given to the National Trust thanks to Ferguson's Gang, a group of young women who used made-up names.

CHO-DID.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Cholsey, on the train's {side}, where Agatha Christie is buried.

CHO-GOR.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Moulsford Railway Bridge, known locally as Four Arches. Brunel set its brick arches at a slant across the river.

CHP-KND.text: Your train passes near Fames Rough, on the train's {side}, a Surrey Wildlife Trust reserve on the Chipstead Downs. Part of its grassland is ploughed now and then to give a home to three very rare plants of arable fields, among them ground pine.

CHP-WME.text: Woodmansterne station, at one end of this stretch, isn't in Woodmansterne: the village lies across the Greater London boundary in Surrey, while the station serves the western side of Coulsdon.

CHR-HNA.text: Your train passes near Christchurch Priory, on the train's {side}, one of the longest parish churches in the country and as big as many cathedrals.

CHR-POK.text: Your train passes near Christchurch Castle, on the train's {side}, a Norman castle by the lowest crossing of the River Avon. The Constable's House beside it, of about 1160, is a rare Norman home.

CHY-VIR.text: Your train passes near St Ann's Hill, on the train's {side}, the highest point in Chertsey. Its summit was a key viewing point for the survey of the 1780s that linked the Greenwich and Paris observatories by a chain of triangles.

CIL-CRT.text: Your train passes near Julliberrie's Grave, on the train's {side}, a long barrow probably built in the fourth millennium BC. No human remains have been found in it, but a broken polished stone axe had been placed at its centre.

CIL-WYE.text: Your train passes Godmersham Park, on the train's {side}. Its house, built in 1732, came to Edward Austen Knight, Jane Austen's brother, and she often stayed there.

CIR-HHY.text: Your train passes near HM Prison Pentonville, on the train's {side}, opened in 1842 with four wings radiating from a central hall, so that staff could see along them all. It became the model for British prisons: 54 more were built to similar designs within six years.

CIT-ESD.text: Your train passes near Elmstead Pit, on the train's {side}, a small geological Site of Special Scientific Interest opposite Elmstead Woods station. It shows a layer of the Blackheath Beds laid down about 50 million years ago in an estuary, rich in fossils such as molluscs, sharks' teeth and fish scales; there is no public access.

CIT-PET.text: Your train passes near the Daylight Inn, on the train's {side}, a pub built at Petts Wood in 1935 for Charrington's Brewery. It is named after William Willett, who lived in Petts Wood and came up with the idea of daylight saving, and for many years old legal restrictions meant no other pub could be built within a mile of it.

CIT-SMY.text: Your train passes near Chislehurst Caves, on the train's {side}, some 22 miles of man-made tunnels and caverns dug as chalk and flint mines and first mentioned in a ninth-century Saxon charter. In the Second World War they became an air-raid shelter for up to 15,000 people, who paid a penny to go in, with electric lighting, a chapel and a hospital.

CKN-YVJ.text: Your train passes near the Church of All Saints at Sutton Bingham, on the train's {side}, from the 1100s and 1200s. Its wall paintings of the 1300s were whitewashed over at the Reformation.

CLA-HSY.text: Your train passes near West Horsley Place, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house of the 15th century with 50 rooms. It is best known as the filming location of the BBC series Ghosts.

CLA-LRD.text: Your train passes near Abbot's Hospital on Guildford's High Street, on the train's {side}, founded in 1619 by George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury, as homes for the town's elderly. Its first residents moved in on his 60th birthday in 1622.

CLC-TAU.text: Your train passes near Athelney, on the train's {side}, where Alfred the Great hid before defeating the Vikings at Edington in 878, and where he later founded an abbey.

CLC-YVP.text: Your train passes near the Haynes Motor Museum at Sparkford, on the train's {side}, with more than 300 cars and motorcycles. It was founded in 1985 by John Haynes, of the Haynes workshop manuals, in a disused sawmill.
