CLD-KCK.text: Your train passes near Hewitt's Chalk Bank, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve run by the Kent Wildlife Trust on a former refuse tip. Its large mound is the soil dug out when a railway tunnel was made, and its grassland has unusual plants such as grass vetchling and dark mullein.

CLD-ORP.text: Your train passes near Crofton Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, beside Orpington station. Lived in from about AD 140 to 400 as the centre of a farming estate, it was found in 1926 by workmen making a drive for new council offices; the remains of ten rooms can be seen, with tiled floors and underfloor heating.

CLG-HYW.text: Your train passes near the Scilly Isles, on the train's {side}: not the islands, but a double roundabout built in the 1930s. Drivers called its unfamiliar traffic islands the "silly islands", and the name stuck.

CLG-OXS.text: Your train passes near Oxshott Heath, on the train's {side}, common land of woods and heath on a sandy hill. From its top, which has a war memorial, you can see as far as Box Hill.

CLJ-EAD.text: Your train passes Wandsworth Common Windmill, on the train's {side}, a small smock mill built in 1837 to drain water from this railway's cutting. It pumped the water into an ornamental lake on the common called the Black Sea, and stopped work after the lake was filled in around 1884.

CLJ-IMW.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Battersea Railway Bridge, dating from 1863 and one of the oldest crossings of the river in London. It was first called the Cremorne Bridge, after the Cremorne pleasure gardens in Chelsea, and once carried broad-gauge track for Great Western trains to Victoria.

CLJ-WNT.text: Your train passes near the Falcon, on the train's {side}, a pub on St John's Hill recorded as an inn in 1733; the present building dates from 1882 to 1883. The Campaign for Real Ale describes its curved bar counter as the longest in Britain.

CLJ-WSW.text: Your train passes near the Royal Victoria Patriotic Building, on the train's {side}, built in 1859 beside Wandsworth Common as a school for girls orphaned in the Crimean War. In the Second World War it became the London Reception Centre, where 34,000 people arriving from occupied Europe were questioned to find spies among them.

CLK-ELE.text: Your train passes near the Bowie Bandstand, on the train's {side}, put up in 1905 in Croydon Road Recreation Ground and believed to be the only surviving bandstand by the McCallum and Hope Iron Foundry of Glasgow. On August 16th 1969 David Bowie helped organise, compere and perform at a free festival there.

CLK-NBC.text: Your train passes near the HSBC Sports and Social Club ground, on the train's {side}, set up in 1920 and known as the Midland Bank Sports Ground until 1992. Kent played a single one-day match there, beating Lancashire in a rain-affected game in 1970, and the River Pool runs along its western edge.

CLL-COB.text: Your train passes Gillham Wood, on the train's {side}, a Sussex Wildlife Trust reserve of oak with hazel, birch and holly. An old bomb crater in it is now a pond, and 74 kinds of bird have been recorded there.

CME-FIN.text: Your train passes near North Leigh Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, which grew from the late first century into a very large, luxurious house with 19 mosaic floors. It is in the care of English Heritage.

CME-HND.text: Your train passes near the park of Blenheim Palace, on the train's {side}, built between 1705 and 1722 and now a World Heritage Site. Winston Churchill was born there.

CNM-GCR.text: Your train passes near the remains of Greyfriars in Gloucester, on the train's {side}, a friary founded about 1231. Around 1518 the Berkeleys of Berkeley Castle paid for its church to be rebuilt.

CNM-SHU.text: Your train passes near Dean Close School, on the train's {side}, opened in 1886. Its grounds, some 50 acres, are the largest single private area of land in Cheltenham.

CNN-HHY.text: Your train passes near Canonbury Tower, on the train's {side}, the oldest building in Islington: the main surviving part of a manor house built for the canons of St Bartholomew's Priory between 1509 and 1532. Thomas Cromwell, Francis Bacon and Oliver Goldsmith were among its owners or occupants.

CNO-MDN.text: Your train passes near the church at Cattistock, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 1800s by Sir George Gilbert Scott and his son. The son's tall tower earned it the name "Cathedral of the Frome Valley".

CNO-YET.text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church in Yetminster, on the train's {side}, listed Grade I and mostly from the mid-1400s. Its faceless clock, some 300 years old, chimes the national anthem every three hours.

COB-NSB.text: Your train passes Normans Bay, a coastal hamlet on the train's {side}, called Pevensey Sluice until the railway halt opened in 1905. In 2005 divers found cannons offshore, perhaps from a Dutch warship sunk in the Battle of Beachy Head in 1690.

COE-LSK.text: Your train passes beneath Liskeard Viaduct, 150 feet high, which carries the main line. The Looe branch has run under it since 1901.

COE-SKN.text: At Coombe Junction Halt, at one end of this stretch, trains between Liskeard and Looe change direction: the driver and guard swap ends.

COH-ERI.text: Your train passes near Jarvis Brook, on the train's {side}, the village where Crowborough station actually stands; the village grew when the station opened. Its brickworks closed in 1980, and the quarry that fed them became a local nature reserve in 2009.

COO-FZP.text: Your train passes near Cannoncourt Farm Pit, on the train's {side}, old gravel pits where Stone Age tools were found in the early 1900s, among them the largest hand axe ever found.

COP-MRD.text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary the Virgin at Down St Mary, on the train's {side}, listed Grade I and rebuilt in the 1400s. One of the two old crosses in its churchyard was found being used as a paving slab in Bow, and put back up between 1897 and 1909.

COP-YEO.text: Your train passes Copplestone Cross, on the train's {side}, an ancient carved granite pillar listed Grade I, standing where three old parishes meet.

CPM-MKM.text: Your train passes near the Yelde Hall in Chippenham's Market Place, on the train's {side}, built in about 1450 and once the meeting place of Chippenham Borough Council. It is listed Grade I.

CPM-SWI.text: Your train passes near STEAM, the Museum of the Great Western Railway, on the train's {side}. It is in a workshop of Swindon Works, built around 1842 with stone from Box Tunnel.

CPN-UMB.text: Your train passes near Umberleigh House, on the train's {side}, a Georgian farmhouse listed Grade I with the ruins of the medieval chapel of the Holy Trinity beside it. The Devon historian Tristram Risdon wrote that the site was once a palace of the Saxon king Æthelstan.

CPT-HAC.text: Your train passes near the Clapton Cinematograph Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened on December 16th 1910 and one of the earliest purpose-built cinemas in London. It was built after new safety rules of 1909, as film then was highly flammable, and seated 750.

CPT-TOM.text: Your train passes Walthamstow Marshes, on the train's {side}, one of the last pieces of near-natural wetland in Greater London. In 1909 Alliott Verdon Roe made the first all-British powered flight across them, in his Roe I Triplane; he went on to found Avro.

CPW-LYD.text: Your train passes near Offa's Dyke at Sedbury, on the train's {side}, the earthwork that roughly follows the border between England and Wales, named after Offa, king of Mercia from 757 to 796.

CRH-HGY.text: Your train passes near Railway Fields, on the train's {side}, a railway goods yard until 1967 and now a nature reserve of about one hectare. More than 200 kinds of wild flower have been recorded there, among them the Haringey knotweed, a hybrid first found in 1987.

CRH-HRY.text: Your train passes near the site of Harringay Arena, on the train's {side}, an eight-sided arena put up in eight months in 1936. It held the basketball and wrestling of the 1948 Olympics and Billy Graham's first crusade in Britain in 1954, and closed in 1958.

CRH-UHL.text: Your train passes near Whittington Park, on the train's {side}, named, like the nearby Whittington Hospital, after Dick Whittington. A large topiary cat, after his legendary pet, stands at the Holloway Road entrance.

CRN-SND.text: Your train passes near Wellington College, on the train's {side}, built as a national monument to the first Duke of Wellington. Queen Victoria laid its foundation stone in 1856 and opened it in 1859.

CRN-WKM.text: Your train passes near the Lucas Hospital, on the train's {side}, almshouses founded in 1663 for 16 elderly men from the parishes around, and listed Grade I.

CRW-IFI.text: Your train passes near the George in Crawley, on the train's {side}, once the most important coaching inn in Sussex, halfway between London and Brighton. Its inn sign, which reaches across the High Street, began as a gallows.

CRW-TBD.text: Your train passes near Tree House on Crawley's High Street, on the train's {side}, the town's original manor house, built in the early 15th century. It is named after an ancient elm that stood outside for hundreds of years, and is now home to Crawley Museum.

CRY-DFD.text: Your train passes near what is left of Dartford Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Dominican nuns founded by Edward III. Henry VIII took it for himself and turned it into a royal manor house; its gatehouse survives in a farmhouse.

CRY-SGR.text: Your train passes near the site of Crayford Stadium, on the train's {side}, a greyhound stadium that opened on September 1st 1986, built to replace the older Crayford & Bexleyheath Stadium beside it. Its last race meeting was held on January 19th 2025.

CSA-HLS.text: Your train passes through the Hilsea Lines, fortifications of the 1700s and 1800s built to guard the way onto Portsea Island, on which most of Portsmouth stands.

CSA-PTC.text: Your train passes near Wymering Manor, on the train's {side}, the oldest building in Portsmouth. The manor is first recorded in 1042, when it belonged to King Edward the Confessor.

CSB-SUO.text: Your train passes near the Cock sign, on the train's {side}, which stands over a crossroads in Sutton High Street. It was put up in 1907 as the sign of the Cock Hotel, later became a road sign and lamp post, and was listed in 2018.

CSB-WLT.text: Your train passes near Carshalton Park, on the train's {side}, now about a tenth of its original size, as the rest was sold for housing from 1892. There were deer in the park until 1898.

CSD-EFF.text: Your train passes near Chelsea Football Club's training ground, on the train's {side}. The first team have trained here at Stoke d'Abernon since 2005.

CSD-OXS.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Stoke d'Abernon, on the train's {side}, parts of which date from the 7th century. In front of the altar rail is the brass of Sir John d'Abernon, who died in 1277, one of the finest in existence.

CSH-HCB.text: Your train passes near Wilderness Island, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of almost three hectares on the island between the rivers Wandle and Wrythe in Carshalton. A fish pond survives from a public garden that was once here, and kingfishers and the rare hornet clearwing moth can be found.

CSH-SUO.text: Your train passes near Carshalton House, on the train's {side}, built around 1710 for a tobacco merchant who went bankrupt a few years later. In its grounds a water tower of about 1721 pumped water to the house and fountains, and has a bathroom still lined with Delft tiles; the house is now St Philomena's School.

CSK-GSL.text: Your train passes near Morwellham Quay, on the train's {side} across the Tamar in Devon, a river port that grew up to serve the local mines. It is now an open-air museum.

CSN-CSS.text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin's Church in Chessington, on the train's {side}, whose chancel dates from the 12th century; a chapel here is mentioned in Merton Priory's records from 1174 to 1189. When the plaster ceiling was taken down in its Victorian restoration, the date 1636 was found and the old chestnut roof revealed.

CSN-TOL.text: Your train passes near the ground of Corinthian-Casuals, on the train's {side}, an amateur club formed in 1939 by joining Corinthian, founded in 1882, with Casuals. On a tour of Brazil in the 1988 to 1989 season they played Corinthians, and Sócrates turned out for both teams.

CST-LBG.text: Your train passes near Southwark Cathedral, on the train's {side}, a place of Christian worship for more than a thousand years. It became a cathedral only when the Diocese of Southwark was created in 1905, and the building keeps the form of the Gothic church built between 1220 and 1420, though its nave was rebuilt in the late 19th century.

CSW-HNB.text: Your train passes Swalecliffe, on the train's {side}, recorded in the Domesday Book. In 1581 a farm here called Bodkin's was given to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and most of its income paid for four scholars.

CSW-WHI.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Whitstable, on the train's {side}, where there has been a church for at least 800 years. Its oldest brass remembers Thomas Brede, who died in 1444, and a priest's tomb slab still shows the outline of a chalice.

CTM-GLM.text: Your train passes near the Chatham Naval Memorial, on the train's {side}, an obelisk on the Great Lines unveiled in 1924. It names sailors and marines of the Royal Navy lost in the First World War who have no known grave, and of the three such memorials (the others are at Portsmouth and Plymouth) it's the only one on a hill.

CTM-RTR.text: Your train passes Fort Pitt, on the train's {side}, a fort built between 1805 and 1819 on the high ground between Chatham and Rochester. With the Napoleonic Wars over, it became a military hospital, from 1824 to 1857 the only General Military Hospital in England. Its surviving buildings now house a girls' grammar school.

CTN-WCB.text: Your train passes near Woodlands House, on the train's {side}, a Georgian villa built from 1774 to 1776 for John Julius Angerstein, whose art collection was bought in 1824 to form the core of the National Gallery. It was designed by the local architect George Gibson and now houses a Steiner school.

CTN-WWD.text: Your train passes near The Valley, on the train's {side}, home of Charlton Athletic since 1919. Supporters dug out the pitch themselves in an old sand and chalk pit; it now holds 27,111.

CUM-RAD.text: Your train passes near the Culham fusion research site, on the train's {side}. Its Joint European Torus began work in 1983 and in 1991 became the first reactor in the world to run on the deuterium and tritium fuel meant for future power stations.

CUS-CWX.text: Your train passes near Billingsgate Fish Market, on the train's {side}, the largest inland fish market in the United Kingdom. It moved here, by the West India Docks, from the City of London in 1982; in the 19th century, Billingsgate was the largest fish market in the world.

CUS-WWC.text: Your train passes near the Woolwich Ferry, on the train's {side}, a free vehicle and foot ferry across the Thames. A ferry has run at Woolwich since the 14th century; the free service began in 1889, and about two million passengers use it each year.

CUX-HAI.text: Your train passes near Ranscombe Farm, on the train's {side}, a working farm and Plantlife nature reserve. It is known for rare plants of farmland and chalk grassland, such as hairy mallow, ground pine and the lady orchid.

CUX-SOO.text: Your train passes Temple Manor in Strood, on the train's {side}, built in the early 13th century for the Knights Templar. When the Templars were suppressed in 1312 it passed to the Knights Hospitaller; English Heritage now opens it to visitors.

CWH-GDH.text: Your train passes near Lavender Hill Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1872 with two facing Gothic chapels, one for Anglicans and one for nonconformists. Its gates were “Cemetery Gates”, the end of Stan and Jack's bus route in the sitcom On the Buses.

CWL-GMV.text: Your train runs through the Colwall Tunnel under the Malvern Hills. The first tunnel here opened in 1861; it was replaced on August 2nd 1926 by the wider one in use today.

CWL-LED.text: Your train runs through Ledbury Tunnel, bored through the limestone of Dog Hill and opened in 1861. It has never been widened, and carries a single track for its whole length of 1,323 yards.

CWN-HEV.text: Your train passes near Markbeech, on the train's {side}, a small village on the northern ridges of the High Weald, in the parish of Hever, whose castle was the childhood home of Anne Boleyn.

CWU-WLD.text: Your train passes near the site of St Leonards West Marina station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1846 and caught up in a feud between two rival railway companies over the way into Hastings. It closed in 1967.

CWX-ZLW.text: Your train passes near St Anne's Limehouse, on the train's {side}, designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor and consecrated in 1730. Being so close to the river, it was given the right to fly the White Ensign of the Royal Navy.

CYP-GIP.text: Your train passes near the Crystal Palace transmitting station, on the train's {side}, the main television transmitter for London, on the site of a television station run by John Logie Baird from 1933. Standing on a hill 109 metres high, it is the highest structure above sea level in London.

CYP-NWD.text: Your train passes near the Church of St John the Evangelist, Upper Norwood, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Gothic Revival church built from 1878 to 1887 to the designs of John Loughborough Pearson. It replaced a large iron church moved to the site in 1875 to serve the new suburb.

CYP-SYD.text: Your train passes the Crystal Palace Dinosaurs, on the train's {side}, unveiled in 1854 as the first dinosaur sculptures in the world. Designed by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins with Sir Richard Owen, they show 15 kinds of extinct animal, only three of them true dinosaurs, and are listed Grade I.

DAT-SNY.text: Your train passes near where Datchet Bridge crossed the Thames, on the train's {side}. Berkshire and Buckinghamshire argued for decades over its upkeep, and in 1836 each built its own half, one in wood and one in iron, not touching in the middle. It was pulled down in 1848.

DAT-WNR.text: Your train passes Eton College, on the train's {side}, founded by Henry VI in 1440. It is the largest boarding school in England, and has been called "the nurse of England's statesmen".

DBG-DEN.text: Your train passes near West Dean, on the train's {side}, a village with the border between Wiltshire and Hampshire running through it. A Roman villa site here lies across the border too.

DBG-ROM.text: Your train passes near Romsey Abbey, on the train's {side}, the church of a Benedictine nunnery until the Dissolution and now the largest parish church in Hampshire. Earl Mountbatten of Burma is buried there.

DCH-MTN.text: Your train passes near Max Gate, on the train's {side}, the house Thomas Hardy designed for himself. He lived there from 1885 until his death in 1928.

DCH-UPW.text: Your train passes near Ridgeway Hill, on the train's {side}, where in June 2009 archaeologists found a pit holding the remains of 54 Scandinavian men, executed some time between 970 and 1025. They are thought to have been Vikings killed by the local Anglo-Saxons.

DCW-MDN.text: Your train runs in a tunnel beneath Poundbury Camp, an Iron Age hillfort above Dorchester. Brunel wanted a cutting through it, but local outrage meant the more expensive tunnel was built instead.

DCW-UPW.text: Your train passes near Maumbury Rings, on the train's {side}, a Neolithic henge that the Romans made into an amphitheatre and the Civil War into an artillery fort. In 1846 the route planned for the Southampton and Dorchester Railway was changed to spare it.

DEA-SDW.text: Your train passes near Deal Castle, on the train's {side}, an artillery fort built by Henry VIII in 1539 and 1540 against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire. Its moated stone bastions had 66 firing positions for guns.

DEA-WAM.text: Your train passes near Old St Mary's Church in Upper Walmer, on the train's {side}, built in 1120 as the chapel of Walmer Manor. The Duke of Wellington worshipped here when he stayed at Walmer Castle as Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, and his hatchment hangs inside.

DEN-GRT.text: Your train passes near Borbach Chantry at West Dean, on the train's {side}, a chapel built in about 1333. When the church it belonged to was pulled down in 1868, the chapel was kept, and it is all that remains.

DEN-SAL.text: Your train passes near Salisbury Cathedral, on the train's {side}, built in just 38 years from 1220. Its spire is the tallest in England, and it holds one of the four surviving original copies of Magna Carta.

DEP-GNW.text: Your train passes near St Paul's, Deptford, on the train's {side}, designed by Thomas Archer and built between 1712 and 1730. It is one of the 12 churches actually built of the 50 planned by the New Church Commissioners, and the Buildings of England calls it one of the most moving 18th-century churches in London.

DEP-LBG.text: Your train runs along the viaduct of the London and Greenwich Railway, built between 1834 and 1836 and one of the oldest railway viaducts in the world. With 851 semi-circular arches and 27 skew arches or road bridges between London Bridge and Deptford Creek, it is the longest run of arches in Britain.

DFD-SCG.text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church in Dartford, on the train's {side}, begun in about 1080 by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester. A painting of St George slaying the dragon, from about 1485, can still be seen on one of its walls.

DFD-SGR.text: Your train passes near Slade Green Depot, on the train's {side}, a railway depot on Crayford marshes whose brick shed of ten roads was finished on October 27th 1899, at first under the name Whitehall, Erith. Its budget allowed for building 145 houses for railway workers.

DGC-DNM.text: Your train passes near Denham Place, on the train's {side}, a Dutch-style house built between 1688 and 1701 for Sir Roger Hill. Capability Brown landscaped its park in 1773, and later residents included members of the Bonaparte family and the American banker J. P. Morgan.

DGC-GER.text: Your train crosses the M25 on the Chalfont Viaduct, five brick arches built between 1902 and 1906, long before the motorway passed beneath. A second, longer viaduct just to the west spans the A413.

DID-SWI.text: Your train passes near the village of Uffington, on the train's {side}, where Thomas Hughes, author of Tom Brown's School Days, was born in 1822. The poet John Betjeman lived there from 1934 to 1945.

DIG-NCO.text: Your train passes near Sandy Park, on the train's {side}, home of the Exeter Chiefs rugby club since 2006, beside junction 30 of the M5.

DIG-POL.text: Your train passes near the headquarters of the Met Office, on the train's {side}. The national weather service moved here from Bracknell in 2003; it was founded in 1854 as a service to sailors.

DKG-HLM.text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary at Pixham, on the train's {side}, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens in 1903. Inside, it has a barrel-vaulted ceiling.

DKT-DPD.text: Your train passes near the Dorking Cockerel, on the train's {side}, a large sculpture of 2007 on the Deepdene roundabout. It shows a Dorking chicken, a local breed, complete with the breed's fifth toe.

DKT-GOM.text: Your train passes near Denbies, on the train's {side}, an estate bought in 1734 by Jonathan Tyers of Vauxhall Gardens. Much of its south-facing land is now planted with the vines of Denbies Wine Estate.

DLH-TOK.text: Doleham station, at one end of this stretch, is a single-platform halt that opened as Guestling Halt in 1907. It serves only a handful of houses, and before the pandemic about eight people a day used it.

DLH-WSE.text: Your train passes near Winchelsea, on the train's {side}, a town planned on a grid on higher ground after storms ravaged the old town on the shingle. Edward I granted it a charter in 1281.

DLJ-DLK.text: Your train passes near the Vortex Jazz Club, on the train's {side}, founded by David Mossman in 1988 in Stoke Newington Church Street. It moved to Gillett Square in Dalston in 2005, and the square opened the next year with a performance by 200 saxophonists.

DLJ-HGG.text: Your train passes near the Clowns Gallery and Archives, on the train's {side}, set up in 1959 in the vestry of Holy Trinity Church, Dalston, and closed since 2018. It keeps the Clown Egg Register: since 1946, clowns' face designs have been painted on eggs so that no two clowns share a face.

DLK-HKC.text: Your train passes near the Rio Cinema, on the train's {side}, which opened as the Kingsland Palace in 1909 and was rebuilt as the Kingsland Empire in 1915. F. E. Bromige gave it its Art Deco look in 1937; it was renamed the Rio in 1976, and from 1979 local people ran it as a community cooperative.

DLK-SFA.text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Tower, on the train's {side}, all that is left of Hackney's early 16th-century parish church. A working 16th-century turret clock has been inside since at least 1608, and the tower appears on the London Borough of Hackney's coat of arms.

DMH-WMN.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Old Dilton, on the train's {side}, built in the 14th century beside the Biss Brook and listed Grade I. It is now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

DMH-WSB.text: Your train passes Dilton Marsh station, opened as a halt in 1937 with no staff. A sign sent passengers to the seventh house up the hill, where Mrs H. Roberts sold tickets from her home until 1947.

DMK-PMR.text: Your train passes near the Maudsley Hospital, on the train's {side}, the largest mental health training institution in the UK. The psychiatrist Henry Maudsley offered £30,000 in 1907 towards a hospital for early and acute cases, with teaching and research.

DMP-RAM.text: Your train passes near the Montefiore Synagogue in Ramsgate, on the train's {side}, the private synagogue Sir Moses Montefiore had built on his estate, finished in 1833. He first came to Ramsgate on his honeymoon in 1812, and his mausoleum stands beside it.

DMS-EGR.text: Your train passes near the Queen Victoria Hospital in East Grinstead, on the train's {side}, where in the Second World War Archibald McIndoe pioneered reconstructive surgery for badly burned airmen. His patients formed the Guinea Pig Club here in 1941.

DMS-LFD.text: Your train passes Lingfield Park Racecourse, on the train's {side}, best known for flat racing in winter on an all-weather Polytrack rather than turf. Lingfield station adjoins the course.

DNG-KCK.text: Your train passes near the site of the Polhill Anglo-Saxon cemetery, on the train's {side}, used in the seventh and eighth centuries. It held between 180 and 200 graves; its east end was dug in 1984, ahead of work on the M25.

DNG-SEV.text: Your train passes near the Vine Cricket Ground in Sevenoaks, on the train's {side}, one of the oldest cricket grounds in England, first known to be used in 1734. The Duke of Dorset gave it to the town in 1773, for a rent of one peppercorn a year.

DNM-WRU.text: Your train passes the site of Harefield Road, a station planned in the late 1930s for the Central line's extension to Denham. The war stopped the work, and afterwards the green belt ruled out the new houses it was meant to serve, so it was never built.

DOC-DPT.text: Your train passes near Devonport Park, on the train's {side}, laid out in the 1850s on former military land.

DOC-KEY.text: Your train passes near Devonport naval base, on the train's {side}, the largest naval base in Western Europe.

DPT-PLY.text: Your train passes near Mount Pleasant Redoubt, on the train's {side}, an earthwork fort built around 1780 to guard the dockyard against a French and Spanish invasion.

DRG-WEA.text: Your train passes near the Drayton Court, on the train's {side}, opened in 1894 and a hotel until the 1940s. In 1914 Ho Chi Minh, later the leader of Vietnam, worked in its kitchens.

DUR-GBS.text: Your train passes near English Martyrs' Church in Goring-by-Sea, on the train's {side}, whose ceiling is a copy of Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted by hand by the sign-painter Gary Bevans between 1987 and 1993. The church is the same width as the Sistine Chapel, and a little shorter.

DUR-WWO.text: Your train passes near West Tarring, on the train's {side}, a village given to the archbishops of Canterbury in the 10th century, with a 13th-century Archbishop's Palace. Tradition says Thomas Becket visited, and it had a much-visited fig garden from 1745 or earlier.

DVP-FKC.text: Your train passes Samphire Hoe, on the train's {side}, a country park at the foot of the White Cliffs made from 4.9 million cubic metres of chalk dug out for the Channel Tunnel. It opened in 1997 and is named after rock samphire, which Shakespeare mentions in King Lear.

DVP-KSN.text: Your train passes the remains of Dover Priory, on the train's {side}; the railway was built across the western part of its site. Dover College uses its old buildings, and the 12th-century Strangers' Refectory is still in use.

DVP-MTM.text: Your train passes near the Maison Dieu, on the train's {side}, now the oldest part of Dover Town Hall. Hubert de Burgh, Constable of Dover Castle, founded it in 1203 as a hospital for pilgrims arriving from the Continent on their way to Becket's shrine at Canterbury.

DWL-DWW.text: Your train passes Langstone Rock, on the train's {side}, a red sandstone headland that the sea, and then Brunel's railway, cut off from the mainland.

DWL-TGM.text: As your train goes through Parson's Tunnel, the two rock stacks it is named after, the Parson and Clerk, stand just off the headland on the train's {side}.

DWW-SCS.text: Your train passes Brunel's pumping house at Starcross, on the train's {side}, built in 1845 for his atmospheric railway, whose trains ran for less than a year. It is the only complete pumping house left from the three atmospheric lines in the British Isles.

DYP-FPK.text: Your train passes near the Emirates Stadium, on the train's {side}, Arsenal's home since 2006. The club built it on an industrial and waste site at Ashburton Grove after being refused permission to enlarge Highbury; it seats more than 60,000.

DYP-HHY.text: Your train passes near Islington Central Library, on the train's {side}, opened in 1907 as the largest municipal library in London, partly paid for by Andrew Carnegie. Its architect, Henry T. Hare, was known for putting a hare somewhere in his designs.

EAD-WIM.text: Your train passes Wimbledon Traincare Depot, on the train's {side}, where South Western Railway's trains are looked after. Opened in 1974, it is one of the busiest depots in the country, with about 250 carriages maintained here each night.

EAL-WEA.text: Your train passes near Pitzhanger Manor, on the train's {side}, the country house that the architect Sir John Soane designed and built for himself between 1800 and 1804.

EAR-RDG.text: Your train passes near the centre of Reading, on the train's {side}, which a Parliamentarian army of 19,000 under the Earl of Essex besieged for 11 days in April 1643, until the Royalist garrison gave up the town.

EAR-WTI.text: Your train passes near Sol Joel Park in Earley, on the train's {side}, given to Reading in 1927 by Solomon Joel and opened by the Duke of York, later King George VI.

EBD-GRV.text: Your train passes near Baker's Hole, on the train's {side}, a filled-in quarry by Ebbsfleet. Quarrymen there found many Stone Age flint tools from 1909, and it has been called the best known site in Britain from its part of the Old Stone Age.

EBN-HMD.text: Your train passes through Eastbourne, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. The seaside resort lies just east of Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in Great Britain.

EBR-GDN.text: Your train passes near the Crowhurst Yew, on the train's {side}, in the churchyard at Crowhurst. It is thought to be about 4,000 years old; when a hollow was cut into it in 1820, a cannonball was found embedded in its side.

EBR-PHR.text: Your train passes near Jaques of London, on the train's {side}, a games maker dating from 1795 that moved to Edenbridge in 2000. In 1849 it brought out the Staunton chess set, which became the international standard.

EBT-HEV.text: Your train passes near the church of St Peter and St Paul in Edenbridge, on the train's {side}, whose oldest walls date from the 11th or early 12th century. Inside is stained glass by Edward Burne-Jones.

EBT-HUR.text: Your train passes near the Eden Valley Museum in Edenbridge, on the train's {side}, in a medieval farmhouse. Its collections include cricket-ball making, and a needlework box made by a German prisoner of war that featured in the BBC's A History of the World in 100 Objects.

ECR-SCY.text: Your train passes near Fairfield Halls, on the train's {side}, an arts centre opened in 1962 with a large concert hall often used for BBC recordings. It stands on Croydon's old "Fair Field", home to a well-known fair until about 1860, above disused railway cuttings that once led from the line to Brighton to Croydon Central station.

ECR-SRS.text: Your train passes near the "50p Building", on the train's {side}, the 24-storey tower next to East Croydon station that was first called the NLA Tower and is also known as the "Threepenny Bit". Designed by Richard Seifert and Partners and finished in 1970, it gets its distinctive look from floors with cut-off corners, set one above another at alternating angles.

EDN-ELE.text: Your train passes near Long Lane Wood, on the train's {side}, 15 acres of ancient woodland, mostly English oak with the odd beech. It was part of the Great North Wood, and has a small fenced-off bird sanctuary at the back.

EDN-WWI.text: Your train passes near the site of the Wellcome Research Laboratories, on the train's {side}. Henry Wellcome bought the 105-acre site in 1919 for £32,000, and its scientists developed the antibiotic trimethoprim; it closed in 1995, after Glaxo took Wellcome over.

EDR-SBU.text: Your train passes near the Ripaults Factory, on the train's {side}, a listed art deco building designed by A. H. Durnford for a firm that made electrical cables and parts for motor vehicles. Built in the 1930s, it has since been used by the lorry maker MAN and then a builders' merchant.

EDR-SLV.text: Your train passes near Pymmes Park, on the train's {side}, named after Pymmes House, built there by William Pymme in 1327. William Cecil, Lord Burghley, bought the estate in 1582; the council bought it for a public park, which opened in 1906.

EDW-NDL.text: Your train passes near James Allen's Girls' School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1741 and the second-oldest independent girls' school in Great Britain. It began as part of Edward Alleyn's charity, with Dulwich College and Alleyn's School.

EDW-PMR.text: Your train passes near the House of Dreams, on the train's {side}, an ordinary terraced house that the designer Stephen Wright has turned into his own art museum since 1998. It is a memorial to his late partner and his parents, and opens to visitors about ten times a year.

EFF-HSY.text: Your train passes near the Forest and the Highlands, on the train's {side}, a wood owned by East Horsley's parish council where almost 180 kinds of plant and more than 50 kinds of bird have been recorded, among them tawny owls and nuthatches.

EFL-MDW.text: Your train passes East Farleigh Bridge, on the train's {side}, probably built in the 14th century and still carrying traffic, one way at a time, over the Medway. It has been described as probably the finest medieval bridge in the south of England.

EFL-WTR.text: Your train passes Teston Bridge, on the train's {side}, a narrow bridge over the Medway built in the 14th or 15th century. The line crosses its road on the level, where Teston Crossing Halt stood from 1909 to 1959.

EGG-KGN.text: Your train passes near the gatehouse at Colleton, on the train's {side}, probably from the 1400s and listed Grade I. Its upper floor was once a chapel, licensed in 1402.

EGG-LAP.text: Your train passes near Lapford's church of St Thomas of Canterbury, on the train's {side}, listed Grade I. Inside is a late 15th-century screen, carved on both sides.

EGH-SNS.text: Your train crosses the River Thames on Staines Railway Bridge, completed in 1856. Its wrought iron girders rest on six cast iron pillars set in the river bed.

EGH-VIR.text: Your train passes near the old Holloway Sanatorium, on the train's {side}, built between 1873 and 1885 for the philanthropist Thomas Holloway to treat people with temporary mental illness. Pevsner called it and its sister, Royal Holloway College, the summit of High Victorian design; it is now homes.

ELD-RDH.text: Your train passes near the Royal Earlswood Hospital, on the train's {side}, the first establishment to care specifically for people with learning disabilities. John Langdon Down, after whom Down's syndrome is named, ran it from 1855 to 1868.

ELD-SAF.text: Your train passes near East Surrey Hospital, on the train's {side}, which began as Reigate Cottage Hospital in 1866. The present hospital opened in 1981 and was formally opened by Margaret Thatcher in 1984.

ELW-FCN.text: Your train passes near Well Hall, on the train's {side}, once a manor owned by William Roper and his wife Margaret, the daughter of Sir Thomas More. The Tudor Barn built for Roper in about 1525 beside the manor house still stands, with the moat, though the house itself was pulled down in the 1730s.

ELW-KDB.text: Your train passes near the ground of Blackheath Football Club, on the train's {side}, a rugby union club founded in 1858 by old boys of Blackheath Proprietary School. It is the oldest open rugby club in continuous existence in the world, and helped to organise the first rugby international, between England and Scotland in 1871.

EML-WMA.text: Your train passes near St James the Great's Church, East Malling, on the train's {side}, with a nave of the 14th century. Sir Thomas Twisden lies here, a judge at the trials of the regicides of Charles I.

EMS-SOB.text: Your train passes near Brook Meadow, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of grassland and woodland between two streams on the edge of Emsworth, looked after by volunteers. Its wildlife includes water voles.

EMS-WBL.text: Your train passes near Emsworth, on the train's {side}, at the head of an arm of Chichester Harbour, with a basin that fills at high tide and can be emptied through a sluice. The River Ems is named after the town, not the other way round: the chronicler Raphael Holinshed gave it the name in the 16th century.

ENC-GDH.text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels church, on the train's {side}, begun in 1873. A year later the money ran out, and the unfinished west end was closed off with a temporary wall that was not replaced until 1963.

ENC-GPK.text: Your train passes near Trinity Church, Enfield, on the train's {side}, a ragstone church with a tall spire, built for the Methodists in 1889. Badly damaged by fire in 1919, it reopened the next year; in the Second World War its basement was an air raid precautions control centre.

ENL-WLC.text: Your train passes near the Eleanor Cross at Waltham Cross, on the train's {side}, one of only three of Edward I's crosses for his queen, Eleanor of Castile, still standing. They marked where her coffin rested on its way from Lincoln to Westminster Abbey in 1290; the town is named after it.

EPS-EWE.text: Your train passes Laine Theatre Arts in Epsom, on the train's {side}, a college for dance and musical theatre founded in 1974 by the dancer Betty Laine. Victoria Beckham trained there.

EPS-EWW.text: Your train passes near Bugby Chapel in Epsom, on the train's {side}, built in 1779 by a Calvinist preacher, William Bugby. It was later a Baptist chapel and, from 1954, a synagogue; since 1994 it has been an office.

ERH-SGR.text: Your train passes near Erith Playhouse, on the train's {side}, which opened as the Oxford Cinema on July 27th 1913, showing silent films. In the Second World War it stored furniture from bombed homes, and from 1947 the volunteers of Erith Theatre Guild spent two years turning it into a theatre, mostly in their spare time.

ESD-GRP.text: Your train passes near Grove Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1935 and listed in 2003 as a Grade II landscape of special historic interest for its carefully planned 1930s layout. It holds 56 Commonwealth war graves of the Second World War, with a memorial wall in the war graves plot at its centre.

ESH-HER.text: Your train passes near Wayneflete Tower, on the train's {side}, the gatehouse of a palace built at Esher in 1462 by William Waynflete, Bishop of Winchester. Most of the palace was pulled down in the 17th century, but the tower survives, listed Grade I.

ESH-SUR.text: Your train passes near Seething Wells, on the train's {side}, where the Lambeth Waterworks opened in 1852 to take cleaner water from the Thames above the tide. It played a part in John Snow's study of cholera in London.

ESL-HDE.text: Your train passes Eastleigh Works, on the train's {side}, opened by the London and South Western Railway in 1891 to build carriages and wagons. Locomotive building moved here from Nine Elms in London in 1910.

ESL-SHW.text: Your train passes near Shawford Down, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of chalk grassland. Its slopes still show strip lynchets, terraces left from the Middle Ages, when it was ploughed as common land.

ESL-SOA.text: Your train passes Southampton Airport, on the train's {side}, where the prototype Spitfire made its first flight on March 5th 1936. A two-thirds-size model of it, K5054, stands at the road entrance.

ETC-RBR.text: Your train passes Robertsbridge, on the train's {side}, a village thought to date from 1176, when a Cistercian abbey was founded there. A 14th-century manuscript found here, the Robertsbridge Codex, holds the earliest surviving music written for keyboard.

ETC-SOG.text: Your train passes near Etchingham's 14th-century church, on the train's {side}, whose spire carries what is probably England's oldest brass weather vane. The village's medieval manor house stood where the railway now runs.

EVE-HYB.text: Your train passes the battlefield of Evesham, on the train's {side}, where on August 4th 1265 the future Edward I defeated Simon de Montfort, who was killed in the fighting.

EVE-PSH.text: Your train passes near the bell tower of Evesham Abbey, on the train's {side}, built in the 1500s. Almost all of the abbey was pulled down at the Dissolution, but the tower still stands.

EWR-LAC.text: Your train passes the site of Lancing Carriage Works, on the train's {side}, where railway carriages and wagons were built and repaired from 1911 to 1965. A special daily train, known as the Lancing Belle, brought the workers from Brighton.

EWR-WRH.text: Your train passes near Beach House in Worthing, on the train's {side}, a Regency villa built in 1820. King Edward VII stayed here several times between 1907 and 1910, and in 1936 it took in children from the Basque country, fleeing the Spanish Civil War.

EWW-SNL.text: Your train passes near Fitznells Manor in Ewell, on the train's {side}, the last surviving manor house in the borough of Epsom and Ewell. Its oldest part is a wing of a timber-framed hall house probably built in the early 16th century.

EXC-EXD.text: Your train passes near Rougemont Castle, on the train's {side}, built into a corner of Exeter's Roman walls from 1068, after the city rebelled against William the Conqueror. In 1682 the three Devon Witches, the last people in England executed for witchcraft, were tried there.

EXC-SJP.text: Your train passes near Exeter Cathedral, on the train's {side}, complete by about 1400. It has the longest unbroken medieval stone vaulted ceiling in the world.

EXD-EXT.text: Your train passes near Exeter Cathedral, on the train's {side}, complete by about 1400, with the longest unbroken medieval stone-vaulted ceiling in the world.

EXD-NTC.text: Your train passes near Cowley Bridge, on the train's {side}, a three-arched classical bridge built in 1813 and 1814 by James Green, surveyor to the county of Devon.

EXD-TVP.text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church, Cullompton, on the train's {side}, mostly 15th-century and known for its fan-vaulted Lane Aisle.

EXM-LYM.text: Your train passes near the grounds of A la Ronde, on the train's {side}, a 16-sided house built for two cousins, Jane and Mary Parminter, who came home from a tour of Europe and set up house together in Devon in 1795. It now belongs to the National Trust.

EXN-LYC.text: Your train passes the Commando Training Centre Royal Marines, on the train's {side}, the main training centre of the Royal Marines. Lympstone Commando station, opened in 1976, is there to serve it.

EXN-TOP.text: Your train passes near the Bridge Inn at Topsham, on the train's {side}, a pub since at least 1797 on a site recorded in the Domesday Book. In 1998 Queen Elizabeth II paid what was reported as her first official visit to a pub there.

EXR-HHY.text: Your train passes near Union Chapel, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed Gothic Revival church of the late 19th century that is still a working Congregational church. It is also a music venue known for its acoustics, and a drop-in centre for people facing homelessness.

EXR-OLD.text: Your train passes near Bunhill Fields, on the train's {side}, a burial ground from 1665 to 1854 that took about 123,000 burials. John Bunyan, Daniel Defoe and William Blake are among those buried there; most of it is now a public garden.

EXT-MBT.text: Your train passes near Exeter's Custom House, on the train's {side}, built in the late 17th century, the first in England built for the purpose.

EYN-SAY.text: Your train passes near Eynsford Castle, on the train's {side}, a ruin now looked after by English Heritage. William de Eynsford built it, probably between 1085 and 1087, to protect the lands of the Archbishop of Canterbury.

EYN-SEH.text: Your train passes near Lullingstone Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, first built around AD 82. In the fourth century one of its rooms became a Christian chapel or house church, the earliest known in the British Isles.

FAL-FMT.text: Your train passes near Pendennis Castle, on the train's {side}, an artillery fort built for Henry VIII between 1540 and 1542. In the Civil War its Royalist garrison held out through a long siege until August 1646.

FAV-SEG.text: Your train passes St Catherine's Church, Preston-next-Faversham, on the train's {side}. It dates from the Norman period, and John Betjeman described it as “high and distinguished among the railways and breweries”.

FAV-TEY.text: Your train passes the Maison Dieu at Ospringe, on the train's {side}, beside Watling Street. Henry III commissioned it in 1234 as a hospital and a place for pilgrims and the poor to stay, with a chamber kept for the king to rest in when he passed this way.

FAV-WHI.text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church, Goodnestone, on the train's {side}, a small Norman church of the 12th century. Its porch had to be rebuilt in 1837 after an earth tremor damaged it; it's now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

FCN-WLI.text: Your train passes near Shoulder of Mutton Green, on the train's {side}, an open space at Welling beside the old London to Dover road, named for its triangular shape. In the Second World War it held a large public air-raid shelter, and part of its entrance can still be seen near the bus stop on Bellegrove Road.

FEL-HOU.text: Your train passes near Hounslow Heath, on the train's {side}, all that remains of a heath that once spread across Feltham, Hounslow, Twickenham and what is now Heathrow. Armies camped on it, Cromwell's in 1647 among them, and in the 17th and 18th centuries it was notorious for highwaymen.

FEL-WTN.text: Your train passes the site of Feltham marshalling yard, on the train's {side}, a hump yard built with the help of about 200 German prisoners of war and opened in 1918 to sort freight for south-west London. It closed in 1969, and part of the site is being rebuilt to stable South Western Railway's trains.

FGT-IFI.text: Your train passes near Ifield Water Mill, on the train's {side}, a weatherboarded 19th-century mill on the site of an earlier iron forge. It fell out of use in the 1930s; volunteers later restored it to working order.

FGT-LVN.text: Your train passes the site of Roffey Road Halt, opened in 1907 for steam railmotors in the hope that houses would be built nearby. They weren't, and it closed in 1937; a few concrete posts from its platforms are all that remain.

FIT-PWY.text: Your train passes Stoke Gifford depot, on the train's {side}, opened in 2016 on a triangle of land between three railway lines. It looks after Great Western Railway's Class 800 trains.

FKC-FKW.text: Your train passes near the Cheriton Road sports grounds in Folkestone, on the train's {side}, home of Folkestone Invicta. Cricket has been played there since 1901, and Kent County Cricket Club has used the ground.

FKW-SDG.text: Your train passes near Saltwood Castle, on the train's {side}, which belonged to the archbishops of Canterbury until 1540. In 1953 the art historian Kenneth Clark bought it, and his son, the diarist Alan Clark, lived there later.

FLE-FNB.text: Your train passes Fleet Pond, on the train's {side}, a fishery first recorded in 1324. The London and Southampton Railway bought it for £50 in the 1830s because it stood in the way, and built an embankment across its northern end.

FLE-WNF.text: Your train passes near the Elvetham Heath nature reserve, on the train's {side}, where heather and gorse are coming back by themselves. Its wet woodland has bog myrtle, a rare plant.

FLW-HMP.text: Your train passes near Bushy Park, on the train's {side}, the second largest of London's Royal Parks, which Henry VIII made a deer-hunting ground. In the Second World War General Eisenhower planned the D-Day landings from his headquarters in the park, and herds of red and fallow deer still live here.

FLW-STW.text: Your train passes near Fulwell bus garage, on the train's {side}, built in 1902 and 1903 as a tram depot for London United Tramways. London's first trolleybuses arrived here in 1931, and it later became London Transport's main trolleybus works.

FMR-LWS.text: Your train crosses the Greenwich meridian on the edge of Lewes, a town that sits on the line of zero longitude. The Greenwich Meridian Trail, a long walk from Peacehaven to East Yorkshire, passes through the middle of the town.

FMR-MCB.text: Your train passes near Falmer Stadium, known as the Amex, on the train's {side}: home of Brighton & Hove Albion since 2011, with room for 32,500. It has also held matches in the 2015 Rugby World Cup and the Women's Euro 2022.

FMT-PNM.text: Your train passes near the National Maritime Museum Cornwall, on the train's {side}, in a harbourside building that opened in February 2003. It looks after the National Small Boat Collection, which came from the National Maritime Museum in Greenwich.

FNC-GLD.text: Your train passes near the ruined chapel on St Catherine's Hill, on the train's {side}, built early in the 14th century; the railway runs through a tunnel under the hill. J. M. W. Turner drew the hill and chapel, and in 2020 work on the line uncovered a small sandstone cave with carved niches, thought to be a medieval shrine.

FNC-GOD.text: Your train passes near Charterhouse, on the train's {side}, a school founded by Thomas Sutton in 1611 on the site of a Carthusian monastery in London. It moved here in 1872, to a hilltop site just outside Godalming.

FNN-NCM.text: Your train passes near Farnborough Hill, on the train's {side}, a house built for the publisher Thomas Longman and bought in 1880 by the exiled Empress Eugénie of France. It is now a girls' school.

FNR-LGF.text: Your train crosses the viaduct at South Darenth, built in 1859 and 1860 to a design by Joseph Cubitt. It has ten arches, each about 20 metres high, and one of them spans the River Darent.

FNR-SAY.text: Your train passes near St John's Jerusalem, on the train's {side}, set up in 1199 by the Knights Hospitaller. Its 13th-century chapel and a garden moated by the River Darent belong to the National Trust and are open to the public.

FNT-HON.text: Your train passes near Pomeroy Wood, on the train's {side}, where a Roman military site, probably a fort or a marching camp, was found when the A30 was improved in the 1990s. Its garrison seems to have included cavalry.

FNT-WHM.text: Your train passes near Whimple, on the train's {side}, home of Whiteway's cider until 1985. The village is still surrounded by cider apple orchards.

FNY-HDH.text: Your train passes near Keats House, on the train's {side}, where the poet John Keats lodged from 1818 to 1820. According to his friend Charles Brown, 'Ode to a Nightingale' was written under a plum tree in the garden, and here Keats fell in love with Fanny Brawne, who lived next door.

FNY-WHD.text: Your train passes near JW3, on the train's {side}, the Jewish Community Centre London, opened on Finchley Road in 2013. Its name plays on its postcode, NW3, and the idea came from Vivien Duffield's visit to a Jewish community centre in Manhattan in 2003.

FOD-LIT.text: Your train passes near St Mary Magdalene's Church at Tortington, on the train's {side}, founded in the 12th century and little changed since. Its chancel arch and doorway are carved with rare beakhead figures, described as "grotesque, boggle-eyed monsters".

FOG-MNP.text: Your train passes near Manor Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1874. Among those buried here are Jack Cornwell, who was given the Victoria Cross after his death, and Sarah Chapman, a leader of the matchgirls' strike of 1888 at Bryant & May.

FOG-MYL.text: Your train passes near the Cart and Horses, on the train's {side}, a pub at Maryland Point that moved here in about 1805. The heavy metal band Iron Maiden played here from 1976, with its founder Steve Harris, and a sign at the pub has called it the band's birthplace.

FOG-WGR.text: Your train passes near Woodgrange Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened on February 12th 1889 on land owned by the Marquess of Salisbury. The local MP objected to it in the House of Commons, as two other cemeteries were already close by.

FOH-HPA.text: Your train passes near the Horniman Museum, on the train's {side}, opened in 1901 by the tea trader Frederick Horniman for his collection of some 30,000 objects. Designed by Charles Harrison Townsend, it is known for its natural history displays and musical instruments, and it was Museum of the Year in 2022.

FOH-SYD.text: Your train passes near Mayow Park, on the train's {side}, opened in 1878 as Sydenham Recreation Ground on land owned by the Mayow family. It is the oldest park in the borough of Lewisham, and the tea merchant Frederick Horniman was on the committee formed to find the money and the land for it.

FPK-HGY.text: Your train passes near New Beacon Books, on the train's {side}, founded in 1966 by John La Rose and Sarah White as the first Caribbean publishing house in England. Its bookshop has been at 76 Stroud Green Road since 1973, with the George Padmore Institute on the floors above.

FRM-PTC.text: Your train passes near Cams Hall, on the train's {side}, a Palladian mansion of about 1770 overlooking Portsmouth Harbour. Listed as derelict in 1989, it was restored in the 1990s.

FRM-SNW.text: Your train passes near Titchfield Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1222. After the abbey was closed in 1537 it became a mansion, later the home of Henry Wriothesley, a patron of Shakespeare.

FRO-PEW.text: Your train passes near Swanborough Tump, on the train's {side}, a mound where King Aethelred and his brother, the future Alfred the Great, met in 871 on their way to fight the Danes.

FRO-WSB.text: Your train passes near Berkley House, on the train's {side}, home of Squire Thomas Prowse, who built the church of St Mary beside it in 1751. The church has a glazed cupola over its nave.

FRT-TBW.text: Your train passes near the Pantiles in Tunbridge Wells, on the train's {side}, a Georgian colonnade leading from the iron-rich spring, found in 1606, that gave the town its name. In summer, costumed 'dippers' serve the water to visitors.

FRT-WAD.text: Frant station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1851. It stands in the hamlet of Bells Yew Green, about two kilometres from the village of Frant itself.

FSG-PLD.text: Your train passes near Portslade Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1928 as the Ronuk Hall, a social club for the workers of a local polish factory. It later became the meeting place of the town's council.

FSG-SWK.text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels Church in Southwick, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 12th and 13th centuries with some Anglo-Saxon work still in place. A church may have stood here as early as the 10th century.

FST-LHS.text: Your train passes near the Tower of London, on the train's {side}, founded towards the end of 1066 as part of the Norman Conquest. Its White Tower was built by William the Conqueror, and over the centuries the Tower has been a royal palace, an armoury, a treasury, a menagerie and the home of the Royal Mint.

FTN-HLS.text: Your train passes near Fratton Park, on the train's {side}, home of Portsmouth Football Club since 1899. Being on Portsea Island, it is the only professional English football ground not on the mainland of Great Britain.

FTN-PMS.text: Your train passes near Portsmouth Guildhall, on the train's {side}, built in 1890 as the town hall. It was badly damaged by bombing in the Second World War and largely rebuilt in the 1950s.

FZP-MAI.text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church at Boyne Hill in Maidenhead, on the train's {side}, completed in 1857 and one of the finest early works of the architect G. E. Street. It is listed Grade I.

GCR-LYD.text: Your train passes near Gloucester Cathedral, on the train's {side}. Edward II was buried there in 1327, and it stood in for Hogwarts in the Harry Potter films.

GCR-SHU.text: Your train passes near the centre of Gloucester, on the train's {side}, which held out against Charles I's army for nearly four weeks in 1643, until a Parliamentarian army under the Earl of Essex arrived and the siege was lifted.

GDN-NUF.text: Your train passes near Lyttel Hall at Nutfield, on the train's {side}, bought in 1948 for the Brewing Industry Research Foundation. Its squash court became a pilot brewery, and brewing research went on there until 2024.

GER-SRG.text: Your train passes near Jordans, on the train's {side}, whose Quaker meeting house was built in 1688 and is one of the oldest in the country. William Penn, the founder of Pennsylvania, is buried in its burial ground.

GFD-SGN.text: Your train passes Greenford station. It was the first London Underground station with an escalator up to the platforms, and until 2014 it had the last wooden escalator on the Underground.

GIL-TIS.text: Your train passes near the park of Wardour Castle, on the train's {side}, with the ruins of Old Wardour Castle, built in the 1390s and left uninhabitable after fighting in the Civil War in 1643 and 1644.

GIL-TMC.text: Your train passes near the site of Templecombe Preceptory, on the train's {side}, founded by the Knights Templar in 1185. A face painted on oak panels in about 1280, found in an outhouse in the village, may come from it.

GIP-WNW.text: Your train passes near West Norwood Cemetery, on the train's {side}, consecrated on December 7th 1837 and one of London's "Magnificent Seven" Victorian cemeteries. Its 69 listed monuments and buildings include a Greek Orthodox burial ground with 19 listed mausoleums and monuments.

GLD-LRD.text: Your train passes near the Royal Grammar School in Guildford, on the train's {side}, founded in the will of Robert Beckingham, who died in 1509. Its Old Building, put up between 1557 and 1586, holds a rare chained library.

GLD-SFR.text: Your train passes near Guildford Castle, on the train's {side}, built soon after the Norman Conquest of 1066. Its keep still stands.

GLD-WAN.text: Your train passes near the University of Surrey, on the train's {side}, which began as the Battersea Polytechnic Institute in London in 1891 and became a university in 1966.

GLD-WPL.text: Your train passes near Guildford Cathedral, on the train's {side}, on top of Stag Hill. Designed by Edward Maufe and built between 1936 and 1961, it was the last Church of England cathedral to be consecrated on a new site.

GLM-RAI.text: Your train passes near Priestfield Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Gillingham Football Club since the club began as New Brompton in 1893. Brighton & Hove Albion also played their home games here for two seasons in the 1990s.

GLY-LWS.text: Your train passes near Mount Caburn, on the train's {side}, a 150-metre hill with an Iron Age hill fort on top. It has been dug so often, with 170 trenches, that it may have had more excavations than any other site in Britain.

GMN-WND.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Wendover, on the train's {side}. Early Wendover seems to have been centred near the church, south of today's town centre; the town was granted a market charter in 1214.

GMV-MVL.text: Your train passes near Great Malvern Priory, on the train's {side}, a Benedictine monastery from about 1075 and now the parish church. It has the largest display of 15th-century stained glass in England.

GNH-SCG.text: Your train passes near Ingress Abbey, on the train's {side}, a mansion built by the Thames in 1833 for the solicitor James Harmer. Harmer served as a model for Jaggers, the lawyer in Dickens's Great Expectations.

GNH-SWM.text: Your train passes near the Swanscombe Skull Site, on the train's {side}, an old gravel pit. In 1935 and 1936 an amateur found pieces of a human skull there, about 400,000 years old, probably from an early Neanderthal or Homo heidelbergensis.

GNW-MZH.text: Your train passes near the National Maritime Museum, on the train's {side}, created by an Act of Parliament in 1934 and based largely on gifts from Sir James Caird. King George VI opened it on April 27th 1937.

GOD-MLF.text: Your train passes near the Pepperpot in Godalming High Street, on the train's {side}, a little market hall with a clock tower and cupola, finished in 1814. Markets were held under its arches, and the room upstairs housed the town's museum from 1921 to 1987.

GOR-PAN.text: Your train passes near Basildon Park, on the train's {side}, an 18th-century house that played Netherfield, Mr Bingley's home, in the 2005 film of Pride & Prejudice.

GPK-WIH.text: Your train passes near Grange Park Methodist Church, on the train's {side}, also known as the Church in the Orchard. Designed by Charles H. Brightiff in the Art Deco style, it opened in 1938.

GPO-HDH.text: Your train passes near Parliament Hill Lido, on the train's {side}, an open-air pool first opened in 1938. It is unheated and open all year, though from September to April only for early-morning swims.

GPO-KTW.text: Your train passes over Camden Town Brewery, which began brewing in 2010 in five Victorian railway arches beneath Kentish Town West station. Its founder, Jasper Cuppaidge, first brewed at The Horseshoe, his pub in Hampstead, using one of his grandfather's recipes.

GPO-UHL.text: Your train passes Little Green Street, on the train's {side}, a tiny Kentish Town street of houses built in the 1780s, eight on one side and two on the other. It is one of the few intact Georgian streets left in London, and its houses are listed at Grade II.

GRP-SUP.text: Your train passes near Chinbrook Meadows, on the train's {side}, a park of about half a mile from north to south on Lewisham's border with Bromley. The River Quaggy flows north through it, and both the Green Chain Walk and the Capital Ring cross it.

GRT-SAL.text: Your train passes near John Halle's Hall in Salisbury, on the train's {side}, a merchant's hall of the 1400s that is now the foyer of a cinema.

GRV-HGM.text: Your train passes the Guru Nanak Darbar Gurdwara in Gravesend, on the train's {side}, one of the largest Sikh gurdwaras outside India. It opened in 2010, at a cost of £12 million.

GRV-NFL.text: Your train passes near St George's Church in Gravesend, on the train's {side}, where Pocahontas was buried in 1617. She died in Gravesend aged 20 or 21, on her way home to America; a bronze statue of her stands by the church.

GTW-HOR.text: Your train passes near the site of Gatwick Racecourse, on the train's {side}, now part of the airport. The course opened in 1891 beside the railway, and during the First World War it held a stand-in for the Grand National.

GTW-TBD.text: Your train passes near the Beehive, on the train's {side}, Gatwick's first terminal: a round building opened in 1936, when passengers came by fast train from London Victoria to fly to Paris. It is now offices.

GUN-KWG.text: Your train passes near the National Archives at Kew, on the train's {side}, the UK government's official archive, whose first building here was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1977. Its records span 1,000 years, from Domesday Book to the present, and the site was once a First World War hospital.

GUN-SAT.text: Your train passes near Gunnersbury Triangle, on the train's {side}, a patch of woodland hemmed in by three railway lines. In 1983 it became the first place in Britain where a public inquiry stopped building because of the land's value for nature, and it opened as a nature reserve in 1985.

HAC-LOF.text: Your train passes near the Hackney Empire, on the train's {side}, designed by Frank Matcham and built in 1901 as a music hall. Charlie Chaplin, Stan Laurel, Marie Lloyd and Gracie Fields all performed there.

HAC-REC.text: Your train passes near Mossbourne Community Academy, on the train's {side}, opened in 2004 on the site of Hackney Downs School. Sir Clive Bourne founded it as one of England's first city academies, and its buildings were designed by Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners.

HAF-HXX.text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 4, on the train's {side}, built for £200 million south of the southern runway and opened by the Prince and Princess of Wales on April 1st 1986. British Airways was based here until 2009, when it moved to the airport's newest terminal.

HAI-SDA.text: Your train passes Holborough Marshes, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of 35 hectares on the edge of Snodland, run by Kent Wildlife Trust. It has reedbeds and wet grassland, with water voles, reed buntings and sedge warblers.

HAM-HOL.text: Your train passes near the site of the Royal Naval Cordite Factory, on the train's {side}, set up in the First World War to make cordite for the Navy. Much of it became a nature reserve in 1981.

HAM-POO.text: Your train passes Poole Stadium, on the train's {side}, a speedway track built in the early 1930s to give the town some entertainment during the Great Depression.

HAN-STL.text: Your train crosses the Wharncliffe Viaduct over the Brent valley, Isambard Kingdom Brunel's first major design for the railway, built in 1836 and 1837. Lord Wharncliffe's coat of arms is carved on its south side.

HAN-WEA.text: Your train passes near the Kensington and Chelsea cemetery in Hanwell, on the train's {side}, opened in 1855. One of its tombs, for the shell expert Edgar Smith, is decorated with a large conch shell.

HAV-RLN.text: Your train passes the remains of Rowland's Castle, on the train's {side}, a motte-and-bailey castle built at some time between 1066 and 1189, where Henry II spent several days hunting. The railway and quarrying damaged the site in the 19th century, and only earthworks and a few bits of wall are left.

HAV-WBL.text: Your train passes near Warblington Castle, on the train's {side}, a moated manor built between 1515 and 1525 for Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury. Most of it was destroyed in the Civil War, and only a gate tower, part of a wall and a gateway still stand.

HAY-HXX.text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 1, on the train's {side}, designed by Frederick Gibberd and opened by Queen Elizabeth II in April 1969, when it was the largest new airport terminal in western Europe. It closed in 2015 to make way for a bigger Terminal 2.

HAY-STL.text: Your train passes near Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, on the train's {side}. When it opened in 2003, Guinness World Records named it the largest Sikh temple outside India.

HAY-WDT.text: Your train passes near the Old Vinyl Factory, on the train's {side}: EMI's old record works, which pressed vinyl records from 1952 until the 1970s.

HBN-HRM.text: Your train passes within a kilometre of the parkland of Leeds Castle, on the train's {side}. The castle stands on islands in a lake made by the River Len; Henry VIII used it as a home for his first wife, Catherine of Aragon.

HCB-MIJ.text: Your train passes near BedZED, the Beddington Zero Energy Development, on the train's {side}. Designed by the architect Bill Dunster and built from 2000 to 2002, its 82 homes made up the first large community designed to give off no carbon emissions, and it was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2003.

HCN-PLC.text: Your train passes near Headcorn Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, a grass airfield that opened in 1943 as RAF Lashenden, a name chosen to confuse the enemy. Today it is home to Kent's only skydiving club.

HCN-SPU.text: Your train passes near Headcorn's parish church, on the train's {side}. By its south door are the remains of the Headcorn Oak, said to be up to 1,200 years old, though one expert reckoned it nearer 500.

HDL-HRW.text: Your train passes near Kodak's former Harrow works, on the train's {side}, opened in 1891 as the company's first factory outside the United States. At its peak in the mid-20th century it employed up to 6,000 people; film-making ended in 2005 and the plant closed in 2016.

HDL-HTE.text: Your train passes Hatch End station, rebuilt in 1911 to a design by the architect Gerald Horsley. It opened as Pinner, and took its present name in 1956; Bakerloo line trains called here from 1917 until 1982.

HDM-PRR.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Haddenham, on the train's {side}, of 12th-century Norman origin. Haddenham is one of only three wychert villages in England, with walls built of white clay mixed with straw.

HDN-SBP.text: Your train passes near the Ace Cafe, on the train's {side}, opened in 1938 for traffic on the new North Circular Road and famous in motorcycle culture. It closed in 1969 and reopened on the same site in 1997.

HDN-WIJ.text: Your train passes near Our Lady of Willesden Church, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church built from 1929 to 1931 in the Romanesque Revival style. It houses a shrine to Our Lady of Willesden, whose statue dates from 1892.

HDW-NBA.text: Your train passes near Monken Hadley Common, on the train's {side}, a wedge of common land between Monken Hadley and Cockfosters. It is a remnant of the royal forest of Enfield Chase, enclosed by an Act of Parliament in 1777.

HER-WAL.text: Your train passes near Ashley Park, on the train's {side}, where a grand country house stood from 1605 until the early 1920s. Its owners included the Duke of Dorset and members of the Sassoon family; its grounds are now streets of detached houses.

HFD-LED.text: Your train passes near Hereford Cathedral, on the train's {side}, home of the Mappa Mundi, a map of the world made around 1300, and of the largest library of chained books in the world.

HGD-KIT.text: Your train passes near the church of St Mark and St Luke at Avington, on the train's {side}, an unspoilt Norman church listed Grade I.

HGG-HOX.text: Your train passes near Hoxton Hall, on the train's {side}, built as MacDonald's Music Hall in 1863. It lost its licence in 1871 after complaints by the police, and was later a Quaker meeting house for many years, which is why its galleried auditorium survives largely as it was built.

HGM-SOO.text: Your train runs through the Higham and Strood tunnel, 3.5 km long, dug by hand for the Thames and Medway Canal. From 1845 trains shared it with the barges, on a single track resting partly on the towpath. In 1846 the railway bought the tunnel, filled in the canal and laid two tracks.

HGR-LEE.text: Your train passes near the River Quaggy, on the train's {side}, which rises near Locksbottom and joins the River Ravensbourne near Lewisham station. In its upper reaches, through countryside near Chislehurst, it is known as the Kyd Brook.

HGS-ORE.text: Your train passes near Hastings Castle, on the train's {side}, begun in 1066 on William of Normandy's orders, before the Battle of Hastings. It stands on the West Hill cliffs, and large parts of it have fallen into the sea.

HGS-SLQ.text: Your train passes near Hastings Museum and Art Gallery, on the train's {side}, founded in 1892. Its Durbar Hall was part of an Indian palace built for the Indian and Colonial Exhibition of 1886.

HGY-HRN.text: Your train passes near Konk, on the train's {side}, the recording studio the Kinks set up in Hornsey in the early 1970s, a mile from their home ground of Muswell Hill. Ray and Dave Davies paid for it partly with money from hits such as 'Lola', and the band recorded there full-time from about 1973.

HHE-WVF.text: Your train passes near Muster Green in Haywards Heath, on the train's {side}, where Parliamentarians beat a larger Royalist army in December 1642. It was the furthest any large Royalist force got into Sussex during the Civil Wars.

HIB-TBW.text: Your train passes near Trinity Theatre in Tunbridge Wells, on the train's {side}, which was Holy Trinity Church from 1829 to 1972. Decimus Burton designed it, in sandstone from Calverley Quarry; it is now a theatre and arts centre.

HIB-TON.text: Your train passes near Tonbridge Castle, on the train's {side}, first built after the Norman Conquest to guard the crossing of the River Medway. Its twin-towered gatehouse took 30 years to build and was finished in 1260.

HIG-WOR.text: Your train passes near the Helicopter Museum, on the train's {side}, with more than 80 helicopters and autogyros from around the world. It began as the private collection of the aviation writer Elfan ap Rees and opened to the public in 1978.

HIG-WSM.text: Your train passes near the Tropicana, a disused lido in Weston-super-Mare, on the train's {side}, where Banksy secretly built Dismaland, his "bemusement park", in 2015. It was open for 36 days and had 150,000 visitors.

HKC-HMN.text: Your train passes near Sutton House, on the train's {side}, built in 1535 by Sir Ralph Sadler, Henry VIII's Principal Secretary of State. The oldest home in Hackney, it is a rare red-brick Tudor house and belongs to the National Trust.

HKW-HMN.text: Your train passes near St Mary of Eton church, on the train's {side}, built in 1890 to 1892 for a mission that Eton College set up in Hackney Wick, to help local people and show its pupils how they lived. The 59 Club, a Church of England youth club, was founded there.

HKW-SRA.text: Your train passes near the London Aquatics Centre, on the train's {side}, designed by Zaha Hadid for the swimming and diving at the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Under its wave-like roof are two swimming pools and a diving pool; it opened to the public in 2014.

HLB-SEV.text: Your train passes near Knole Park, on the train's {side}, a deer park of 1,000 acres. Its house, Knole, was once an archbishop's palace and is one of the five largest houses in England; the National Trust owns it.

HLB-TON.text: Your train passes the site of Tonbridge Priory, on the train's {side}, founded in 1124. Its last remains were demolished in 1842 when the South Eastern Railway came through, and Tonbridge's first station was built on the site.

HLM-OLY.text: Ockley station, at one end of this stretch, opened as Ockley & Capel in 1867. Next to brickworks, it carried bricks for many years, and milk until the 1930s; it is listed Grade II.

HMC-THD.text: Your train passes near Hampton Court Palace, on the train's {side}. Building began in 1514 for Cardinal Wolsey, who gave it to Henry VIII in 1529; in the 1690s William III rebuilt much of it to rival the Palace of Versailles.

HMD-PEV.text: Your train passes near Stone Cross Windmill, on the train's {side}, built in 1876 and worked by wind until 1937. It was a lookout post in the Second World War, and after a long restoration it was making wholemeal flour again in 2000.

HMD-PLG.text: Your train passes through Hampden Park, a suburb of Eastbourne on the train's {side}. Trains on the East Coastway Line often pass through its station twice, and its level crossing is thought to be one of the busiest in Europe.

HME-NTL.text: Your train passes near the chapel of the Royal Victoria Hospital, on the train's {side}, a military hospital begun in 1856. Its main building was the longest in the world when finished; all but the chapel and one other building were knocked down in 1966.

HMN-SFA.text: Your train passes near V&A East, on the train's {side}, the Victoria and Albert Museum's outpost in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. Its storehouse opened in May 2025 and its museum on April 18th 2026, the V&A's sixth site.

HMP-KMP.text: Your train passes near the Kempton Park waterworks, on the train's {side}, home to two triple-expansion steam engines of the late 1920s that each weigh more than 800 tons. One, the Sir William Prescott, still runs: the largest working engine of its kind in the world.

HMW-KNG.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Kingston Railway Bridge, built in 1907 to replace a cast-iron bridge of 1863. Three of its five arches span the river, and the other two are over dry land.

HMW-TED.text: Your train passes near Normansfield, on the train's {side}, opened in 1868 by Dr John Langdon Down, after whom Down syndrome is named, as a home for children with learning disabilities. Its Victorian theatre opened in 1879, and the building now houses the Langdon Down Museum of Learning Disability.

HNA-NWM.text: Your train passes near Chewton Glen, on the train's {side}, now a hotel. Captain Frederick Marryat stayed there in the 1840s while writing The Children of the New Forest.

HND-OXF.text: Your train passes near St Barnabas Church in Jericho, Oxford, on the train's {side}, built like an Italian basilica with a bell tower. It appears in Thomas Hardy's Jude the Obscure, and John Betjeman wrote a poem about it.

HNH-TUH.text: Your train passes near the South London Botanical Institute, on the train's {side}, founded in 1910 by Allan Octavian Hume in a large Victorian house on Norwood Road. It has changed little since, keeping its library, a herbarium of pressed plants and a small botanic garden with more than 500 species.

HNH-WDU.text: Your train passes the Half Moon, on the train's {side}, a corner pub of 1896 that is one of only 270 pubs on CAMRA's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors. The poet Dylan Thomas drank there, and for nearly 50 years it was a live music venue: U2 played there three times in 1980.

HOH-MYB.text: Your train passes near Abbey Road Studios, on the train's {side}, opened by the Gramophone Company in November 1931 behind a Georgian townhouse. The Beatles were its most famous clients, working mostly in Studio Two, and the building was listed in 2010 when it was under threat of sale.
