HOH-RIC.text: Your train passes near the site of The More, on the train's {side}, a palace owned by Cardinal Wolsey and then Henry VIII, where Catherine of Aragon lived in the winter of 1531 to 1532. In 1527 the French ambassador thought it more splendid than Hampton Court; nothing now remains above ground.

HOK-WNF.text: Your train passes near Hook Common and Bartley Heath, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest with large areas of wet heath, a habitat that rarely survives in the Thames Basin.

HOL-WRM.text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church in Wareham, on the train's {side}, built in about 1020: the most complete Anglo-Saxon church in Dorset. Inside is a stone effigy of T. E. Lawrence.

HOR-SAF.text: Your train passes the Archway Theatre in Horley, on the train's {side}, an amateur theatre under the railway arches of the Victoria Road bridge, built in 1909. It has a 95-seat main auditorium and stages ten main productions a year.

HOT-SHI.text: Your train passes near Henley Bridge, on the train's {side}, built in 1786 with five stone arches across the Thames.

HOU-ISL.text: Your train passes near Worton Hall, on the train's {side}, a house of 1783 that became a film studio in 1914. Alexander Korda made Things to Come here in 1936, from H. G. Wells's screenplay; the studios closed in 1952.

HOU-WTN.text: Your train passes near the site of Whitton Park, on the train's {side}, the estate of the 3rd Duke of Argyll, whom Horace Walpole nicknamed the Treemonger. After his death in 1761 many of his trees went to the Princess of Wales's new garden at Kew; a black locust planted there in 1762 still survives.

HOV-PRP.text: Your train passes near Preston Manor, on the train's {side}, a manor house rebuilt in 1738 around part of a 13th-century building. It has been a museum of Edwardian life since 1932, and is said to be one of the most haunted buildings in Britain.

HOX-SDC.text: Your train passes near the Museum of the Home, on the train's {side}, formerly the Geffrye Museum, in almshouses built in 1714 for the widows of ironmongers with money left by Sir Robert Geffrye, a Lord Mayor of London. It explores home life from 1600 to the present day.

HRH-LVN.text: Your train passes near Horsham Museum, on the train's {side}, founded in 1893 by volunteers from the town's Free Christian Church. It has been in Causeway House, a building listed Grade II*, since 1941.

HRH-WNH.text: Your train passes near the College of Richard Collyer, on the train's {side}, founded in the will of Richard Collyer, a Horsham man who became a wealthy London mercer, in 1532. The Mercers' Company are still its trustees.

HRM-LEN.text: Your train passes near Bell Farm House in Harrietsham, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed farmhouse built around 1500. Its hall wall is still blackened by smoke from the days before it had a chimney.

HRW-KNT.text: Your train passes near Harrow Skate Park, on the train's {side}, opened on July 15th 1978. It is one of only two concrete skateparks from the 1970s still in use in Britain, and its pool was modelled on one in Spring Valley, California.

HSK-PRP.text: Your train goes through Clayton Tunnel, more than a mile long and finished in 1841, the longest tunnel on the line to Brighton. Its northern entrance is turreted like a castle, with a small cottage perched on top.

HSL-LIP.text: Your train passes near Haslemere, on the train's {side}, thought to have begun as a planned town in the 12th century, with a market charter from 1221. The Dolmetsch Early Music Festival was founded here in 1925, and at the west end of Shottermill, in the same parish, Surrey, Hampshire and West Sussex meet.

HSL-WTY.text: Your train passes near Haslemere Educational Museum, on the train's {side}, founded in 1888 by the surgeon Sir Jonathan Hutchinson for his natural history collection. It holds nearly half a million specimens, artefacts, papers and images, among them the mummy of Pa-Er-Abu, thought to have been an Egyptian priest.

HUR-LFD.text: Your train passes near the church of St Peter and St Paul in Lingfield, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in 1431. Its brasses and monuments, including the tomb of Reginald de Cobham, 1st Baron Cobham, are among the finest in England.

HUR-OXT.text: Your train runs through Limpsfield Tunnel, 551 yards long, at the southern end of Oxted station. The line through it opened in 1884.

HWV-HXX.text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 5, on the train's {side}, opened in 2008 after the longest public inquiry in British history. Its main building, designed by the Richard Rogers Partnership, is the largest free-standing structure in the UK.

HWY-SDR.text: Your train passes near the Hellfire Caves, on the train's {side}, man-made chalk and flint caverns running 260 metres into the hill above West Wycombe. They were dug between 1748 and 1752 for Sir Francis Dashwood, co-founder of the Hellfire Club, which met in them.

HYB-MIM.text: Your train runs past the site of a small Roman town at Dorn, the largest of five defended towns on the Fosse Way between Cirencester and Lincoln. Here the line reaches its highest point between Oxford and Worcester.

HYD-KGS.text: Your train passes near St James' Church in Somerton, on the train's {side}. In 1512 the Crown granted the manor to William Fermor, and in the 16th century the church's south aisle became the Fermor family's chapel.

HYD-TAC.text: Your train passes near Rousham House, on the train's {side}, built in about 1635 and attacked by Parliamentary soldiers in the Civil War. Its gardens were laid out by Charles Bridgeman and then by William Kent.

HYL-SER.text: Your train passes the old offices of Harvey & Co, on the train's {side}, the foundry John Harvey set up in Hayle in 1779.

HYR-TOO.text: Your train passes near Wandle Meadow Nature Park, on the train's {side}, beside the River Wandle. Part of a sewage works from 1877 to 1970, it was proposed as a site for a Wimbledon football stadium, but local people opposed it and it became a nature reserve in 1989.

HYR-WIM.text: Your train passes near the site of Plough Lane, on the train's {side}, Wimbledon Football Club's ground from September 1912 until 1991. It was demolished in 2002, and the houses built there are named Reynolds Gate after the Wimbledon striker Eddie Reynolds.

HYS-WWI.text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary the Virgin in Hayes, on the train's {side}, built in the 12th century and much enlarged in Victorian times to designs by Sir George Gilbert Scott and his son John Oldrid Scott.

HYW-SUR.text: Your train passes near the site of Surbiton Studios, on the train's {side}, a film studio opened in 1918 whose first film came out in January 1919. It belonged to Stoll Pictures, one of the largest British film companies of the early 1920s.

IMW-WBP.text: Your train passes near Stamford Bridge, on the train's {side}, home of Chelsea since the club was founded in 1905. The ground opened in 1877 for the London Athletic Club, and its record crowd, 82,905, came to see Chelsea play Arsenal in 1935.

ISL-SYL.text: Your train passes near the Quaker meeting house in Isleworth, on the train's {side}, built in 1785 on land bought for £35. It is one of the oldest purpose-built meeting houses in London, with a Quaker burial ground and a garden around it.

ISP-OXP.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas' Church in Islip, on the train's {side}. Edward the Confessor was born in Islip and baptised in a church here; the font is now at Middleton Stoney.

IVR-LNY.text: Between Iver and Langley, your train passes from Buckinghamshire into Berkshire.
IVR-LNY.textReverse: Between Langley and Iver, your train passes from Berkshire into Buckinghamshire.

IVR-WDT.text: Your train crosses the River Colne, and about here passes between Greater London and Buckinghamshire.

IVY-PLY.text: Your train passes near Saltram House, on the train's {side}, which Nikolaus Pevsner called "the most impressive country house in Devon", with interiors by Robert Adam.

IVY-TOT.text: Your train passes near Totnes Castle, on the train's {side}, one of the best-preserved Norman motte-and-bailey castles in England.

KEM-STD.text: Your train passes near one end of the Sapperton Canal Tunnel, on the train's {side}. When it opened in 1789 it was the longest tunnel of any kind in England, and it kept the title until 1811. Boats were legged through it until 1911.

KEM-SWI.text: Your train passes near the Mechanics' Institute in Swindon, on the train's {side}, founded in 1843 to give evening classes and a library to the Great Western Railway's workers. Its building of 1854 and 1855 has stood empty since the works closed in 1986.

KEY-SBF.text: Your train passes near HMS Drake, on the train's {side}: not a ship but a "stone frigate", the naval barracks for Devonport.

KGM-MIM.text: Your train passes the site of Adlestrop station, closed in 1966. On June 24th 1914 the poet Edward Thomas's express made a stop here, and he wrote the poem "Adlestrop" about it; a station sign and a bench are now in the village bus shelter.

KGM-SIP.text: Your train passes near Bruern Abbey, on the train's {side}, where Nicholas Basset founded a Cistercian abbey in 1147. The country house there now was built in 1720.

KGN-PMA.text: Kings Nympton station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1854 as South Molton Road. It was renamed in 1951 to avoid confusion with South Molton station on the line to Taunton.

KIT-NBY.text: Your train passes near the Litten Chapel, on the train's {side}, an early 16th-century chapel of Newbury's medieval St Bartholomew's hospital, with finely carved timber roof trusses.

KLY-PUR.text: Your train passes near Foxley Wood, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve of more than 11 hectares, partly ancient woodland of oak and ash, with patches of chalk grassland. The local council bought it in the 1930s to keep it as Green Belt, and badgers and roe deer live there.

KLY-WHY.text: Your train passes near Whyteleafe, on the train's {side}, a village in a dry valley of the North Downs with three railway stations on two lines. It takes its name from the whitebeam trees that grow here, whose leaves are white underneath.

KML-NGT.text: Your train passes Bobbing, on the train's {side}. In 1673 the local squire made Titus Oates, later the inventor of the Popish Plot, vicar here, but his drunkenness and blasphemy so horrified the parishioners that they put him out before the end of the year.

KML-SIT.text: Your train passes Kemsley, on the train's {side}, a garden village built in 1924 by Edward Lloyd for the workers at his new Kemsley Paper Mill. The narrow-gauge railway that served the mill survives as the Sittingbourne and Kemsley Light Railway.

KML-SWL.text: Your train passes near Ridham Dock on the Swale, on the train's {side}, planned to give the Sittingbourne paper mills deeper water than the silted Milton Creek. Work began in 1913; during the First World War it was used for loading ammunition, and it was finished in 1919.

KMP-SUU.text: Your train passes Kempton Park, on the train's {side}, first enclosed as a royal park in 1246; Henry VIII later hunted here. It is now home to Kempton Park Racecourse and a nature reserve.

KMS-OTF.text: Your train passes near Greatness Brickworks, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest in Sevenoaks for its Cretaceous rocks, which are rich in fossils, above all ammonites. It is private land.

KND-TAD.text: Your train passes near Tadworth Court, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed house built in 1700 in the Queen Anne style for Leonard Wessels, lord of the manor of Banstead. It is now home to The Children's Trust, a charity for disabled children.

KNG-NBT.text: Your train passes near the Lovekyn Chapel, on the train's {side}, founded by Edward Lovekyn in 1309, with later gifts from his son John and from William Walworth. It is still used by Kingston Grammar School, whose roots go back to at least the 13th century.

KNL-WIJ.text: Your train passes near Kensal Green Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1833 and one of London's 'Magnificent Seven' cemeteries. Among those buried there are the engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel and the novelists William Makepeace Thackeray and Anthony Trollope.

KNR-WIJ.text: Your train passes near Kensal Rise Library, on the train's {side}, opened by Mark Twain in 1900 on land given by All Souls College, Oxford. When it was threatened with closure, Alan Bennett, Philip Pullman and Zadie Smith were among those who campaigned to save it.

KNT-SOK.text: Your train passes near Northwick Park, on the train's {side}, for centuries part of Sheepcote Farm in the manor of Harrow. The land passed to Harrow School, and in the 1930s Middlesex County Council bought 192 acres of it from the school for a public park.

KPA-SPB.text: Your train passes near Olympia, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1886, built as the National Agricultural Hall. Its Grand Hall, with an iron roof made by Handyside of Derby, is listed at Grade II*.

KPA-WBP.text: Your train passes the site of the Earls Court Exhibition Centre, on the train's {side}, an art moderne hall built between 1935 and 1937. For decades it hosted the Royal Tournament, the Ideal Home Show and Crufts, and events of the 1948 Olympics; its demolition was finished in 2017.

KSN-SPH.text: Your train passes Lydden and Temple Ewell Downs, on the train's {side}, some of the richest chalk downland in Kent, with adonis blues and silver-spotted skippers. In June 2025 the Dover twist moth was found here, not seen in England since 1952.

KTH-PNE.text: Your train passes near the Royal Watermen's Almshouses, on the train's {side}, built in 1840 and 1841 by the Company of Watermen and Lightermen of the City of London for retired freemen and their widows. They are the oldest Victorian almshouses in Penge; the residents moved to Hastings in 1973, and the buildings became private homes.

KWG-RMD.text: Your train passes near the Palm House at Kew Gardens, on the train's {side}, finished in 1848 and the first greenhouse built on such a scale. It was also the first large-scale use of wrought iron in a building, and many of its tropical plants are endangered or extinct in the wild.

KYN-LWH.text: Your train passes near Brislington House, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1806 as one of the first purpose-built asylums in England. Its design influenced later asylums and Acts of Parliament.

KYN-OLF.text: Your train passes near Saltford Brass Mill, on the train's {side}, the last survivor of more than 30 mills that once worked along this stretch of the Avon.

LAC-SSE.text: Your train passes near Shoreham Airport, on the train's {side}, the oldest airport in the UK. The first flight from here was in 1910, it opened officially in 1911, and its terminal is a listed 1930s Art Deco building.

LAP-MRD.text: Your train passes near the site of a Roman fort at Bury Barton, on the train's {side}, thought to be a large early fort that was followed by a smaller one.

LBG-NWX.text: Your train passes near Maltby Street Market, on the train's {side}, a weekly street-food and provisions market near Tower Bridge. The street was roughly the site of a ropewalk, in an area once known for making rigging and cable for sailing ships, and the market's yard is still called the Ropewalk.

LBG-NXG.text: Your train passes near St James's Church, Bermondsey, on the train's {side}, designed by James Savage and consecrated in 1829, one of the churches paid for under the Church Building Acts. Its spire was inspired by Sir Christopher Wren's St Stephen Walbrook, and needed an Act of Parliament of its own in 1831 to borrow more money.

LBG-SBM.text: Your train passes near Neckinger Mills, on the train's {side}, a warehouse of the tanners Bevington & Sons, completed in 1864 and named after the River Neckinger, which now runs underground. A paper mill stood here before the firm took over the site in 1806.

LEB-SRA.text: Your train passes near the Lee Valley VeloPark, on the train's {side}, with its velodrome built for the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. It also has a BMX track, a one-mile road course and five miles of mountain bike trails, and opened to the public in March 2014.

LEB-TOM.text: Your train passes near the Markfield Beam Engine, on the train's {side}, built in 1886 to pump Tottenham's sewage towards Beckton. Its flywheel is 27 feet across, and it is the only Wood Brothers eight-column engine still where it was installed.

LEE-MTG.text: Your train passes near Eltham College, on the train's {side}, a school founded in Victorian times for the sons and orphans of missionaries; David Livingstone sent his son Robert there in the 1850s. It moved here in 1912, to an 18th-century mansion called Fairy Hall that had been the Royal Naval School.

LEL-LTS.text: Your train runs beside Lelant Saltings, on the train's {side}, part of the Hayle Estuary, where the RSPB manages a nature reserve.

LEW-NHD.text: Your train passes near Telegraph Hill, on the train's {side}, once called Plowed Garlic Hill. It takes its name from a semaphore telegraph station built on top in about 1795, one of the points from which news of Wellington's victory at Waterloo was passed to London.

LEW-SAJ.text: Your train passes near Brookmill Road Local Nature Reserve, on the train's {side}, on the embankment of a disused railway: its trains stopped in 1916 and the tracks were lifted in 1929. Lewisham Council bought the land in 1979 and made it a nature reserve, with three small ponds.

LGF-MEP.text: Your train passes Longfield, on the train's {side}, recorded as Langanfelda in Saxon charters. In the mid-1940s the planner Patrick Abercrombie proposed building a new town here as part of the Greater London Plan, but other places around London were chosen instead.

LHS-SRA.text: Your train passes near Tower Hamlets Cemetery Park, on the train's {side}, one of London's Magnificent Seven Victorian cemeteries, opened in 1841 and known as Bow Cemetery. It closed in 1966 after 350,000 burials and is now a public park and local nature reserve, looked after by a friends' group.

LHS-WEH.text: Your train passes near the House Mill, on the train's {side}, a tide mill on the River Lea built in 1776 by Daniel Bisson and thought to be the largest tidal mill standing in Britain. Mills on this site are recorded in the Domesday Book, and much of its machinery survives, including four waterwheels; it is listed Grade I.

LIH-PHR.text: Your train passes the park of Penshurst Place, on the train's {side}. The house was built in 1341 for Sir John de Pulteney, four times Lord Mayor of London, and the poet Sir Philip Sidney was born there in 1554.

LIH-TON.text: Your train passes Haysden Country Park, on the train's {side}, opened in 1988 on the edge of Tonbridge. It has two lakes, Barden Lake and Haysden Water, and the River Medway runs through it.

LIP-LIS.text: Your train passes near Liss Riverside Railway Walk, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve whose footpath runs through willow and alder woodland along the route of the Longmoor Military Railway, from Liss to Liss Forest.

LIS-PTR.text: Your train passes near the statue of William III in Petersfield's square, on the train's {side}, a lead figure of the king as a Roman senator on horseback, made in about 1757 and once gilded. It first stood at the entrance to Petersfield House and was moved to the square when the house was pulled down in the 1790s.

LKE-SAN.text: Your train passes near Sandown Barrack Battery, on the train's {side}, one of the Palmerston Forts built to defend the Isle of Wight against a feared French invasion. It was built between 1861 and 1863 for £6,233.

LKE-SHN.text: Your train runs into Shanklin, whose town is on the train's {side}, a seaside resort known for its Old Village and Shanklin Chine, a wooded ravine. The poet John Keats lodged in the High Street in the summer of 1819.

LNG-SNG.text: Your train passes near the site of Bromhall Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Benedictine nuns from 1200. The Pope suppressed it in 1524, and its lands went to St John's College, Cambridge.

LNG-VIR.text: Your train passes near Longcross Studios, on the train's {side}, opened in 2006 where military vehicles were tested from 1942 to 2005 and Chobham armour was developed. The James Bond film Skyfall was made here.

LNY-SLO.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Langley, on the train's {side}. Inside is the Kedermister Library, a parish library from the 1600s still kept in the painted cupboards made for it in 1620.

LOO-SDP.text: Your train passes near the Old Guildhall in East Looe, on the train's {side}, believed to date from around 1450.

LOS-PAR.text: Your train passes near the Duchy Palace in Lostwithiel, on the train's {side}, once the centre from which the Dukes of Cornwall ran their estates.

LRB-MCB.text: Your train passes near Moulsecoomb Place, on the train's {side}, a farmhouse remodelled as a Neoclassical mansion in 1790. The council bought it between the wars, when Moulsecoomb became a large council estate, and it later became part of the University of Brighton.

LSK-MEN.text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church, Liskeard, on the train's {side}, the second-largest parish church in Cornwall.

LSY-NBC.text: Your train passes near the County Ground, Beckenham, on the train's {side}, set up by Lloyds Bank in 1918 as its main sports ground near London. It was first used for first-class cricket in 1954, hosted two matches in the 1993 Women's Cricket World Cup, and has been a regular Kent outground since 2003.

LTK-MRS.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas' Church in Great Kimble, on the train's {side}. It was in this parish that John Hampden refused to pay his ship money in January 1636.

LTS-SER.text: St Erth station, at one end of this stretch, is listed Grade II and is the junction for the St Ives Bay Line.

LUX-PAR.text: Your train passes beneath the Treffry Viaduct, built of granite by Joseph Treffry between 1839 and 1842 to carry his tramway, and water for his Fowey Consols mine, across the Luxulyan Valley.

LWH-SRD.text: Your train passes near Bristol's Northern Storm Water Interceptor, on the train's {side}: a tunnel about 16 feet across that carries floodwater from the River Frome at Eastville three miles under the city to the Avon Gorge. It was finished in 1962.

LWS-SEE.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Lewes Priory, on the train's {side}, the first Cluniac priory in England. In 1264, after losing the Battle of Lewes, Henry III retreated there and was forced to accept a council that marked the start of parliamentary government in England.

LYC-LYM.text: Your train passes near Nutwell Court, on the train's {side}, a neo-classical house of about 1800 on the bank of the Exe estuary, almost facing Powderham Castle on the far side. It was built for a nephew of the last of the Drake baronets, who had lived in the older house here.

LYP-LYT.text: Your train passes near Lymington Lifeboat Station, on the train's {side}, on the west bank of the Lymington River. The RNLI first stationed an inshore lifeboat here in 1965.

MAI-TAP.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Brunel's Maidenhead Railway Bridge, whose two main brick arches are thought to be the longest and flattest ever built. Turner painted a train crossing it in Rain, Steam and Speed (1844).

MAI-TWY.text: Your train passes near the Church of St James, Ruscombe, on the train's {side}. Its flint chancel dates from the 12th century; the nave and tower were rebuilt in brick in 1638 and 1639.

MAL-MOT.text: Your train passes near the manor house of Malden, on the train's {side}, beside St John's church and mentioned in the Domesday Book. In 1264 Walter de Merton founded a college here, which later moved to Oxford as Merton College.

MAL-TOL.text: Your train passes near Tolworth Tower, on the train's {side}, a 22-storey office block 81 metres high beside the Kingston bypass, opened in 1964. The supermarket on its ground floor, first a Fine Fare, was the largest in England when it opened.

MAR-WGA.text: Your train passes near the Royal Sea Bathing Hospital in Margate, on the train's {side}, founded in 1791 by the Quaker doctor John Coakley Lettsom to treat poor Londoners with scrofula. Its patients were given fresh air, sunshine and sea bathing, and slept on its verandas whenever the weather allowed.

MBK-RDB.text: Your train passes near the King George V Graving Dock in Southampton, on the train's {side}, opened by King George V and Queen Mary in 1933. It was then the largest dry dock in the world, and stayed so for nearly 30 years.

MBK-SOU.text: Your train passes near the Mayflower Theatre, on the train's {side}. It opened in 1928 as the Empire, and with seats for 2,300 it is the largest theatre in the south of England outside London.

MBT-SCS.text: Your train passes near Powderham Castle, on the train's {side}, a fortified manor house on the bank of the Exe estuary, listed Grade I.

MDB-MDW.text: Your train passes near the Archbishop's Palace in Maidstone, on the train's {side}, by the River Medway. It was a resting place for archbishops travelling between London and Canterbury, and work on the present building began in 1348.

MDG-THA.text: Your train passes near Midgham Lock, on the train's {side}, one of the locks built between 1718 and 1723 under the engineer John Hore of Newbury, when the River Kennet was made navigable.

MDS-SIH.text: Your train passes near St Lawrence Church, on the train's {side}, Morden's parish church, built in 1636 at the highest point of Morden, overlooking Morden Park. It is listed at Grade I.

MDS-SMO.text: Your train passes Baitul Futuh, on the train's {side}, one of the largest mosque complexes in Europe, completed in 2003 for the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community. Paid for entirely by donations, it can hold 13,000 worshippers.

MEN-SGM.text: Your train passes near St Germans church, on the train's {side}, once the seat of the Saxon bishops of Cornwall.

MEP-SOR.text: Your train passes near St Mildred's, the small 14th-century church of Nurstead, on the train's {side}, its walls built of oblong flints. A quarter of a mile north of it is Nurstead Court, called one of the most famous small medieval houses in the country.

MHM-RDH.text: Your train passes near Gatton, on the train's {side}, now just a few houses and two farms. It once sent two members to Parliament: by 1831 it had only seven voters, one of the most notorious rotten boroughs, until the Reform Act of 1832 abolished it.

MIC-WIN.text: Your train passes near the gateway of Hyde Abbey, on the train's {side}, where Alfred the Great, his wife and his son were reburied in 1110. Their remains were lost after the abbey was pulled down in 1538.

MIJ-MTC.text: Your train passes near Mitcham Cricket Green, on the train's {side}, where cricket has been played since 1685. Touring Australian teams of the 19th century stayed at the Cricketers pub, which overlooked the green, and practised on the green, and its pavilion, built in 1904, is one of the few cut off from their ground by a road.

MKC-WOL.text: Your train passes near the Concrete Cows, on the train's {side}, the replicas by the line at Bancroft of Liz Leyh's three cows and three calves of 1978. The originals, made from scrap and skinned with concrete, are now at Milton Keynes Museum.

MKM-TRO.text: Your train passes near Staverton Mill, on the train's {side}, a mill on the River Avon since the Domesday Book. Once a woollen mill and later a Nestlé milk factory, it makes breakfast cereals: Shredded Wheat and Shreddies moved there in 2007.

MLF-WTY.text: Your train passes near Tigbourne Court, on the train's {side}, a country house by Edwin Lutyens, finished in 1901 and called "probably his best" building. Edgar Horne, who had it built, never moved in, and it was let to the fraudster Whitaker Wright.

MOG-OLD.text: Your train passes near John Wesley's House, on the train's {side}, built in 1779 beside Wesley's Chapel on City Road. John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, lived there for the last 12 years of his life and died in his bedroom.

MOG-ZFD.text: Your train passes near the London Charterhouse, on the train's {side}, founded as a Carthusian priory in 1371 on the site of a Black Death burial ground. Thomas Sutton bought it in 1611 for a school and an almshouse; the almshouse is still lived in, while the school moved to Godalming in 1872.

MOG-ZLW.text: Your train passes near Christ Church Spitalfields, on the train's {side}, built between 1714 and 1729 to Nicholas Hawksmoor's design. It was one of the first churches of the commission set up in 1711 to build 50 new churches for London's new districts.

MOR-RGP.text: Your train passes Reading Green Park station, which opened on May 27th 2023, later than planned because of the Covid-19 pandemic. It serves Reading Football Club's stadium and the Green Park business area.

MOT-RAY.text: Raynes Park station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1871. Its platforms aren't opposite each other, so its long footbridge crosses the four main-line tracks at an angle.

MOT-WCP.text: Your train passes near Sir Joseph Hood Memorial Wood, on the train's {side}, a small nature reserve of oaks planted in the middle of the 19th century, probably as cover for hunting. It is named after Sir Joseph Hood, a former MP and Mayor of Wimbledon.

MRN-PDW.text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels Church, Marden, on the train's {side}, built at the end of the 12th century. The church is the picture on the village sign.

MRN-SPU.text: Your train passes Marden Meadows, on the train's {side}, three fields of unimproved grassland that are a Site of Special Scientific Interest. They are mown for hay once a year, and green-winged orchids grow there.

MRS-PRR.text: Your train passes near The Mount, on the train's {side}, now a car park but once the site of Risborough's royal manor house. The Black Prince was lord of the manor, and after his death the town became known as Prince Risberge, later Princes Risborough.

MRW-NUM.text: Your train passes near the site of Glover and Main's Gothic Works, on the train's {side}, where gas meters were made from 1897. Thomas Glover had invented the diaphragm gas meter in 1843, and the firm became one of Britain's biggest makers of gas cookers.

MRW-PON.text: Your train passes near Wright's Flour Mill, on the train's {side}, Enfield's oldest working industrial building, with parts dating from 1789. There has been a mill there since at least the late 16th century; the Wright family still own it.

MSR-SDW.text: Your train passes Richborough Roman Fort, on the train's {side}, whose walls still stand several metres high. As Rutupiae it was a main gateway to Roman Britain after the conquest of AD 43 and the start of Watling Street; the coast is now miles away.

MSR-STU.text: Your train passes near Minster Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in about 670 by the Kentish princess Domne Eafe; legend says her land was as much as her pet deer could mark out in a day. Since 1937 Benedictine nuns have lived here, beside the ruins.

MSR-THP.text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Cross, on the train's {side}, put up in 1884 to mark Augustine's arrival in England in 597. It's believed to stand where he first met King Ethelbert of Kent.

MTC-STE.text: Your train passes Oakleigh Way, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve of less than a hectare in Mitcham. It was once a railway depot and sidings, and is now birch woodland with scrub and grassland, where weld and zigzag clover grow.

MTG-NEH.text: Your train passes near the Tarn, on the train's {side}, a garden, bird sanctuary and lake among woodland between Mottingham and Eltham. The lake, once called Starbuck's Pond, was in the Great Park of Eltham Palace, a royal deer park until the Civil War; it opened as a garden in 1935 and has an 18th-century ice well.

MTL-NSH.text: Your train passes near Mortlake Brewery, on the train's {side}, where brewing is recorded as early as 1487. As it grew in the 1850s it supplied India Pale Ale to the British army in India, and it brewed Budweiser from 1995 to 2011, before closing in 2015.

MTM-WAM.text: Your train passes near Ripple Mill, on the train's {side}, a smock mill first built at Drellingore and moved here in the early 19th century, its corner posts cut in half lengthways and bolted back together. Trinity House once helped pay for repairs, as it was a landmark for ships.

MTN-WOO.text: Your train passes near Woolbridge Manor, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century house by the old bridge over the River Frome. Its two wall portraits appear in Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles as Tess's ancestors.

MTP-RDA.text: Your train passes near Redland Chapel, on the train's {side}, built in 1742 as a private chapel for John Cossins of Redland Court and listed Grade I. Now the parish church, it is unusual in having no patron saint.

MTP-SRD.text: Your train passes near St Paul's Church in Portland Square, on the train's {side}, begun in 1789 and listed Grade I. It closed in 1988 and is now Circomedia, a circus school.

MVL-WOF.text: Your train passes near Worcester Racecourse, known locally as Pitchcroft, on the train's {side}, beside the River Severn. Horses have raced there since at least 1718.

MYB-WCX.text: Your train passes near Lord's Cricket Ground, on the train's {side}, the third ground Thomas Lord opened, in 1814: his second had to go when the Regent's Canal was cut through its outfield. The pitch has a pronounced slope, running down from north to south.

MYL-SRA.text: Your train passes near Stratford East, once the Theatre Royal, on the train's {side}, a Victorian theatre that opened on December 17th 1884. From 1953 it was the home of Joan Littlewood's Theatre Workshop, which staged A Taste of Honey and Oh, What a Lovely War! there, and her statue stands outside.

MZH-WCB.text: Your train passes near East Greenwich Pleasaunce, on the train's {side}, a park that was once the graveyard of Greenwich Hospital. When a railway tunnel was built, the remains of about 3,000 sailors and officers, including men who had fought at Trafalgar, were moved here from the hospital's own grounds in 1875.

NBA-OKL.text: Your train passes near New Barnet War Memorial, on the train's {side}, built in 1921 with a bronze figure of winged victory on top. It names 277 men and one woman of the district who died in the First World War; 136 names from the Second World War were added later.

NBT-NEM.text: Your train passes near Kingsmeadow, on the train's {side}, a football ground built by Kingstonian in 1989. AFC Wimbledon played here from 2002 until 2020, and it is now the home ground of Chelsea Women.

NBY-NRC.text: Your train passes near the West Berkshire Museum, on the train's {side}, partly housed in Newbury's Cloth Hall, built in 1627 as a cloth factory.

NCO-TOP.text: Your train passes near Broadway House in Topsham, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Georgian house of 1776. In the 1800s a naval officer who lived there opened it to the public as a museum of antiquities and fossils.

NDL-TUH.text: Your train passes near Herne Hill Velodrome, on the train's {side}, built in 1891 and one of the oldest cycle tracks in the world. It hosted the track cycling at the 1948 Olympics, and Crystal Palace football club played there during the First World War.

NEH-SID.text: Your train passes near the Metropolitan Police Museum, on the train's {side}, at Marlowe House in Sidcup, where a new gallery opened in 2023. Its collection began with an appeal for objects in 1949, to mark 200 years since the Bow Street Runners, and was first kept at Bow Street police station.

NEM-RAY.text: Your train passes near New Malden's war memorial, on the train's {side}, a three-tiered cenotaph in the High Street unveiled in 1924 by a soldier who had been blinded in the First World War. It was slightly damaged in 1940 when a bomb fell close by during the Blitz.

NFL-SWM.text: Your train passes near Stonebridge Road, on the train's {side}, the football ground built in 1905 for Northfleet United. It is the home of Ebbsfleet United, and holds 4,769 people.

NGT-RAI.text: Your train passes Newington, on the train's {side}. Its parish church was built between 1163 and 1177 by Richard de Lucy, and a stone in the church car park, the Devil's Stone, is said to bear the Devil's footprint. The village also holds the national collection of witch hazel.

NGT-SIT.text: Your train passes near Watling Temple in Newington, on the train's {side}: the remains of a temple in a Roman town found during a dig in 2019, along with pottery kilns and a Roman road. A reconstruction of its foundations, the same size and facing the same way, was unveiled near the spot in 2021.

NHD-PMR.text: Your train passes near Nunhead Cemetery, on the train's {side}, consecrated in 1840 as All Saints' Cemetery. One of two of London's “Magnificent Seven” Victorian cemeteries south of the Thames, it is now a local nature reserve.

NHE-SDA.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church in Snodland, on the train's {side}, which stands where the Pilgrims' Way crosses the River Medway. It is mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086, and the church standing today was begun in the 12th century.

NLS-PSN.text: Your train passes near the park of Tyntesfield, on the train's {side}, around a Victorian Gothic house remodelled in the 1860s for William Gibbs, whose fortune came from guano. The National Trust bought it in 2002.

NLS-YAT.text: Your train passes near the Strawberries and Cream Tree in Backwell, on the train's {side}, a cherry tree with white blossom on one side and pink on the other: a wild cherry grafted with a Japanese one. Children in Backwell gave it its name.

NLT-SDH.text: Your train passes near Orley Farm School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1850 to prepare boys for Harrow School. In 1862 it took its name from Anthony Trollope's novel Orley Farm, which describes the buildings and grounds the Trollope family once owned and the school later used.

NLT-SRU.text: Your train passes the site of RAF South Ruislip, on the train's {side}, the headquarters of the US Air Force's Third Air Force from 1949 to 1972. In 1970 three teenagers whose fathers were stationed here, Dewey Bunnell, Dan Peek and Gerry Beckley, formed the band America.

NQY-QUI.text: Your train crosses Trenance Viaduct, 141 metres long, over the Trenance valley in Newquay. The first, of timber on stone piers, opened in 1849; today's masonry viaduct dates from 1939.

NRB-SRC.text: Your train passes near the Norbury Estate, on the train's {side}, a London County Council cottage estate built from 1901 to 1920 and influenced by the garden city movement. It stands on an old brickfield, whose clay was fired to make bricks for the estate.

NRB-TTH.text: Your train passes near the site of J. W. Hobbs' Ground, on the train's {side}, a cricket ground laid out in 1885 in the grounds of Norbury Hall. Its only first-class match was against the touring Australians in 1888, and cricket went on here until a leisure centre was built on it in the 1990s.

NRC-THA.text: Your train passes near Monkey Marsh Lock, on the train's {side}, a turf-sided lock from the 1720s that is now a scheduled monument.

NSB-PEB.text: Your train passes near St Nicolas' Church in Pevensey, on the train's {side}, built between 1205 and 1216 and named after the patron saint of seafarers. Its size reflects Pevensey's importance as a seaport then; the sea is now about half a mile away.

NSG-OKL.text: Your train passes near the former Friern Hospital, on the train's {side}, opened in 1851 as Colney Hatch Lunatic Asylum. At its height it held 2,500 patients and had the longest corridor in Britain; it closed in 1993 and became housing.

NSH-RMD.text: Your train passes near the Station Hotel, on the train's {side}, whose back room became the Crawdaddy Club in 1963. The Rolling Stones were its house band in its first year, followed by the Yardbirds; the club took its name from Bo Diddley's song Doing the Craw-Daddy.

NTA-TGM.text: Your train runs beside the Teign estuary, with the village of Shaldon across the water on the train's {side}.

NTA-TOT.text: Your train passes near Forde House, on the train's {side}, a manor house of about 1550, enlarged around 1610 and known for its 17th-century carving and plasterwork.

NTA-TRR.text: Your train passes near Forde House, on the train's {side}, enlarged around 1610. Charles I stayed there in 1625, and William of Orange in 1688, a few days after landing at Brixham.

NTL-SHO.text: Your train passes near Netley Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1239 for Cistercian monks, who were known for their kindness to travellers. Its ruins later inspired Romantic poets and artists.

NUF-RDH.text: Coming into Redhill, your train passes over the covered way at the end of Redhill Tunnel. The tunnel, opened in 1899, takes the Quarry Line of the Brighton Main Line under the east of the town, so that its trains avoid Redhill station.

NUM-TOM.text: Your train passes near Tottenham Marshes, on the train's {side}, part of the Lee Valley Park since 1972. Tottenham Hotspur played their first matches there, in 1882, before moving to an enclosed ground.

NUT-SOB.text: Your train passes near Southbourne, on the train's {side}, a village that began in 1876, when its church of St John was consecrated. It sits in the western corner of West Sussex, with the Hampshire border just to the west.

NVH-NVN.text: Your train passes the Port of Newhaven, on the train's {side}, where ferries sail to Dieppe in France. Newhaven was a fishing village of little importance as a port until the railway arrived in 1847.

NVN-SEE.text: Your train passes near St John's Church at Piddinghoe, across the River Ouse on the train's {side}. Its round Norman tower is one of three in the Ouse valley, the others being at Southease and St Michael's in Lewes.

NWB-SOK.text: Your train passes near the Windermere, on the train's {side}, a pub built in about 1938 and listed at Grade II. Its interior is on the Campaign for Real Ale's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors.

NWB-WMB.text: Your train passes near the Hirst Research Centre, on the train's {side}, set up by the General Electric Company and formally opened in 1923 as one of the first specialised industrial research laboratories built in Britain. In the Second World War its engineers made the cavity magnetron far more powerful, helping to make radar small enough to fit in fighter aircraft.

NWD-SRS.text: Your train passes near Holy Innocents Church, South Norwood, on the train's {side}, built in 1894 and 1895 to the designs of George Frederick Bodley, in imitation of the late Gothic Perpendicular style. The tower he planned for it was never built.

NWM-SWY.text: Your train passes Sway, on the train's {side}, which the railway reached in 1888. At the southern edge of the village stands Sway Tower, a concrete folly 66 metres tall built from 1879 to 1885, still the tallest unreinforced concrete structure in the world.

NWX-SAJ.text: Your train passes near Stone House, on the train's {side}, built between 1771 and 1773 by the architect George Gibson the younger for himself. Its design is so unusual that in the 19th century it was commonly known as the Comical House, and some maps of the time labelled it so.

NWX-SQE.text: Your train passes near SELCHP, on the train's {side}, an energy-from-waste plant that can burn up to 420,000 tonnes of rubbish a year and generate up to 35 megawatts. It grew from Lewisham, Southwark and Greenwich councils coming together in 1986 to find an alternative to landfill.

NXG-SQE.text: Your train passes near Sanford Housing Co-operative, on the train's {side}, the first purpose-built housing co-operative in the United Kingdom, which has run without a break since it opened in 1974. About 120 people live there, in a street of shared houses and studio flats run by its members.

OKE-OKI.text: Your train passes near Okehampton Castle, on the train's {side}, built between 1068 and 1086 after a revolt in Devon against Norman rule. It is now a ruin.

OKI-YEO.text: Your train passes near the site of Roman forts at North Tawton, on the train's {side}, where the Romans crossed the River Taw. The fort is thought to have been called Nemetostatio.

OLY-WNH.text: Your train passes the site of Shiremark Mill, on the train's {side}, a windmill built in 1774 just inside Surrey, close to the border with Sussex. It worked by wind until 1919, and burnt down in 1972.

ORE-TOK.text: Your train passes near Speckled Wood, on the train's {side}, a steep-sided, wet woodland park in Ore. It is thought to take its name from the speckled wood butterflies that thrive there.

ORP-PET.text: Your train passes Orpington's former engine shed, beside the line just north of the station, where the main line's four tracks narrow to two at the end of the suburban belt. The steam depot had a 55-foot turntable; after electrification it closed and became offices for train drivers, and since 2007 it has held a training centre with a driving simulator.

OTF-SEH.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Otford Palace, on the train's {side}, rebuilt by Archbishop Warham from 1514. Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon stayed there in 1520 on their way to the Field of the Cloth of Gold, and in 1537 Henry made Archbishop Cranmer hand it over to the Crown.

OVR-WCH.text: Your train passes near Laverstoke Mill, on the train's {side}. From the 1720s the Portals made the paper for Bank of England banknotes here; it is now the Bombay Sapphire gin distillery.

OXF-OXP.text: Your train passes near the Radcliffe Observatory, on the train's {side}, Oxford University's observatory from 1773 until 1934. Its octagonal tower is based on the Tower of the Winds in Athens and is topped by a statue of Atlas holding up the world.

OXF-RAD.text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin, Iffley, on the train's {side}, built in the second half of the 12th century and one of the best-preserved Norman churches in England.

OXF-TAC.text: Your train passes Port Meadow, on the train's {side}, a great stretch of common grazing land beside the Thames. The Freemen of Oxford's right to graze their animals here free of charge is recorded in the Domesday Book, and has been used ever since.

OXT-WOH.text: Your train runs through Oxted Tunnel, more than a mile long. It was dug in the 1860s, but work on the line stopped in 1869 and it did not open until 1884.

PAL-WIH.text: Your train passes near the Intimate Theatre, on the train's {side}, the name long used for St Monica's church hall on Green Lanes. The actor John Clements made it a theatre in 1935; Roger Moore later acted in its repertory company, and David Bowie appeared on its stage in 1968.

PAN-TLH.text: Your train passes near Mapledurham Watermill, on the train's {side} across the Thames, the last working watermill on the river.

PAR-SAU.text: Your train passes near Charlestown harbour, on the train's {side}, a port that grew in the late 18th century from the fishing village of West Polmear and has changed little since.

PDW-TON.text: Your train passes near Somerhill House, on the train's {side}, a Jacobean mansion built from 1611 to 1613 for the Earl of Clanricarde. Turner painted it in 1811, and it is now a school.

PEB-PEV.text: Your train passes near Pevensey Castle, on the train's {side}, a Roman fort called Anderitum built around 290 AD. The Normans reoccupied it in 1066 and built a castle inside its walls; it was besieged several times but never taken by storm.

PEW-TRO.text: Your train passes near St James's Church in Trowbridge, on the train's {side}, built in the 1400s. The poet George Crabbe, rector from 1814 to 1832, is buried there.

PEW-WSB.text: Your train passes near Edington Priory church, on the train's {side}, built by William Edington, Bishop of Winchester, and consecrated in 1361.

PGN-TQY.text: Your train passes near Oldway Mansion, on the train's {side}, built for the sewing-machine maker Isaac Singer and rebuilt by his son Paris in the style of the Palace of Versailles.

PIL-PWY.text: Your train passes near The Wave, on the train's {side}, an artificial lake for surfing that opened in 2019, with wave machines from the Spanish company Wavegarden.

PIL-STJ.text: Your train passes near Severn Beach, on the train's {side}, farmland until the railway came. In the 1920s it became a seaside resort for Bristol, with an open-air pool called the Blue Lagoon, a boating lake and donkey rides.

PIN-SJP.text: Your train passes near Exeter's underground passages, on the train's {side}, built to bring water into the medieval city. The oldest date from the 1200s, and you can take a guided tour.

PKS-POO.text: Your train passes near Scaplen's Court, on the train's {side}, a merchant's house of the late 1400s built of Purbeck and Bath stone and cobbles from Poole Quay. It is now a museum.

PLU-WWA.text: Your train passes near the site of the Manor Ground, on the train's {side}, home from 1888 of Royal Arsenal, the club that became Arsenal. The pitch was famously muddy, and with no stands, wagons borrowed from army bases nearby held the crowds.

PMA-UMB.text: Your train passes near Brightley Barton, on the train's {side}, on a hillside above the River Taw. From the early 1500s to 1715 it was the seat of the Giffard family, and the medieval stone walls of their house's moat still survive, a great rarity in North Devon.

PMH-PMS.text: Your train passes near HMS Warrior, on the train's {side}. Built in 1859 to 1861, she and her sister ship were the first armour-plated, iron-hulled warships. For more than 50 years she served as an oil jetty.

PMP-WVF.text: Your train passes near Plumpton Racecourse, on the train's {side}, where racing began in 1884. The Queen Mother had her first winner here in 1963, and AP McCoy won his 3,000th race here in 2009.

PMR-QRP.text: Peckham Rye station, at one end of this stretch, opened on December 1st 1865 and was designed by Charles Henry Driver, the architect of the Abbey Mills and Crossness pumping stations. Its platforms are on two separate viaducts, with a single ticket hall at ground level.

PNE-SYH.text: Your train passes near Six Pillars, on the train's {side}, a modernist house built from 1932 to 1934 for John Leakey, headmaster of Dulwich College Preparatory School. Its architect, Valentine Harding of the Tecton group, based it on Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye, but used London stock brick so it wouldn't stand out among its Victorian neighbours.

PNM-PYN.text: Your train crosses Collegewood Viaduct, 954 feet long. When it was rebuilt in stone in 1934, it was the last timber viaduct in Cornwall to be replaced; the piers of the old one still stand.

PNW-SYD.text: Your train passes near St Christopher's Hospice, on the train's {side}, founded in 1967 by Cicely Saunders, whose work is the basis of the modern hospice movement. Its early staff began the first hospice home care, and one of them, Florence Wald, took the idea to the United States.

PNZ-SER.text: Your train passes near Penzance Heliport, on the train's {side}, where helicopters to the Isles of Scilly started flying again in 2020 after an eight-year gap.

POL-SJP.text: Your train passes near what remains of Polsloe Priory, on the train's {side}, a Benedictine nunnery founded around 1159. At the time it was the only religious house for women in Devon.

PRI-SHH.text: Your train passes near the Avonmouth Bridge, on the train's {side}, which carries the M5 over the River Avon. It is 4,554 feet long, with a main span of 538 feet.

PRR-SDR.text: Your train passes near Saunderton's church of St Mary and St Nicholas, on the train's {side}. It took its second saint in 1452, when the village's other church, St Nicholas, was pulled down After its walls began to lean in 1886 it was largely taken down and rebuilt.

PRW-PYN.text: Your train crosses Ponsanooth Viaduct over the River Kennal. At 139 feet high, it is the tallest viaduct west of Truro.

PRW-TRU.text: Your train crosses Carnon Viaduct, 96 feet high, over Restronguet Creek. The first viaduct here had timber on stone piers; a new stone viaduct replaced it in 1933.

PSH-WOP.text: Your train passes near Mucknell Abbey, on the train's {side}, an Anglican Benedictine monastery of monks and nuns on what was a farm. The community moved here from Burford Priory.

PTR-RLN.text: Your train passes near St Hubert's Church at Idsworth, on the train's {side}, the only place of worship of an isolated hamlet in the South Downs, with medieval paintings on its north wall and around the east window. The diocese calls it "the little church in the field".

PUO-PUR.text: Your train passes near Purley War Memorial Hospital, on the train's {side}. It began as a cottage hospital with eight beds, opened by Princess Helena, and after the First World War it reopened in 1922 as the district's war memorial hospital, with 22 beds.

PUO-SCY.text: Your train passes near Whitgift School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1596 by John Whitgift, Archbishop of Canterbury, and opened in 1600. It moved here in 1931 to Haling Park, once the home of Lord Howard of Effingham, who commanded the English fleet against the Spanish Armada.

PUR-RHM.text: Your train passes near the former Purley Council Offices, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Neo-Georgian building that cost £30,000. The Lord Mayor of London opened it on November 8th 1930 as the headquarters of the Coulsdon and Purley Urban District Council.

PUT-WNT.text: Your train passes near where the Surrey Iron Railway began, on the train's {side}, at a dock on the Thames at Wandsworth. From 1803 its horse-drawn wagons carried coal, lime and building materials about nine miles to Croydon, until it closed in 1846.

QBR-SSS.text: Your train passes the site of Queenborough Castle, on the train's {side}, built for Edward III from 1361 and named, like the town, after his wife Queen Philippa. It was the first concentric castle built in England; it was pulled down soon after 1650, and only low earthworks remain in what is now a park.

QBR-SWL.text: Your train crosses the Swale, between the Isle of Sheppey and the mainland, on the Kingsferry Bridge, which carries road and railway together. Its middle span lifts straight up to let ships through; it replaced a bascule bridge of 1860, whose span tipped up instead.

QRP-SBM.text: Your train passes near The Den, on the train's {side}, home of Millwall Football Club since 1993, when it replaced the Old Den a quarter of a mile away. It is the sixth ground the club has had since it was formed on the Isle of Dogs in 1885.

QRP-SQE.text: Your train passes near the site of New Cross Stadium, on the train's {side}, opened on June 1st 1933 for greyhound racing and later used for speedway. Its tight, banked speedway track was known as "The Frying Pan". The stadium closed in 1969 and was demolished in 1975.

QUI-SCR.text: St Columb Road station, at one end of this stretch, was first called Halloon; it took its present name in 1878. It is a request stop.

RAM-THP.text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church, on the train's {side}, founded in 1062 and the oldest church in Ramsgate. After lightning struck it in 1439 it was rebuilt, and its tower raised to the height it is today.

RAY-WIM.text: Your train passes near the New Wimbledon Theatre, on the train's {side}, an Edwardian theatre that opened on Boxing Day 1910 with the pantomime Jack and Jill. Lionel Bart's Oliver! had its world premiere here in 1960, and it seems to have been the only British theatre with a Turkish bath in the basement.

RDB-ROM.text: Your train passes near Broadlands, on the train's {side}, the country house that was home to Lord Palmerston, the 19th-century prime minister. In 1767 Capability Brown began remaking the house and its garden.

RDB-TTN.text: Your train passes near the old bridge of 1793 at Redbridge, on the train's {side}, at the mouth of the River Test, where merchant ships and Royal Navy ships were built in the 1700s and 1800s.

RDD-SNR.text: Your train passes near Riddlesdown, on the train's {side}, a place recorded as Ridelesdowne in 1331; the "Riddle" part is thought to come from Middle English for "cleared woodland". Most of its houses were built in the 1930s by John Laing, some with an Art Deco touch, and Fred Perry opened its tennis club in June 1938.

RDD-UWL.text: Your train runs beside Riddlesdown Common, on the train's {side}, 43 hectares near the northern end of the North Downs, owned by the City of London Corporation, most of it a Site of Special Scientific Interest. Neolithic stone axes have been found there, and a trig point on top shows it is 525 feet above sea level.

RDG-RDW.text: Your train passes near Greyfriars Church, on the train's {side}, the oldest Franciscan church in the UK still used for worship.

RDG-TLH.text: Your train passes near Chazey Court Barn, on the train's {side} across the Thames: a huge seven-bay brick barn from about 1700, listed Grade I.

RDG-TWY.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Reading Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded by Henry I in 1121. He was buried there in 1136.

RDH-REI.text: Your train passes near the site of Reigate Castle, on the train's {side}, now a public park. None of the castle buildings survive, but a cave below it, Baron's Cave, is sometimes open for tours.

RDW-RGP.text: Your train passes near the site of Elm Park, on the train's {side}, home of Reading Football Club from 1896 to 1998.

RDW-THE.text: Your train passes near Garston Lock, on the train's {side}, one of only two working turf-sided locks left on the Kennet and Avon Canal. Its sloping grass sides use more water than brick ones.

RDW-TLH.text: Your train passes near the place where the Reading Festival bridge crosses the Thames, on the train's {side}: a temporary footbridge first built in 2008 and put up each year for festival-goers only.

REC-SKW.text: Your train passes near Gibson Gardens, on the train's {side}, tenement flats built in 1880 by the Metropolitan Association for Improving the Dwellings of the Industrious Classes. They were some of the first good-quality homes in London for working and lower-middle-class families.

RED-TRU.text: Your train passes near Wheal Busy, on the train's {side}, a mine that produced huge amounts of copper in the 18th century, now part of the Cornish mining World Heritage Site.

RMD-SMG.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Richmond Railway Bridge, one of the first railway bridges over the river, opened in 1848 to Joseph Locke's design. Doubts about its cast iron led to a rebuilding in steel from 1906 to 1908, keeping much of the original look.

ROC-SCR.text: Your train crosses Goss Moor, a national nature reserve and the largest continuous mire in south-west Britain. The A30 once ran through the middle of it.

ROE-WPE.text: Your train runs through the Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel known to have been built successfully under a navigable river. Marc Brunel and his son Isambard built it between 1825 and 1843 for horse-drawn carriages, but it was mostly used by people on foot until it became a railway tunnel in 1869.

ROE-ZCW.text: Your train passes near the Brunel Museum, on the train's {side}, in the engine house Marc Brunel designed for the Thames Tunnel. The tunnel's shaft beside it was the world's first caisson: a brick tower 50 feet across, built above ground and then sunk under its own weight.

RTR-SOO.text: Your train crosses the River Medway on the railway bridge, one of the four bridges that together make up Rochester Bridge. The Romans built the first bridge here to carry Watling Street, and for centuries it was the lowest fixed crossing of the river.

RTR-SOR.text: Your train passes Rochester Castle, on the train's {side}, on the bank of the Medway. Its 12th-century keep, built by William de Corbeil, Archbishop of Canterbury, is one of the best preserved of its time in England or France.

RVB-SRT.text: Your train passes near Bromley Reform Synagogue, on the train's {side}, whose congregation was founded in 1964 and moved here in 1967. Its sanctuary was refurbished in light wood and glass to reflect the community's Hebrew name, Beit Or, House of Light.

RYD-RYP.text: Your train runs along Ryde Pier, the world's oldest seaside pleasure pier, opened in 1814. Before it was built, passengers were carried ashore on a porter's back and might have to walk up to half a mile across wet sand.

RYD-RYR.text: Your train passes near the Royal Victoria Arcade in Ryde, on the train's {side}, built in 1835 and 1836 and one of the first purpose-built shopping centres. It was named after Princess Victoria, later Queen Victoria, who had stayed at nearby Norris Castle.

RYE-WSE.text: Your train passes near Ypres Tower in Rye, on the train's {side}, built in the 13th or 14th century to defend the town and once called Baddings Tower. It was later a prison, and is now part of Rye Castle Museum.

RYR-SAB.text: Smallbrook Junction station, at one end of this stretch, can't be reached except by train: it exists only for changing trains between Island Line and the Isle of Wight Steam Railway. It opened in 1991.

SAL-TIS.text: Your train passes near Place Farm at Tisbury, on the train's {side}, once a grange of Shaftesbury Abbey. Its medieval barn is said to be the largest in England.

SAL-WMN.text: Your train passes near Wilton House, on the train's {side}, home of the Earls of Pembroke for more than 400 years. It stands on the site of Wilton Abbey, which Henry VIII gave to William Herbert after the Dissolution.

SAR-SVB.text: Your train passes near the Lawrence Weston wind turbine, on the train's {side}, owned by the community it helps to fund. When it started turning in May 2023 it was the tallest onshore wind turbine in England, 150 metres to the tip of its blades.

SAU-TRU.text: Your train passes near Truro Cathedral, on the train's {side}, built between 1880 and 1910 on the site of St Mary's parish church.

SAY-SMY.text: Your train passes near the Warren, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve at St Mary Cray managed by the London Wildlife Trust. It is mainly ancient oak and silver birch woodland, with bluebells and foxgloves, and a pond with plants rare in London such as blue fleabane and hare's-foot clover.

SBF-SBV.text: Your train uses a link between the two railways at St Budeaux, put in on March 21st 1941 so that trains could get round bomb damage. Since 1964, when the old line into Devonport closed, all trains from Victoria Road have used it.

SBF-STS.text: Your train crosses the Tamar from Devon into Cornwall on Brunel's Royal Albert Bridge, its two 455-foot iron spans 100 feet above the water.
SBF-STS.textReverse: Your train crosses the Tamar from Cornwall into Devon on Brunel's Royal Albert Bridge, its two 455-foot iron spans 100 feet above the water.

SBP-WMB.text: Your train passes near Wembley Central Mosque, on the train's {side}, built in 1904 as St Andrew's Presbyterian Church, in a style influenced by the Arts and Crafts movement. With the Muslim Welfare Association next door, it can hold up to 2,200 people.

SBU-TUR.text: Your train passes near St James' Church, Enfield Highway, on the train's {side}, consecrated on October 15th 1831. Built by subscription as a chapel of ease, it was the first Anglican church in the parish of Enfield besides the parish church itself.

SBV-STS.text: Your train passes the Tamar Bridge, on the train's {side}, which carries the A38 beside the Royal Albert Bridge. When it opened in 1961 it was the longest suspension bridge in Britain.

SCY-SNR.text: Your train passes near Elmhurst School, on the train's {side}, a preparatory school that grew from two schools founded in 1869. One of them, run by the sisters Clarissa and Florence Prince, counted the young P. G. Wodehouse among its pupils in the 1880s, and moved into the house called Elmhurst in 1894.

SDC-ZLW.text: Your train passes near the site of The Theatre, on the train's {side}, built by James Burbage in 1576 as the first permanent theatre in England made only for plays. Shakespeare's company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, played there; after a dispute with the landlord its timbers went to build the Globe on Bankside.

SDE-WPE.text: Your train passes near St George in the East, on the train's {side}, one of the six churches Nicholas Hawksmoor designed in London, built from 1714 to 1729. Its walls and distinctive "pepper-pot" towers hold a modern church interior built inside them in 1964.

SDE-ZLW.text: Your train passes near Trinity Green Almshouses, on the train's {side}, built by Trinity House in 1695 for retired sailors and their widows. Saved from demolition in the 1890s by a public campaign, they were the first buildings on the register that grew into today's listed buildings.

SDG-WHA.text: Your train passes near Folkestone Racecourse at Westenhanger, on the train's {side}, where racing began in 1898. It closed in 2012, and its grandstand can be seen from the station.

SDH-SUD.text: Your train passes near Sudbury Town Underground station, on the train's {side}, rebuilt by Charles Holden in brick, concrete and glass in the early 1930s. It first opened in 1903, on the first of the Underground's surface lines to run electric trains instead of steam.

SDN-SOU.text: Your train passes near the Bargate, on the train's {side}, the main gateway through Southampton's medieval town walls, built in about 1180. It was used as a prison from at least 1439.

SDN-SWG.text: Your train passes near South Stoneham House, on the train's {side}, an early 18th-century manor house thought to be by Nicholas Hawksmoor. What is now the University of Southampton bought it in 1921 for students and added a 17-storey tower in 1964; it has stood empty since 2005.

SDW-THP.text: Your train passes near White Mill, on the train's {side}, a smock mill west of Sandwich built in 1760. It last worked by wind in 1926 and by an oil engine until 1957, and is now a rural heritage centre, with the miller's cottage furnished as it was between 1900 and 1939.

SFA-SRA.text: Your train passes near the site of Stratford Works, on the train's {side}, where the Great Eastern Railway built 1,702 locomotives. In 1891 the works built a complete tender engine in nine hours and 47 minutes, a record that still stands; the last of the works closed in 1991.

SGM-STS.text: Your train passes near Trematon Castle, on the train's {side}, a Norman motte-and-bailey castle with a 12th-century keep, overlooking the River Lynher.

SHE-TMC.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Sherborne Old Castle, on the train's {side}, built in the 1100s as the palace of Roger, Bishop of Salisbury. Walter Raleigh leased it in 1592, and Parliament's army took it after a siege in 1645.

SHE-YVJ.text: Your train passes near Sherborne Abbey, on the train's {side}, a Saxon cathedral from 705 to 1075, then a Benedictine abbey church, and a parish church since 1539.

SHH-SML.text: Your train passes near Kings Weston House, on the train's {side}, built between 1712 and 1719 to designs by Sir John Vanbrugh for the lawyer and politician Edward Southwell.

SHI-WGV.text: Your train passes near St Mary's churchyard in Wargrave, on the train's {side}, where the Hannen family's columbarium, a resting place for ashes, was designed by Edwin Lutyens.

SHO-WLS.text: Your train passes near Jesus Chapel on Peartree Green, on the train's {side}, consecrated in 1620. Its service is said to have set the pattern for later Church of England consecrations.

SHP-UPH.text: Shepperton station, at one end of this stretch, is the terminus of a branch that opened in 1864. It was first meant to carry on to the River Thames by Chertsey Bridge, but that plan was dropped in 1862.

SHU-STD.text: Your train passes near Stanley Mills, on the train's {side}, a woollen mill built in 1813 to be fireproof, with cast-iron columns holding up brick vaults. Five waterwheels on the River Frome once drove it, and its main building is listed Grade I.

SHW-WIN.text: Your train passes near the Great Hall of Winchester Castle, on the train's {side}, all that stands of the castle William the Conqueror founded in 1067 besides its Westgate. On its wall hangs the Round Table, made in the 13th century and repainted for Henry VIII, whose young face is King Arthur's.

SIH-SUC.text: Your train passes near the Pyl Brook, on the train's {side}, a small stream that rises in Sutton Common and flows through Merton to join the Beverley Brook in New Malden. Its name probably comes from the Old English pyll, a pool or small stream.

SIT-TEY.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Murston, on the train's {side}, designed by William Burges and built in 1873 and 1874. Fumes from the brickworks and gasworks round the old church made it hard to breathe during services, so the rector paid £500 of his own money towards a new one away from them.

SKM-WND.text: Your train passes near the village of Stoke Mandeville, on the train's {side}, whose name comes from the Norman de Mandeville family, first recorded here in 1284. Its old church stood alone a kilometre from the village; excavations for HS2 on its site found two Roman statues.

SKW-SMH.text: Your train passes near Abney Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, one of London's “Magnificent Seven” cemeteries, opened in 1840 as a non-denominational garden cemetery and arboretum. Nearly 197,000 burials had taken place there by 2000; it is now a local nature reserve.

SLO-WNC.text: Your train passes near Windsor Castle, on the train's {side}, used by the monarch since the time of Henry I, who reigned from 1100 to 1135: the longest-occupied palace in Europe.

SLQ-WLD.text: Your train passes near Marine Court on the seafront at St Leonards, on the train's {side}, a block of flats built from 1936 to 1938 to look like the liner Queen Mary. Its curved eastern end steps back as it rises, like the forecastle of a ship.

SLV-WHL.text: Your train passes near Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, on the train's {side}, opened on April 3rd 2019 on the site of the club's old ground, White Hart Lane, and land beside it. With 62,850 seats it is the largest club ground in London, and its pitch slides away to reveal an artificial one for American football.

SMG-TWI.text: Your train passes near Sandycombe Lodge, on the train's {side}, the country retreat J. M. W. Turner designed and built in 1813 and lived in from 1814 to 1826. It is the only surviving building he designed.

SMH-SVS.text: Your train passes near St Ignatius Church, on the train's {side}, a large Roman Catholic church run by the Jesuits. Cardinal Herbert Vaughan invited them to found the parish, which they did in 1894, after nearly 300 local people had asked for one.

SMO-WBO.text: Your train passes near Rutlish School, on the train's {side}, named after William Rutlish, embroiderer to Charles II, who left £400 when he died in 1687 to educate poor children of the parish. John Major, Prime Minister from 1990 to 1997, was a pupil at the school.

SNL-WCP.text: Stoneleigh station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1932. It is in London fare zone 5, and is the only National Rail station in that zone that isn't in a London borough.

SNS-WRY.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Staines, on the train's {side}, standing on a rise above the Thames at the west end of the town. A plaque on its tower, built in 1631, says it was designed by Inigo Jones.

SNY-WRY.text: Your train passes near the site of a palace of the Saxon kings at Old Windsor, on the train's {side}. Edward the Confessor held a royal manor here, and the palace was later replaced by the Norman castle at what became Windsor; Old Windsor was the first place to bear the name.

SOA-SWG.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at South Stoneham, on the train's {side}, one of the two medieval churches left in Southampton. Parts of it are Norman, and its chancel arch dates from the 1100s.

SOG-WAD.text: Your train passes near Wadhurst Castle, on the train's {side}, a castle-style mansion first built between 1818 and 1820 and remodelled for Benjamin Harding, who bought it in 1838. It is now a wedding venue.

SPB-WIJ.text: Your train passes near the site of White City Stadium, on the train's {side}, built in 10 months for the 1908 Olympics and demolished in 1985. The Olympic marathon finished there, and the race's distance was fixed at those Games, measured from a start at Windsor Castle.

SPH-SWO.text: Your train passes the East Kent Railway's station at Shepherdswell, on the train's {side}. It opened in 1916 as the end of the East Kent Light Railway, closed to passengers in 1948, and reopened as a heritage line in 1993.

SQE-ZCW.text: Your train passes near the lake of Canada Water, on the train's {side}, the surviving northern third of Canada Dock, which was mainly used by ships from Canada. After the docks closed in the 1970s, about half of the dock was filled in for the Surrey Quays Shopping Centre, and the rest became a lake and wildlife refuge.

SRA-ZLW.text: Your train passes near St Dunstan's, Stepney, on the train's {side}, believed to have been founded or refounded by St Dunstan in about 952. It is known as the Mother Church of the East End, and as the Church of the High Seas.

SRC-STE.text: Your train passes near St Leonard's Church, Streatham, on the train's {side}, the parish church of a parish named in the Domesday Book. The lower part of its tower dates from the 14th century; almost all the rest was rebuilt in 1830 and 1831, and the church was restored after a fire gutted it on May 5th 1975.

SRS-TTH.text: Your train passes near the BRIT School, on the train's {side}, a school for the performing and creative arts, free to attend, that opened in 1991. Adele and Amy Winehouse are among its former pupils.

SRS-WCY.text: Your train passes the site of the Nest, on the train's {side}, home ground of Croydon Common from 1908 to 1917 and of Crystal Palace from 1918 to 1924. A train depot now stands on the site, and the ground's front wall still stands along Selhurst Road.

SRU-WRU.text: Your train passes the site of RAF West Ruislip, on the train's {side}, a depot chosen in 1917 for the Royal Flying Corps and split in two by this line. The US Air Force took it over in 1955 and the US Navy in 1975; after the Navy left in 2006 it was cleared for housing.

SSE-SWK.text: Your train passes near Shoreham Fort, on the train's {side}, built at the mouth of the River Adur and finished in June 1857, at a time of political alarm. Its gun platform is shaped like a straight-sided crescent, ringed by a ditch with a loopholed wall along the middle.

STE-TOO.text: Your train passes near St Barnabas' Church, Mitcham, on the train's {side}, designed by H. P. Burke Downing and finished on November 14th 1914. It replaced a simple one-room “tin church” used by the mission set up there in 1906.

STE-TUH.text: Your train passes near Streatham Ice and Leisure Centre, on the train's {side}, London's only Olympic-sized ice rink and home of the Streatham ice hockey teams. It replaced Streatham Ice Arena, opened on the site on February 26th 1931.

STW-TWI.text: Your train passes near Strawberry Hill House, on the train's {side}, the Gothic villa Horace Walpole built up in stages from 1749 to suit his collection of antiquities. Its style, Strawberry Hill Gothic, foreshadowed the Victorian Gothic Revival.

SUC-WSU.text: Your train passes Gander Green Lane, on the train's {side}, the home ground of Sutton United. On January 7th 1989 Sutton beat Coventry City, then in the top division, by two goals to one here, one of the biggest upsets in FA Cup history.

SUD-WCX.text: Your train passes near Wembley Stadium, on the train's {side}, England's national football stadium, opened in 2007 where the old Wembley stood from 1923 to 2000. With 90,000 seats it is the largest stadium in the UK, and its arch carries more than three quarters of the roof's weight.

SUO-WSU.text: Your train passes The Messenger, on the train's {side}, a life-size bronze by David Wynne of a horse and a young rider, put up beside Sutton station in 1981. The rider raises one hand as if calling out, and the horse looks towards the station.

SUR-THD.text: Your train passes near Giggs Hill Green in Thames Ditton, on the train's {side}, a triangular green where the village has played cricket since 1833. Despite its name, there is no hill.

SUU-UPH.text: Upper Halliford station, at one end of this stretch, opened as a halt in 1944 for a wartime factory of the British Thermostat Company that made munitions. Its second platform followed in 1946.

SYH-WDU.text: Your train passes near Dulwich College, on the train's {side}, founded on June 21st 1619 by the Elizabethan actor Edward Alleyn as the College of God's Gift, to educate 12 poor scholars. It grew into a large school from 1857, and moved into its present buildings in 1870.

TAD-TAT.text: Your train passes near Tattenham Corner, on the train's {side}, the sharp bend at the top of Epsom Racecourse and the last before the home straight of the Derby. Queen Elizabeth II used to arrive at the station by Royal Train on race days.

TAU-TVP.text: Your train passes near Tonedale Mills in Wellington, on the train's {side}, the largest textile mill in South West England, famous for Taunton serge and later the khaki cloth and puttees of the British Army.

TCR-ZFD.text: Your train passes near Sir John Soane's Museum, on the train's {side}, the architect's own house, full of his drawings, models, paintings and antiquities. An Act of Parliament of 1833 left it to the nation, to be kept as nearly as possible as he left it, partly so that he could disinherit a son he disliked.

THO-YET.text: Your train passes near Upbury Farm in Yetminster, on the train's {side}, where a blue plaque remembers the farmer Benjamin Jesty, born in the village. In 1774, some 20 years before Edward Jenner's vaccine, he used cowpox to give immunity against smallpox.

THO-YVP.text: Your train passes near Newton Surmaville, on the train's {side}, a house built between 1608 and 1612 for the clothier Robert Harbin and listed Grade I.

TQY-TRR.text: Your train passes near Torre Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1196 for Premonstratensian canons and now the best-preserved medieval monastery in Devon and Cornwall.

TRO-WSB.text: Your train passes near the Handle House at Studley Mills in Trowbridge, on the train's {side}, which straddles the River Biss. It was used to dry and store teasels, which were used to raise the nap of cloth.

TUH-WNW.text: Your train passes near St Luke's Church, West Norwood, on the train's {side}, one of four "Waterloo churches" named after the four Gospel writers. Designed by Francis Octavius Bedford as a result of the Church Building Act of 1818, it was consecrated on July 25th 1825, on a triangular site where Norwood Road forks.

TWI-WTN.text: Your train passes near All Hallows church, on the train's {side}, which has the tower of Wren's All Hallows Lombard Street. When that City church was demolished in 1937, its tower, bells, cloister and many fittings were moved here, and a new church was built around them.

TWY-WGV.text: Your train passes near Loddon Nature Reserve, on the train's {side}, 14 hectares run by the Berks, Bucks and Oxon Wildlife Trust.

UPW-WEY.text: Your train passes near the King's Statue in Weymouth, on the train's {side}, put up in 1809 for George III's Golden Jubilee. The king came to Weymouth on holiday 14 times, the first in 1789.

UWL-WOH.text: Woldingham station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1885 as Marden Park, named after the nearby manor, a year after the line itself. It was renamed Woldingham in 1894.
